q.pt: Assess risks associated with venture
q.s: After twelve years as a hospital pharmacist, Leon resigned to open a specialty tea shop. If the shop fails, he may not be able to return to a comparable position. Which type of risk is Leon taking?
q.r: Career risk. Career risk is the chance that an entrepreneur who gives up a secure job, with its steady salary, benefits and advancement, cannot return to a similar position if the venture fails. Leon left an established profession to start his shop, so his career is on the line. Market risk involves whether customers will buy. Emotional risk involves stress and strain on family relationships. Industry risk involves changes that affect every business in an industry.
w: Market risk is the chance customers will not buy the tea, but the question focuses on Leon losing his pharmacist career, not on customer demand.
Emotional risk is stress and strain on family relationships; nothing here describes that, only the chance Leon cannot get his pharmacist job back.
Industry risk comes from changes that hit every business in an industry, while Leon's risk is personal: giving up a secure profession he may not regain.

q.pt: Assess risks associated with venture
q.s: Which of the following is an example of an emotional risk an entrepreneur might face:
o: Rising prices that increase the cost of supplies
Strain on family relationships caused by long work hours
A competitor opening a similar store nearby
Loss of seniority from leaving a former employer
q.r: Strain on family relationships caused by long work hours. Emotional risk is the personal stress, loneliness and pressure on family and marital relationships that running a venture can create. New owners often work very long hours, which can damage relationships at home. Rising supply prices are a financial risk. A new competitor is a market risk. Losing seniority by leaving an employer is a career risk.
w: Rising supply prices threaten the money invested in the business, which makes them a financial risk, not a personal or emotional strain.
A competitor opening nearby could cut into sales, which is a market risk to the business rather than personal stress on the owner's relationships.
Losing seniority from leaving an employer is a career risk, because it affects job security, not the owner's emotional well-being or family life.

q.pt: Assess risks associated with venture
q.s: Sami used his savings to start a food truck. Over the next year, inflation raised his ingredient and fuel costs faster than he could raise prices, shrinking his profits. Sami is experiencing __________ risk.
q.r: Financial. Financial risk is the possibility of losing the money an entrepreneur has invested in a venture. Inflation, debt, unexpected expenses and weak sales all threaten that money; here, rising costs are eating into Sami's profits and savings. Emotional risk involves stress and strain on relationships. Career risk involves giving up a secure job. Reputational risk involves damage to the owner's or brand's good name.
w: Emotional risk involves stress and strain on relationships, but Sami's problem is inflation eating into his profits and the savings he invested.
Career risk means giving up a secure job you may not get back; the question is about rising costs shrinking Sami's profits, not his job prospects.
Reputational risk is damage to a business's good name, and nothing suggests customers think less of Sami's food truck; his costs simply rose.

q.pt: Assess risks associated with venture
q.s: Priya invested heavily in a line of novelty phone cases just as customer interest in them began to fade, leaving her with boxes of unsold inventory. Which type of risk hurt Priya's venture?
q.r: Market risk. Market risk is the possibility that customers will not buy a venture's products or that demand will shift away from them. Priya's product lost popularity, so the demand she planned on did not appear. Career risk involves leaving a secure job. Emotional risk involves stress and strain on family relationships. Reputational risk involves damage to a business's good name, which did not happen here.
w: Career risk is about leaving a secure job, but Priya's problem is that customers stopped wanting her phone cases and left her with unsold stock.
Emotional risk involves stress on family relationships; Priya's loss came from fading customer demand for her product, not from personal strain.
Reputational risk means harm to a business's good name, yet nothing damaged Priya's reputation; customers simply lost interest in novelty phone cases.

q.pt: Assess risks associated with venture
q.s: Why should an entrepreneur assess a venture's risks before launching it?
o: To guarantee that the venture earns a profit in its first year
To remove all uncertainty from future business decisions
To decide whether the potential rewards justify the possible losses
To avoid having to write a business plan
q.r: To decide whether the potential rewards justify the possible losses. Assessing risk means identifying what could go wrong, estimating how likely and how harmful each risk is, and planning how to handle it. That information lets the entrepreneur decide whether the opportunity is worth pursuing. No assessment can guarantee a profit or remove all uncertainty, and assessing risk is part of planning, not a replacement for a business plan.
w: No assessment can promise a first-year profit; studying risks only helps the entrepreneur judge whether the possible rewards are worth the possible losses.
Risk assessment helps manage uncertainty, but every venture still faces unknowns, so it cannot remove all uncertainty from future decisions.
Assessing risks is actually part of business planning, so it supports writing a business plan rather than letting the entrepreneur skip one.

q.pt: Evaluate risk-taking opportunities
q.s: Before signing a lease for a second location, Grace studied foot traffic, estimated the added sales and costs, and set a limit on how much money she could afford to lose. Grace is taking a(n) __________ risk.
q.r: Calculated. A calculated risk is one taken only after carefully weighing the likely gains against the possible losses. Grace gathered information, estimated results and decided in advance how much loss she could tolerate. A reckless risk is taken without that analysis. Emotional risk involves stress on personal relationships, and career risk involves giving up a secure job, neither of which describes Grace's decision.
w: A reckless risk is taken without careful study, but Grace researched foot traffic, estimated sales and costs, and set a loss limit first.
Emotional risk is stress on personal relationships, while Grace's situation is about carefully weighing the money she could gain or lose on a lease.
Career risk means giving up a secure job, but Grace is already a business owner expanding to a second location, not leaving employment.

q.pt: Explain considerations in making the decision to hire staff
q.s: Bianca has decided that her landscaping company needs a worker who can install and repair irrigation systems. What should she decide next as she considers adding staff?
o: Whether the job should be full-time or part-time
Which questions to ask the finalists in their interviews
Whether to offer the new hire a signing bonus
How to word the new hire's first performance review
q.r: Whether the job should be full-time or part-time. After identifying the skills the business needs, an owner should determine how much work there is, because the workload decides whether the job is full-time or part-time. That answer shapes the cost and the job description. Interview questions, signing bonuses and performance reviews all come later, after the position has been defined and candidates have been recruited.
w: Interview questions come later, after the job is defined and candidates are recruited; Bianca has only just identified the skills she needs.
A signing bonus is a detail of the job offer, which Bianca cannot settle until she knows how much work the job involves and what it will cost.
A performance review happens after someone has been hired and working for a while, so it is far beyond Bianca's current step of defining the job.

q.pt: Explain considerations in making the decision to hire staff
q.s: When a small-business owner considers hiring staff, which cost is usually the largest one to evaluate?
q.r: Payroll. Payroll is the total of the wages and salaries a business pays its employees, and it continues every pay period for as long as the employee works there. Because it is ongoing and usually large, owners must be sure sales can support it before hiring. Office supplies, job advertising and background checks are real costs, but they are small or one-time compared with payroll.
w: Office supplies are a real cost of adding staff, but they are small next to the wages a business must pay every pay period.
Job advertising is usually a one-time cost to find candidates, which is minor compared with the ongoing wages paid once the person is hired.
Background checks are a small, one-time screening cost, while payroll continues every pay period for as long as the employee works there.

q.pt: Explain considerations in making the decision to hire staff
q.s: Which pair of factors should a small-business owner weigh most heavily when deciding whether to hire a new employee?
o: The size of competitors' staffs and the local unemployment rate
The number of applicants and the time of year
The skills the business needs and its ability to pay
The owner's free time and the amount of office space
q.r: The skills the business needs and its ability to pay. A hiring decision starts with what work must be done and what skills it requires, and then asks whether the business can pay for the position. If either answer is no, hiring is premature. Competitors' staffing, unemployment rates, applicant numbers, the season, free time and office space may matter somewhat but do not drive the decision.
w: Competitors' staff sizes and unemployment rates say little about whether this business has work that needs doing or money to pay a new worker.
Lots of applicants or a certain season might affect timing, but neither tells the owner whether the needed skills exist or the business can afford the job.
Free time and office space may matter a little, but a hiring decision depends first on what work must be done and whether the business can pay for it.

q.pt: Explain considerations in making the decision to hire staff
q.s: Which of the following is a cost an employer pays in addition to an employee's wages:
o: Matching Social Security and Medicare taxes
The employee's personal income tax refund
The employee's monthly student loan payments
q.r: Matching Social Security and Medicare taxes. Employers must pay payroll taxes, including a matching share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, on top of the wages they pay, along with costs such as workers' compensation insurance. These added costs belong in the hiring decision. An employee's tax refund, commuting expenses and student loan payments are the employee's own personal matters, not employer costs.
w: An employee's income tax refund comes from the government and belongs to the employee, so it is not something the employer pays on top of wages.
Commuting to work is the employee's own personal expense, not an added cost the employer must pay for having that person on staff.
Student loan payments are the employee's personal debt, so they are not part of what a business pays when it adds an employee.

q.pt: Explain considerations in making the decision to hire staff
q.s: Lucia's online gift shop is extremely busy during the November and December holiday rush but slow the rest of the year. Which staffing decision best fits her needs?
o: Hire seasonal workers for the holiday rush
Hire two full-time employees for the entire year
Turn away holiday orders to avoid adding staff
Sign a three-year contract with a staffing agency
q.r: Hire seasonal workers for the holiday rush. When extra work is temporary, part-time or seasonal staff match labor costs to the workload, so Lucia pays only when the help is needed. Full-time, year-round employees would add payroll during slow months. Turning away orders gives up profitable sales, and a three-year staffing contract locks her into costs that do not fit a short seasonal need.
w: Two full-time workers all year would add payroll during the slow months, even though Lucia only needs extra help in November and December.
Turning away holiday orders gives up her busiest, most profitable sales just to avoid hiring, when temporary help would let her fill them.
A three-year staffing contract locks Lucia into long-term costs, which does not fit a need that lasts only about two months each year.

q.pt: Explain factors to consider in determining a venture's human-resources needs
q.s: Martin has turned down three catering jobs this month because his small team could not handle any more events. What does this situation most likely signal?
o: The business should lower its prices
The business has too many employees
The business needs to add staff
q.r: The business needs to add staff. Turning down profitable work because of a lack of capacity is a clear sign that a venture's human-resources needs have grown. Martin is losing sales that additional workers could help him capture. Lowering prices would bring in even more work he cannot handle. Having too many employees would show up as idle time, not lost jobs, and stopping advertising would not solve his capacity problem.
w: Lowering prices would attract even more catering requests, and Martin already cannot handle the jobs he is being offered.
Too many employees would show up as workers sitting idle, but Martin's team is so busy that he is turning work away.
Advertising is not the problem; Martin already has more demand than his team can handle, so cutting ads would not add capacity.

q.pt: Explain the impact of resource productivity on venture success
q.s: The 5 employees at Seaside Surfboards produced 150 surfboards last month. What was the shop's labor productivity per employee for the month?
q.r: 30 surfboards. Labor productivity is found by dividing output by the number of workers: 150 surfboards ÷ 5 employees = 30 surfboards per employee. Tracking this figure shows an owner how well labor is being used. The answer 750 comes from multiplying instead of dividing, and 25 and 35 do not match the data given.
w: Twenty-five boards per worker would total only 125 boards for 5 employees, so this figure does not match the 150 boards the shop made.
Thirty-five boards per worker would total 175 boards for 5 employees, more than the 150 the shop actually produced.
This figure comes from multiplying 150 by 5 instead of dividing, which gives a total far larger than the shop's entire output.

q.pt: Explain the impact of resource productivity on venture success
q.s: New ventures must use their resources productively because a start-up's resources are often
q.r: Limited. Start-ups usually have small amounts of money, time, equipment and people to work with, so every resource must produce as much output as possible. Wasting scarce resources raises costs and can cause the venture to fail. Start-up resources are not unlimited, they are rarely donated, and the government does not guarantee them.
w: Start-ups rarely have plenty of anything, and if resources were unlimited, using them productively would hardly matter to the venture's survival.
Most start-up resources come from the owner's savings, loans or investors rather than donations, and that money must be used carefully.
The government does not guarantee a start-up's money, equipment or workers, so the owner carries the burden of using scarce resources wisely.

q.pt: Explain the impact of resource productivity on venture success
q.s: By rearranging her kitchen and storing ingredients more carefully, Hana reduced wasted food and the time needed to prepare each meal kit. What is the most likely result for her venture?
o: Higher raw-material costs per meal kit
A need to hire more kitchen employees
Lower quality in each meal kit
Lower cost to produce each meal kit
q.r: Lower cost to produce each meal kit. Using resources productively means getting more output from the same inputs. When Hana cuts waste and time, each meal kit costs less to make, which improves profit and gives the venture a greater chance of success. Less waste lowers, not raises, raw-material costs. Saving time reduces the need for added workers, and nothing in her changes lowers quality.
w: Hana is wasting less food, so she needs fewer ingredients per kit, which lowers raw-material costs rather than raising them.
Saving prep time means her current workers can make more kits, which reduces the need for extra kitchen staff instead of increasing it.
Nothing about rearranging the kitchen or storing food more carefully lowers quality; better storage, if anything, helps keep ingredients fresh.

q.pt: Explain the impact of resource productivity on venture success
q.s: Lakeview Print Shop's 6 workers printed 2,400 shirts in March. In April, 5 workers printed 2,250 shirts. How did labor productivity per worker change from March to April?
o: It decreased by 50 shirts per worker
It decreased by 150 shirts per worker
It stayed the same at 400 shirts per worker
It increased by 50 shirts per worker
q.r: It increased by 50 shirts per worker. Labor productivity is output divided by workers. March: 2,400 ÷ 6 = 400 shirts per worker. April: 2,250 ÷ 5 = 450 shirts per worker. Productivity rose by 450 − 400 = 50 shirts per worker, even though total output fell. The 150-shirt figure is the drop in total output, not output per worker, so productivity did not decrease or stay the same.
w: Productivity changed by 50 shirts, but in the opposite direction: output per worker rose from 400 in March to 450 in April.
The 150-shirt drop is the fall in total output (2,400 to 2,250), not the change in shirts produced per worker.
March productivity was 400 shirts per worker, but April's was 2,250 divided by 5, or 450, so the rate did not stay the same.

q.pt: Assess start-up requirements
q.s: Owen's total start-up costs for his phone-repair kiosk are $16,000. Of that amount, $480 is for business registration and license fees. What percentage of his start-up costs do these fees represent?
q.r: 3%. To find one cost's share of the total, divide the cost by the total and multiply by 100: $480 ÷ $16,000 = 0.03, and 0.03 × 100 = 3%. The answer 0.3% misplaces the decimal, 4.8% simply reuses the digits of the fee, and 33.3% comes from dividing the total by the fee instead of the fee by the total.
w: This misplaces the decimal; $480 divided by $16,000 equals 0.03, which becomes 3% after multiplying by 100, not 0.3%.
This just reuses the digits in $480 instead of dividing the fee by the $16,000 total and converting the result to a percentage.
This comes from dividing $16,000 by $480, which flips the fraction; the fee must be divided by the total cost, not the reverse.

q.pt: Assess start-up requirements
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a start-up cost for a new business:
o: State fees to incorporate the business
Monthly utility bills after the business opens
Weekly wages for employees after opening
Quarterly sales tax payments on sales made
q.r: State fees to incorporate the business. Start-up costs are one-time expenses paid before a business can open, such as incorporation or registration fees, professional fees, equipment and initial inventory. Legally forming the business is one of the earliest of these costs. Utility bills, weekly wages and sales tax payments are ongoing operating expenses that occur after the business is up and running.
w: Utility bills arrive every month once the business is running, so they are ongoing operating expenses, not one-time costs of getting started.
Weekly wages are paid after the business opens and keep recurring, which makes them operating expenses rather than start-up costs.
Sales tax payments come from sales the business has already made, so they can only happen after opening and are not start-up costs.

q.pt: Assess start-up requirements
q.s: Before opening, Dante paid an attorney to register a trademark for his brewery's logo. In his list of start-up costs, this expense is classified as a(n)
q.r: Professional fee. Professional fees are payments to experts, such as attorneys and accountants, for services like forming the business or registering a trademark. Dante paid an attorney for a legal service, so the cost is a professional fee. Inventory expenses buy goods to sell, utility expenses cover services like electricity and water, and payroll expenses are wages paid to the business's own employees.
w: Inventory expenses pay for goods to sell, such as beer supplies, but Dante paid an attorney for a legal service.
Utility expenses cover services like electricity and water, not a payment to an attorney for registering a trademark.
Payroll expenses are wages paid to the business's own employees, while the attorney is an outside expert paid a fee for a service.

q.pt: Assess start-up requirements
q.s: How do start-up costs differ from operating expenses?
o: Start-up costs recur monthly; operating expenses are paid only once
Start-up costs include rent; operating expenses include equipment
Start-up costs are one-time; operating expenses are ongoing
Start-up costs are always larger than a year's operating expenses
q.r: Start-up costs are one-time; operating expenses are ongoing. Start-up costs, such as registration fees, equipment and initial inventory, are needed to get the doors open. Operating expenses, such as rent, utilities and payroll, continue for as long as the business runs. Saying start-up costs recur monthly, or that rent is a start-up cost, reverses the two categories, and start-up costs are not always larger than a year of operating expenses.
w: This reverses the two ideas: start-up costs are paid once to open the business, while operating expenses keep coming back every month.
Rent is a typical ongoing operating expense and equipment is a typical start-up cost, so this pairing has the categories switched.
Start-up costs can be large, but they are not always bigger than a year of operating expenses; the real difference is one-time versus ongoing.

q.pt: Determine feasibility of venture ideas
q.s: Theo has an idea for a drone-based roof inspection service. In what order should he complete these two documents?
q.r: Feasibility study, then business plan. A feasibility study tests whether an idea is practical by examining demand, operations and finances. Only if the idea proves workable is it worth the time to write a detailed business plan. Writing the plan first wastes effort on an idea that may fail. Loan applications depend on a business plan, and an exit strategy is developed while writing the plan, both after feasibility is known.
w: Writing a full business plan first could waste a lot of effort if Theo later learns his drone inspection idea is not practical.
A lender will want to see a business plan, and Theo does not yet know whether his idea can even work, so a loan application is premature.
An exit strategy is planned while writing the business plan, which only makes sense after Theo knows his idea is workable.

q.pt: Determine feasibility of venture ideas
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a question found in the financial part of a feasibility study:
o: How will the start-up be financed?
Who are the venture's most likely customers?
What equipment is needed to make the product?
Which competitors already serve the area?
q.r: How will the start-up be financed? A feasibility study looks at an idea from several angles, and its financial part asks how much money is needed, where it will come from and whether the venture can earn a profit. Questions about likely customers and existing competitors belong to the market part of the study. The question about equipment belongs to the operational part.
w: Identifying the most likely customers belongs to the market part of a feasibility study, not the part that looks at money and funding.
Figuring out what equipment is needed is an operational question about how the product will be made, not a financial one.
Studying which competitors already serve the area belongs to the market part of the study, not the part about financing and profit.

q.pt: Determine feasibility of venture ideas
q.s: In which situation might an entrepreneur reasonably decide that a formal feasibility study is unnecessary?
o: When the entrepreneur plans to apply for a bank loan
When the product is new and untested in the market
When the idea's feasibility is already certain
When the entrepreneur has little experience in the industry
q.r: When the idea's feasibility is already certain. The purpose of a feasibility study is to find out whether an idea can work, so if that answer is already known for certain, the study adds little. Planning to borrow, offering an untested product and lacking industry experience all increase uncertainty, which makes a feasibility study more important, not less.
w: Applying for a bank loan makes a feasibility study more useful, since lenders want evidence that the idea can actually succeed.
A new, untested product carries a lot of uncertainty, which is exactly when a feasibility study is most needed.
An entrepreneur with little industry experience knows less about what could go wrong, so a feasibility study becomes more important, not less.

q.pt: Determine feasibility of venture ideas
q.s: Before investing in a new venture, why would an entrepreneur conduct a feasibility study?
o: To describe how the owner will eventually leave the business
To persuade investors with a polished slide presentation
To determine whether the idea is workable
To set step-by-step procedures for daily operations
q.r: To determine whether the idea is workable. A feasibility study tests whether a venture idea is practical and likely to succeed by examining market demand, operations, costs and financing before the entrepreneur commits time and money. Its findings tell the entrepreneur whether to proceed, adjust or drop the idea. Describing how the owner will leave is an exit strategy, a polished slide presentation is a pitch, and step-by-step daily instructions are operating procedures.
w: Describing how the owner will leave the business is an exit strategy, not a test of whether the venture idea can work.
A polished slide presentation for investors is a pitch, which comes after the entrepreneur already knows the idea is worth pursuing.
Step-by-step instructions for daily work are operating procedures, written once a business is running, not a study of whether an idea is workable.

q.pt: Generate venture ideas
q.s: The first stage in generating venture ideas is __________ thinking, in which an entrepreneur produces many ideas without judging them.
q.r: Creative. Creative thinking is producing many new and original ideas while holding back judgment, and it comes first when generating venture ideas. A large pool of ideas raises the chance of finding a strong one. Critical, convergent and evaluative thinking all narrow and judge ideas, which happens later, when the entrepreneur screens the ideas and selects the most promising one.
w: Critical thinking judges and evaluates ideas, which is the opposite of producing many ideas without judging them.
Convergent thinking narrows many ideas down to the best one, which happens later, after a large pool of ideas has been generated.
Evaluative thinking weighs ideas against criteria, while the question describes the earlier step of producing ideas freely without judgment.

q.pt: Generate venture ideas
q.s: During a team idea session for a new smoothie bar, Jasmine keeps the discussion on track, makes sure every member contributes, and does not push her own opinions. Jasmine is serving as the group's
q.r: Facilitator. A facilitator guides a group session objectively, keeps it focused, manages time and draws ideas out of every participant without steering the outcome. That is exactly Jasmine's role. A mentor is an experienced person who advises a less experienced one. A negotiator bargains to reach an agreement. An investor provides money in exchange for a share of the business.
w: A mentor is an experienced person who advises someone less experienced, but Jasmine is guiding a group discussion without pushing her views.
A negotiator bargains to reach an agreement, while Jasmine keeps the session focused and draws ideas from every team member.
An investor supplies money in exchange for part of the business, which has nothing to do with Jasmine running the idea session.

q.pt: Generate venture ideas
q.s: When entrepreneurs generate product ideas, their main goal is to
o: copy the products of successful competitors.
use as much equipment as possible.
q.r: Solve problems that customers have. Strong venture ideas meet a real want or need, so entrepreneurs focus on problems customers will pay to have solved. An idea that solves no problem will struggle to find buyers. Copying competitors gives customers no reason to switch, using more equipment is not a goal in itself, and no venture idea can avoid all risk.
w: Copying successful competitors gives customers no new reason to buy, so it does not solve a problem the market still has.
Using lots of equipment is not a goal in itself; a product idea succeeds because customers want it, not because of the tools behind it.
Every venture idea carries some risk, so avoiding all risk is impossible and is not what generating product ideas is meant to do.

q.pt: Use components of business plan to define venture idea
q.s: In her business plan, Monique describes her ideal customers as working parents aged 30 to 45 who live within ten miles of her store. In which section of the plan does this information belong?
q.r: Market analysis. The market analysis section describes the industry and the target market, the specific customers the venture intends to attract, including their ages, locations and needs. Monique's customer profile fits there. The executive summary is a brief overview of the whole plan. The operations plan covers production and facilities. The management team section describes the owners' and key employees' experience.
w: The executive summary is a short overview of the whole plan, so it would only briefly mention customers, not hold Monique's detailed customer profile.
The operations plan explains how the business produces and delivers its products, not who its ideal customers are or where they live.
The management team section describes the owners' and key staff's experience, not the ages and locations of target customers.

q.pt: Use components of business plan to define venture idea
q.s: Which part of a business plan gives a brief overview of the entire plan and is usually written last?
q.r: Executive summary. The executive summary highlights the main points of every section in a page or two, so it is usually written after the rest of the plan is finished, even though it appears first. Lenders often read it before anything else. The company description explains the business itself, the financial plan presents costs and projections, and the appendix holds supporting documents.
w: The company description explains what the business is and does, but it does not summarize every section of the plan.
The financial plan presents costs, funding and projections for one part of the business, rather than giving a quick overview of the whole plan.
The appendix holds supporting documents such as resumes or charts at the end of the plan, not a brief summary of its main points.

q.pt: Use components of business plan to define venture idea
q.s: How does writing a business plan help an entrepreneur define a venture idea?
o: It legally protects the venture idea from being copied by others
It forces the entrepreneur to think the idea through in detail
It guarantees that a lender will finance the venture
It removes the need to research the competition
q.r: It forces the entrepreneur to think the idea through in detail. Writing each component of a business plan makes the entrepreneur answer specific questions about customers, competitors, operations, management and money, turning a rough idea into a clear concept. A business plan does not legally protect an idea, it does not guarantee financing, and a good plan requires competitive research rather than replacing it.
w: A business plan is a planning document, not a legal tool; protecting an idea from copying requires things like patents, copyrights or trademarks.
A strong plan can help convince a lender, but no plan guarantees financing, and that is not how it helps define the venture idea.
A good business plan requires researching the competition, so writing one increases that research rather than removing the need for it.

q.pt: Explain the need for entrepreneurial discovery
q.s: The process of matching new product ideas with market opportunities is called
q.r: Entrepreneurial discovery. Entrepreneurial discovery is the process of recognizing opportunities and matching product or service ideas with real market needs, so entrepreneurs pursue what customers want instead of untested ideas. Venture harvesting is collecting the value built in a business. Continuation planning prepares a business to keep operating if the owner leaves or disaster strikes. Capital budgeting is planning spending on long-term assets.
w: Venture harvesting means collecting the value an owner has built in an existing business, not matching new ideas to market opportunities.
Continuation planning prepares a business to keep operating if the owner leaves or a disaster hits, not to discover new product opportunities.
Capital budgeting is planning spending on long-term assets like equipment, which has nothing to do with matching product ideas to markets.

q.pt: Explain the need for entrepreneurial discovery
q.s: Before thinking about any product, Ezra spends a week listing the frustrations his neighbors describe about finding reliable after-school care. Which step of entrepreneurial discovery is Ezra completing?
o: Identifying an unmet want or need
q.r: Identifying an unmet want or need. Entrepreneurial discovery begins with spotting a problem or need that customers have and that current businesses are not meeting well. Ezra is gathering evidence of exactly that kind of need. Evaluating feasibility comes after an idea to meet the need has been formed. Exit strategies and capital resources are planning decisions made much later in developing a venture.
w: Evaluating feasibility comes after an entrepreneur has a specific idea, but Ezra has not thought of any product yet.
An exit strategy plans how an owner will eventually leave a business, which is far beyond Ezra's first step of listing his neighbors' frustrations.
Selecting capital resources like equipment happens once a venture is being planned, not while Ezra is still discovering what people need.

q.pt: Discuss entrepreneurial discovery processes
q.s: After listing 30 possible business ideas, Aiyana rates each one against criteria such as start-up cost, customer demand and her own skills, then drops the weakest ideas. Which discovery activity is Aiyana performing?
q.r: Idea screening. Idea screening is the step in the entrepreneurial discovery process in which an entrepreneur compares ideas against set criteria and eliminates the weak ones so that time and money go to the most promising opportunity. Aiyana is judging and narrowing her list. Brainstorming generates many ideas without judging them, which she has already done. Mind mapping diagrams related ideas around a central topic, and venture harvesting collects the value built in an existing business.
w: Brainstorming produces many ideas without judging them, which Aiyana already did when she listed 30 ideas; now she is rating and cutting them.
Mind mapping draws related ideas around a central topic, while Aiyana is scoring ideas against criteria and dropping the weakest ones.
Venture harvesting collects the value from an existing business, but Aiyana has not started a business yet; she is narrowing her list of ideas.

q.pt: Discuss entrepreneurial discovery processes
q.s: Tariq wants to find an idea for a new business in his community. Which activity would best help him discover opportunities?
o: Copying the menu of the busiest restaurant in town
Observing problems people face in daily life
Waiting until he has enough money to buy a franchise
Rereading business plans he wrote in the past
q.r: Observing problems people face in daily life. Observation is a key entrepreneurial discovery activity because watching how people shop, work and live reveals frustrations and unmet needs that a new venture could solve. Copying a busy restaurant offers nothing new, waiting to buy a franchise skips discovery altogether, and rereading old plans looks inward instead of at the market.
w: Copying the busiest restaurant's menu offers nothing new to the community, so it does not uncover an unmet need Tariq could fill.
Waiting to buy a franchise skips discovery entirely, because a franchise is an existing business concept rather than a new opportunity Tariq finds.
Rereading old business plans looks back at past ideas instead of at the community, where new problems and opportunities can be found.

q.pt: Explain the need for continuation planning
q.s: After a ransomware attack shut down a nearby clinic for weeks, Vega Family Dental wrote a plan for backing up patient records and keeping the office running during emergencies. This document is a
q.r: Business continuity plan. A business continuity plan explains how a business will protect its operations and keep running, or quickly resume, after disruptions such as natural disasters, fires or cyberattacks. Vega's backup and emergency procedures fit that purpose. A feasibility study tests whether a new idea can work, an exit strategy plans how the owner will leave, and a marketing plan sets promotion and sales goals.
w: A feasibility study tests whether a new business idea can work, but Vega Family Dental is an existing practice planning for emergencies.
An exit strategy explains how an owner will leave the business, not how the office will back up records and keep running during a crisis.
A marketing plan sets promotion and sales goals, while this document covers backing up records and operating through emergencies like cyberattacks.

q.pt: Explain the need for continuation planning
q.s: Why should the owner of a family-owned hardware store engage in continuation planning?
o: To plan who will run the store if the owner leaves
To decide which new product lines the store should carry
To calculate the store's original start-up costs
To reduce the store's weekly payroll expenses
q.r: To plan who will run the store if the owner leaves. Continuation planning prepares for who will own and run the business when the current owner retires, becomes ill or dies, protecting employees, customers and the family's investment. Choosing product lines is a merchandising decision, start-up costs were settled when the store opened, and reducing payroll is a cost-control decision.
w: Choosing new product lines is a merchandising decision about what to sell, not about who will run the store when the owner leaves.
Start-up costs were settled when the store first opened, so calculating them now has nothing to do with planning for the store's future leadership.
Cutting weekly payroll is a cost-control decision, while continuation planning is about keeping the family business running after the owner is gone.

q.pt: Assess global trends and opportunities for business ventures
q.s: More households are treating their pets as members of the family and spending more on pet care, toys and services. A pet-products entrepreneur would classify this shift as a(n) __________ trend.
q.r: Societal. A societal trend is a lasting change in people's values, lifestyles and habits. Treating pets as family members is a change in how people live and what they value, and it creates opportunities for pet-related businesses. A technological trend involves new tools or technology, an economic trend involves changes in income, prices or interest rates, and a political trend involves government actions and laws.
w: A technological trend involves new tools or technology, but treating pets as family is a change in people's values and lifestyles.
Economic trends involve changes in income, prices or interest rates, while this shift is about how people feel about and care for their pets.
Political trends come from government actions and laws, and nothing in the question involves new rules about pets.

q.pt: Assess global trends and opportunities for business ventures
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a technological trend that could create a business opportunity:
o: Rising interest rates on small-business loans
Growing use of apps to book and pay for services
New state laws requiring businesses to recycle
More families living in multigenerational households
q.r: Growing use of apps to book and pay for services. A technological trend is a lasting shift in the tools and technology people use, and it can open doors for app-based and online ventures. Rising interest rates are an economic trend. New recycling laws are a political or legal trend. Multigenerational households reflect a societal trend in how people live.
w: Rising interest rates on loans are an economic trend involving the cost of borrowing money, not a shift in the technology people use.
New recycling laws come from government action, making them a political or legal trend rather than a technological one.
More families living in multigenerational homes is a change in how people live, which is a societal trend, not a technological one.

q.pt: Assess the need to use external resources for concept development
q.s: Alana is unsure whether her town has enough demand to support a board-game café. What should she do before moving forward?
o: Consult industry experts and local market data
Sign a five-year lease to secure a good location
Order a complete inventory of games and supplies
Hire staff so the café is ready to open quickly
q.r: Consult industry experts and local market data. When an entrepreneur lacks key information, outside sources such as experts, mentors, trade associations and market data can show whether enough customers exist. Getting that information first protects her from costly mistakes. Signing a lease, buying inventory and hiring staff all commit money before she knows the idea has enough demand.
w: Signing a five-year lease commits a lot of money before Alana knows whether her town has enough customers for a board-game café.
Buying a full inventory of games spends start-up money before Alana has answered her main question about whether demand exists.
Hiring staff adds payroll costs before Alana knows if enough customers will come, so it should wait until demand is confirmed.

q.pt: Assess the need to use external resources for concept development
q.s: What is the main benefit of consulting industry experts while developing a venture concept?
o: They guarantee that the venture will receive financing
They take on the venture's legal responsibilities
They provide useful information the entrepreneur may lack
They eliminate the need for a feasibility study
q.r: They provide useful information the entrepreneur may lack. Industry experts know the market, costs, suppliers and common pitfalls, so their insight helps an entrepreneur fill skill and knowledge gaps and refine the concept. Experts cannot guarantee financing, they do not assume the venture's legal responsibilities, and their advice supports a feasibility study rather than replacing it.
w: Experts can share useful advice, but they cannot promise that a lender or investor will fund the venture.
Industry experts give information and advice; the entrepreneur, not the expert, keeps the venture's legal responsibilities.
Expert advice supports a feasibility study by adding knowledge, but it does not replace the study's careful look at demand, operations and money.

q.pt: Describe considerations in selecting capital resources
q.s: Felix needs ovens, mixers and display cases for his new bakery but has a tight start-up budget. Which approach would best reduce his equipment costs?
o: Buy extra equipment for future growth
q.r: Buy good-quality used equipment. Used equipment in good working condition often costs far less than new equipment while doing the same job, which preserves scarce start-up cash. Felix should still check its condition and any warranty. The newest models cost the most, buying extra equipment ties up money in capacity he does not yet need, and rush delivery adds cost without adding value.
w: The newest models usually cost the most, which works against Felix's goal of keeping equipment costs low on a tight budget.
Buying extra equipment for future growth ties up scarce cash in capacity Felix does not need yet, which raises rather than reduces costs.
Rush delivery adds an extra charge without making the equipment any better, so it increases Felix's costs instead of lowering them.

q.pt: Describe considerations in selecting capital resources
q.s: A pottery studio makes a one-time purchase of a kiln that it will use for many years. This purchase is a(n)
q.r: Capital expenditure. A capital expenditure is money spent on a long-term asset, such as equipment, machinery or a building, that will benefit the business for years. The kiln is a one-time purchase of exactly that kind of asset. Operating expenses are recurring costs like rent and utilities, inventory expenses buy goods for resale, and professional fees pay experts such as attorneys.
w: Operating expenses are recurring costs like rent and utilities, but the kiln is a one-time purchase the studio will use for many years.
Inventory expenses pay for goods the business plans to sell, while the kiln is equipment the studio keeps and uses to make pottery.
A professional fee pays an expert such as an attorney or accountant for a service, not for a long-lasting piece of equipment.

q.pt: Develop exit strategies
q.s: Carmen is drafting the business plan for her yoga studio. Her mentor tells her to also plan how she will eventually leave the business. When is the best time to develop this exit strategy?
o: Once the studio earns its first profit
Now, while she is writing the business plan
When a buyer makes her an offer
When she is ready to retire
q.r: Now, while she is writing the business plan. An exit strategy should be developed early, as part of the business plan, because the way an owner plans to leave affects decisions about ownership, financing and how the business is built. Lenders and investors also want to know it. Waiting for a profit, an offer or retirement leaves too little time to shape the business for a successful exit.
w: Waiting for the first profit means Carmen will have already made key decisions about ownership and financing without her exit plan in mind.
Waiting for a buyer's offer leaves too little time to shape the studio for a strong sale, and Carmen may not even want to sell then.
Retirement may be many years away, and planning the exit only then would leave no time to build the business in a way that supports it.

q.pt: Develop exit strategies
q.s: Rafael plans to sell his landscaping company in about five years. Which action would best prepare the business for a successful sale?
o: Cut all marketing to increase the cash on hand in the short term
Keep customer relationships tied only to himself
Stop maintaining equipment to reduce expenses
Build steady profits and systems that run without him
q.r: Build steady profits and systems that run without him. Buyers pay for a business that will keep earning after the owner leaves, so steady profits, loyal customers and documented systems raise the sale price. Cutting marketing and skipping equipment maintenance weaken the business over time. Customer relationships tied only to Rafael may leave with him, which makes the company less valuable to a buyer.
w: Cutting all marketing may raise cash briefly, but it weakens future sales, making the company less appealing to a buyer in five years.
If customers are loyal only to Rafael, they may leave when he does, so a buyer would see the company as worth less.
Skipping equipment maintenance saves money now but leaves worn-out equipment that lowers the company's value and the price a buyer will pay.

q.pt: Select strategies to protect intellectual property
q.s: Nadia wrote an original novel about life on a fishing boat and wants to prevent others from reproducing it without her permission. Which form of protection should she use?
q.r: Copyright. A copyright protects original works of authorship, such as books, music, artwork and software, from being copied or sold without the creator's permission. Nadia's novel is an original written work. A patent protects inventions, a trademark protects brand names, logos and symbols, and a trade secret protects confidential business information, such as a formula, by keeping it private.
w: A patent protects inventions such as new machines or processes, not a written work like Nadia's novel.
A trademark protects brand names, logos and symbols that identify a business, not the text of an original novel.
A trade secret protects private business information by keeping it hidden, but Nadia wants to publish her novel while stopping others from copying it.

q.pt: Evaluate options for continued venture involvement
q.s: After taking her software company public, founder Elise wants to keep a voice in major company decisions without managing daily operations. Which option best fits her goal?
o: Serving on the company's board of directors
Selling all of her shares immediately
q.r: Serving on the company's board of directors. A board of directors oversees a corporation's major decisions, such as strategy and the selection of top executives, without running day-to-day operations. Many founders stay involved this way after an initial public offering. Selling all of her shares would end her involvement, running daily operations is what she wants to avoid, and starting a competitor would conflict with her role.
w: Selling all her shares immediately would end Elise's ownership and her say in the company, which is the opposite of what she wants.
Running daily operations is the exact role Elise wants to give up; she wants a voice in major decisions without the everyday management.
Starting a competing company would put Elise against her own firm, and it would not give her any voice in that company's major decisions.

q.pt: Describe methods of venture harvesting
q.s: A harvest strategy is most often applied to products that are
q.r: Outdated or declining. A harvest strategy collects the remaining value from a product or venture by cutting investment in it while it still produces sales and profit. It fits products whose sales are fading because they are outdated. New, fast-growing and in-development products need continued investment to reach their potential, so harvesting them would waste future opportunities.
w: Newly introduced products need investment to build sales, so cutting spending on them to collect remaining value would make little sense.
Rapidly growing products deserve more investment to keep growing, while harvesting means pulling back investment from products that are fading.
Products still in development have not earned any sales yet, so there is no remaining value to collect through a harvest strategy.

q.pt: Determine opportunities for venture creation
q.s: While working as a hotel desk clerk, Maya noticed that many guests asked where to rent bicycles, but no nearby shop offered rentals. Maya's idea for a bike-rental business came from
q.r: Her work experience. A job exposes people to customers, problems and gaps in an industry, which makes work experience a common source of venture opportunities. Maya saw an unmet need firsthand while doing her job. Nothing in the situation involves a government grant, a franchise company offering its brand, or access to a competitor's business plan.
w: Nothing in the question mentions government money; Maya's idea came from noticing guests' requests while working the hotel desk.
A franchise offer would mean a company inviting Maya to use its brand, but Maya spotted the bike-rental need independently while at work.
Maya never saw a competitor's plan; in fact, no nearby shop offered rentals, and the gap became clear through talking with hotel guests.

q.pt: Describe entrepreneurial planning considerations
q.s: Deciding how a new bakery will mix, bake and package its bread is an example of which type of planning consideration?
q.r: Operational. Operational considerations deal with how a business will produce and deliver its products, including production processes, equipment, facilities and suppliers. Planning how the bread is mixed, baked and packaged is a production decision. Financial considerations involve money and funding, legal considerations involve ownership form, licenses and regulations, and promotional considerations involve communicating with customers.
w: Financial considerations involve money, such as funding and costs, while deciding how to mix, bake and package bread is about production.
Legal considerations involve licenses, regulations and business ownership form, not the steps the bakery uses to make its bread.
Promotional considerations deal with communicating with customers, such as advertising, not with how the bread is produced and packaged.

q.pt: Identify capital resources needed for the venture
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a capital resource for a packaging company:
o: A loan from a local bank
q.r: A shrink-wrap machine. Capital resources are long-lasting goods, such as machinery, equipment, tools, vehicles and buildings, used to produce other goods and services. A shrink-wrap machine is used again and again in production. Cardboard is a raw material used up in each box, wages pay for human resources, and a bank loan is a source of money rather than a capital good.
w: Cardboard is a raw material that gets used up in each box, while capital resources are long-lasting tools and equipment used over and over.
Hourly wages pay for workers, which are human resources, not the long-lasting equipment that counts as a capital resource.
A bank loan provides money that can buy equipment, but the loan itself is a source of financing, not a capital good used in production.

q.pt: Assess the costs/benefits associated with resources
q.s: Cole can buy a pressure washer for his cleaning business for $2,400 or rent one for $150 per month. How many months of renting would cost the same as buying?
q.r: 16 months. Divide the purchase price by the monthly rent: $2,400 ÷ $150 = 16 months. After 16 months, renting costs more than buying, so if Cole expects to use the washer longer than that, buying is the better value. The answers 12, 15 and 24 months do not result from the correct calculation.
w: Twelve months of rent at $150 is only $1,800, which is still less than the $2,400 purchase price, so the costs have not matched yet.
Fifteen months of rent at $150 is $2,250, still $150 short of the $2,400 purchase price, so one more month is needed to break even.
Twenty-four months of rent at $150 is $3,600, far more than buying; this is like dividing by $100 instead of the actual $150 monthly rent.

q.pt: Select sources to finance venture creation/start-up
q.s: Kenji raised $40,000 to develop his mobile app by collecting small contributions from about 800 supporters through an online platform. Which financing source did Kenji use?
q.r: Crowdfunding. Crowdfunding raises money by collecting small amounts from a large number of people, usually through an online platform. Kenji's supporters gave an average of $50 each. Venture capital comes from investment firms that buy ownership in high-growth businesses. An angel investor is one wealthy individual investing personal money. A microloan is a small loan that must be repaid.
w: Venture capital comes from investment firms that buy ownership in high-growth businesses, not from hundreds of small online contributions.
An angel investor is one wealthy person investing personal money, while Kenji gathered small amounts from about 800 different supporters.
A microloan is a small loan that must be paid back to one lender, but Kenji collected contributions from many supporters on an online platform.

q.pt: Describe external resources useful to entrepreneurs during concept development
q.s: Which external resource offers small-business owners free mentoring from experienced volunteer business professionals?
q.r: SCORE. SCORE is a nonprofit organization, supported by the U.S. Small Business Administration, whose volunteer mentors are experienced business professionals who advise entrepreneurs at no charge. The Internal Revenue Service collects federal taxes. The Federal Trade Commission protects consumers and promotes competition. The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates the sale of stocks and other securities.
w: The Internal Revenue Service collects federal taxes; it does not match small-business owners with volunteer business mentors.
The Federal Trade Commission protects consumers and promotes fair competition, rather than offering free mentoring to entrepreneurs.
The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates stocks and other securities, not a program of volunteer mentors for small businesses.

q.pt: Describe the use of operating procedures
q.s: Pedro writes step-by-step instructions that every employee follows when opening his café each morning. These instructions are
q.r: Standard operating procedures. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) are written, step-by-step instructions that tell employees exactly how to perform routine tasks so the work is done correctly and consistently every time. Pedro's opening checklist is an SOP. A mission statement describes a business's purpose, an exit strategy plans how the owner will leave, and a feasibility study tests whether an idea can work.
w: A mission statement describes a business's overall purpose, not the step-by-step tasks employees follow to open the cafe each morning.
An exit strategy plans how the owner will eventually leave the business, not how employees should open the cafe each day.
A feasibility study tests whether a business idea can work, while Pedro's instructions guide routine daily tasks in a cafe that is already running.

q.pt: Adapt to changes in business environment
q.s: When a new competitor began offering same-day delivery, Ruth quickly added her own delivery service so her flower shop would not lose customers. Ruth is
o: developing an exit strategy for the shop.
q.r: Adapting to the business environment. Businesses cannot control outside forces such as competitors' actions, so successful owners monitor them and adjust their products or operations quickly to stay competitive. Ruth responded to a competitor's move by adding delivery. Harvesting collects value from a venture, a feasibility study tests a new idea, and an exit strategy plans the owner's departure.
w: Harvesting means collecting value from a venture, often by cutting investment, but Ruth added a new service to keep her customers.
A feasibility study tests whether a new idea can work before launch, while Ruth quickly reacted to a competitor in a shop already running.
An exit strategy plans how an owner will leave the business, but Ruth is investing in new delivery so her flower shop stays competitive.

q.pt: Describe the need for marketing data
q.s: What is the primary reason the owner of a new business needs marketing information?
o: To avoid spending money on promotion
q.r: To make sound marketing decisions. Marketing information consists of facts and figures about customers, competitors and the market. Entrepreneurs and managers use it to make informed decisions about products, prices, locations and promotion instead of relying on guesses or hunches. Marketing information reduces risk, but it cannot eliminate risk. It does not replace promotion, and businesses do not gather it mainly to satisfy government reporting rules.
w: Marketing information can reduce risk by replacing guesses with facts, but no amount of information can remove all business risk.
Marketing information helps decide where and how to promote, but it does not replace promotion or let the owner skip spending on it.
Owners gather marketing information mainly to guide business decisions about customers and products, not to satisfy government reporting rules.

q.pt: Describe the need for marketing data
q.s: Keisha reviews the monthly sales reports for Lumen Candle Co. Which of the following can she most likely learn from these reports:
o: Why competitors recently changed their prices
How actual sales compare with sales goals
What customers think of the store's decor
How fast the local population will grow
q.r: How actual sales compare with sales goals. Sales reports are internal records showing what a business sold by product, time period, territory or salesperson. Comparing those figures with sales goals tells managers which products and areas are performing well and which need attention. Competitors' reasons for pricing, customer opinions about decor, and population growth projections do not appear in a company's own sales reports; they require other sources, such as surveys or government data.
w: Sales reports show what Lumen sold, but they cannot explain why competitors changed their prices; that requires outside information.
Customer opinions about decor would come from surveys or comments, not from sales figures that show only what was sold and when.
Population growth forecasts come from government or other outside sources, not from a company's own monthly sales records.

q.pt: Describe the need for marketing data
q.s: Before launching a meal-kit delivery service, Ivan studies customer demand, local competitors and delivery costs. The main advantage of gathering this marketing information is that it helps Ivan
o: keep all competitors out of the market.
q.r: Predict and control risks. Starting or expanding a business involves risk, the possibility that a decision will lead to a loss. Marketing information about demand, competitors and costs lets an entrepreneur anticipate problems and plan around them before committing money. No amount of information can guarantee a profit or keep competitors out of a market, and setting wages is a human resources decision rather than the main purpose of marketing information.
w: Information about demand, competitors and costs can improve Ivan's decisions, but no research can promise that the business will be profitable.
Studying competitors helps Ivan plan how to compete with them, but it cannot stop other businesses from entering the market.
Setting wages is a human resources decision, while Ivan's research on demand, competitors and delivery costs is meant to help Ivan plan around risks.

q.pt: Describe the need for marketing data
q.s: Diego, a sales representative for Summit Office Supply, regularly reports back to his manager about the businesses he visits. Which type of marketing information is Diego best positioned to provide?
q.r: Current and potential customers' needs. Salespeople have direct, frequent contact with buyers, so they are an excellent source of information about current customers, potential customers and what those customers want. They also hear about competitors' activities in the field. Payroll costs and tax obligations come from the company's accounting records, and national unemployment statistics come from government sources, not from a sales representative's customer visits.
w: Payroll expenses come from the company's own accounting records, not from what Diego learns while visiting customer businesses.
National unemployment figures come from government sources, so a sales representative's visits are not a good source for them.
Tax obligations are tracked through accounting records and tax rules, not discovered during Diego's conversations with customers.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing research
q.s: When Mara surveyed shoppers for her gift shop, she was careful not to word questions in ways that would steer people toward the answers she hoped to hear. Mara was trying to keep her research
q.r: Objective. Objective research is free of bias, meaning the researcher's personal opinions or hopes do not influence how data are collected or interpreted. Leading questions that push respondents toward a preferred answer introduce bias. Timely research is available when the decision must be made, reliable research produces consistent results when repeated, and inexpensive research simply costs little; none of these describes avoiding leading questions.
w: Timely research is available when a decision must be made, which has nothing to do with Mara avoiding questions that push people toward answers.
Reliable research gives consistent results when repeated; Mara's concern is keeping her own hopes from biasing the answers, which is objectivity.
Inexpensive research simply costs little, while Mara's careful question wording is about keeping bias out of the results.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing research
q.s: To decide which flavors to reorder, the owner of Pop & Pour Ice Pops reviews her own point-of-sale records from last summer. She is using
q.r: Internal secondary data. Secondary data are facts that already exist because they were collected earlier for another purpose. When those facts come from inside the business, such as point-of-sale records, customer accounts or inventory reports, they are internal secondary data. External secondary data come from outside sources like government reports or trade journals. Primary data, including experimental data, are collected firsthand for the problem currently being studied.
w: External secondary data come from outside sources like government reports or trade journals, but these sales records are the shop's own.
Primary data are collected firsthand for the current problem, while these point-of-sale records already existed from last summer.
Experimental data come from changing one factor and measuring the result, but the owner is simply reviewing existing sales records.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing research
q.s: Which marketing-research method involves changing one factor, such as price, and measuring how customers respond?
q.r: Experiment. The experimental method tests cause and effect by changing one variable, such as a product's price, package or display location, while holding other factors constant and measuring the change in customer response. Observation involves watching and recording what people do, a survey asks people questions, and a focus group is a guided discussion with a small group of people about a product or idea.
w: Observation means watching and recording what people do, without deliberately changing a factor like price to test the response.
A survey asks people questions about their opinions or habits, rather than changing a factor and measuring how customers actually respond.
A focus group is a guided discussion with a small group, which gathers opinions instead of testing how a changed factor affects behavior.

q.pt: Explain the nature of marketing research
q.s: Marketing research is described as systematic because it
o: relies on the researcher's personal judgment.
uses only data that are collected online.
follows an orderly, planned series of steps.
is repeated every week without changes.
q.r: Follows an orderly, planned series of steps. Marketing research is the systematic gathering, recording and analyzing of information about a specific marketing problem. Systematic means the work follows a logical process, such as defining the problem, collecting and analyzing data, and recommending action. Relying on personal judgment works against objectivity, research can draw on many sources besides online data, and repeating the same study every week is not what makes research systematic.
w: Relying on personal judgment makes research less objective; being systematic means following an orderly, planned process instead.
Research can use many sources, such as interviews, records and observation, so it is not systematic just because data come from online.
Repeating the same study every week is about frequency, while systematic means the research follows logical, planned steps.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: Belle Rue, a new boutique, uses elegant displays, personal stylists and premium prices to appeal to affluent shoppers. Which of the following products would best fit the boutique's marketing mix:
o: Discount phone cases sold from bulk bins
q.r: Handmade leather handbags priced at $450. A marketing strategy works only when all elements of the marketing mix fit together and support the image the business wants. An upscale boutique with elegant displays, personal service and premium prices should carry high-quality, high-priced goods. Discount phone cases, clearance T-shirts and $5 generic sunglasses would send a bargain message that conflicts with the boutique's image and confuses its target market.
w: Discount phone cases in bulk bins send a bargain message that clashes with Belle Rue's elegant displays and premium prices for affluent shoppers.
Clearance T-shirts marked down 70 percent suggest bargain shopping, which conflicts with the high-end image Belle Rue is building.
Five-dollar generic sunglasses do not match a boutique offering personal stylists and premium prices to wealthy customers.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: The owners of Tread Lightly, a startup that sells recycled-rubber sandals, want to appeal to more price-conscious customers. Which marketing-mix change would best help them reach this goal?
q.r: Lowering the sandals' prices. Price is the marketing-mix element most directly tied to whether price-conscious customers are able and willing to buy. Lowering prices makes the product affordable to more people, which widens the potential customer base. Raising prices narrows the market to fewer buyers, while selling through fewer retailers and cutting back on advertising reduce the number of customers who can find and learn about the product.
w: Raising prices would push the sandals further out of reach for price-conscious buyers, which works against the owners' goal.
Selling through fewer retailers makes the sandals harder to find, which does nothing to make them more affordable for budget-minded customers.
Cutting advertising means fewer people hear about the sandals, and it does not address the price that matters most to these customers.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: Why should an entrepreneur review marketing strategies regularly rather than keep them unchanged indefinitely?
q.r: Market conditions change over time. Customers' needs, competitors' actions, the economy and technology all shift, so a strategy that works well today may not work next year. Businesses monitor the market and adjust their marketing strategies when conditions change. No law requires yearly strategy changes, customers generally value consistent branding, and strategies do not automatically expire after a set period of time.
w: No law requires businesses to change their marketing strategies each year; they review strategies because markets keep changing.
Customers generally value consistent branding, so a dislike of consistency is not the reason strategies need regular review.
Strategies do not automatically expire after a season; they need review because customers, competitors and the economy keep shifting.

q.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a marketing goal rather than a strategy or a tactic:
o: Target college students who live nearby
Post a discount code online each Friday
Sell through campus bookstores and pop-ups
q.r: Increase online sales 15% by June 30. A marketing goal, or objective, states the specific result a business wants to achieve within a set time. A strategy is the overall plan for reaching that goal, such as choosing a target market or a distribution approach. A tactic is a specific action that carries out a strategy. Targeting college students and selling through campus bookstores are strategies, and the weekly discount post is a tactic.
w: Targeting nearby college students is a strategy, because it chooses who to serve rather than stating a measurable result to reach by a date.
Posting a discount code each Friday is a tactic, a specific action that carries out a strategy, not the end result the business wants.
Selling through campus bookstores and pop-ups is a distribution strategy for reaching customers, not a specific result with a deadline.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: All the people or businesses who want a product and have both the ability and the willingness to buy it make up a(n)
q.r: Market. A market consists of all the potential customers, whether consumers or industrial buyers, who share a need or want for a product and have both the ability and the willingness to buy it. A market segment is a smaller group within a market, a channel is the path a product takes to reach its users, and an industry is a group of businesses that produce similar products.
w: A segment is a smaller group within a market, not the full set of everyone who wants the product and can afford to buy it.
A channel is the path a product takes to reach buyers, not the group of people who want and can buy it.
An industry is a group of businesses making similar products, while the question describes the buyers who want and can pay for a product.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: Riverbend Marine sells fishing boats that start at $90,000. Which demographic factor best indicates whether a person can afford the company's boats?
q.r: Income. Demographics are population statistics such as age, gender, income, education and family size. Of these, income is the clearest indicator of a customer's ability to buy, which matters most for expensive goods like boats. Gender, family size and marital status may influence what people want or how they use a product, but they do not show whether a person can afford a $90,000 purchase.
w: Gender may shape what kind of product someone wants, but it says nothing about whether a person can afford a $90,000 boat.
Family size might affect what size boat a buyer wants, but it does not show whether the person has the money for a $90,000 purchase.
Marital status may affect how a boat is used, but it does not tell Riverbend whether someone can actually afford one of its boats.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: Hollis started Paws Pantry, a dog-treat company, after identifying dog owners in her city as her market. Why should she re-examine her market every year or so?
o: Customers' needs and numbers change over time
Her market share cannot change once set
Target markets can be chosen only once
Research findings are legally valid for one year
q.r: Customers' needs and numbers change over time. Markets are not fixed. Over time, customers' needs, tastes, incomes and numbers change, new competitors arrive, and the economy shifts. Periodically re-examining the market lets an entrepreneur spot these changes and adjust products and promotion before sales suffer. Market share can rise or fall, businesses can change their target markets whenever it makes sense, and research findings have no legal expiration date.
w: Market share can rise or fall over time, so Hollis's share is not fixed and is one more reason to keep checking her market.
Businesses can change their target markets whenever it makes sense, so Hollis is not stuck with her first choice.
Research findings have no legal expiration date; Hollis should update her research because customers and conditions keep changing.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: A company that sells commercial cleaning equipment to hotels, hospitals and office buildings for use in their daily operations is serving a(n) __________ market.
q.r: Industrial. An industrial market, also called a business-to-business market, is made up of businesses and organizations that buy goods and services to run their operations or to resell. Hotels, hospitals and offices buying cleaning equipment for daily use are industrial buyers. A consumer market, which includes households, buys for personal use, and a niche is a small, specialized segment, not a broad group of different organizations.
w: A consumer market buys products for personal or household use, while hotels, hospitals and offices buy this equipment to run their operations.
Households buy goods for personal use at home, not cleaning equipment for running hotels, hospitals and office buildings.
A niche is a small, specialized segment, while this company sells to a broad range of different organizations for their daily operations.

q.pt: Identify market segments
q.s: Why do businesses divide a total market into smaller segments?
o: Segments remove the need for research
q.r: Customers' needs and wants differ. Market segmentation divides a total market into smaller groups of customers who share similar characteristics, needs or wants. Because customers in a large market do not all want the same things, a business can serve them better by tailoring its marketing mix to one or more segments. No law requires segmentation, large markets can be very profitable, and segmentation depends on research rather than replacing it.
w: No law requires businesses to segment their markets; they do it because different groups of customers want different things.
Large markets can be very profitable, and segmentation helps a business serve parts of them better rather than avoiding them.
Segmentation depends on research to identify customer groups, so it increases the need for research instead of removing it.

q.pt: Identify market segments
q.s: Fuel Fit Gym groups its members as light, medium and heavy users based on how many times they visit each month. The gym is segmenting its market by
q.r: Rate of use. Rate of use is a behavioral segmentation base that groups customers by how often or how much they use a product. Light, medium and heavy users of a gym are classified by visit frequency. Loyalty status groups customers by how committed they are to a brand, benefits sought groups them by what they want the product to do for them, and lifestyle is a psychographic base.
w: Loyalty status groups members by how committed they are to the gym's brand, not by how many times they visit each month.
Benefits sought groups customers by what they want from a product, such as weight loss, not by how often they come in.
Lifestyle is a psychographic base about how people live and what they value, while Fuel Fit is counting visits per month.

q.pt: Identify market segments
q.s: To be useful to marketers, the members of a market segment should
o: live together in the same household or building.
currently buy from the same competitor.
share similar characteristics, needs or wants.
earn exactly the same annual income.
q.r: Share similar characteristics, needs or wants. A market segment is a group of customers within a larger market who share similar characteristics, needs or wants and therefore respond similarly to marketing.
