That similarity lets a business design one marketing mix for the whole group. Segment members do not need to live together, buy from the same competitor, or earn identical incomes; they only need to be alike in ways that matter for the product.
w: Segment members do not need to live together; they only need to share traits or needs that affect how they respond to marketing.
Buying from the same competitor is not required, because a segment is defined by shared needs and traits rather than current purchases.
Members of a segment can have similar incomes, but they do not need identical incomes; being alike in ways that matter for the product is enough.

q.pt: Develop customer profile
q.s: Why do advertisers develop customer profiles?
o: To understand customers' interests and concerns
To replace the need for a promotional budget
q.r: To understand customers' interests and concerns. A customer profile is a detailed description of the typical customer in a target market, including demographic, geographic, psychographic and behavioral traits. Advertisers use profiles to understand what customers care about so they can choose the right media and create messages that appeal to them. Profiles describe customers, not competitors' prices; they do not replace a promotional budget; and supplier delivery schedules are an operations matter.
w: Customer profiles describe the business's own customers, while competitors' pricing strategies are studied through competitive analysis.
Profiles help an advertiser spend a promotional budget wisely, but they do not replace the need to set aside money for promotion.
Supplier delivery schedules are an operations matter and have nothing to do with understanding what customers care about.

q.pt: Develop customer profile
q.s: Coastal Cowork, a shared-office startup, builds detailed profiles of its typical members and shares them with staff. A key benefit of an effective customer-profiling system is that it helps employees
q.r: Provide better customer service. When employees understand who their customers are and what those customers need and expect, they can anticipate requests, personalize service and solve problems more effectively. That is a major benefit of an effective customer-profiling system. Profiles cannot prevent every complaint, they do not replace training, and pricing decisions still require research on costs, competition and demand.
w: Knowing members better helps staff prevent many problems, but no profiling system can stop every single customer complaint.
Customer profiles help employees understand who they serve, but new staff still need training on how to do their jobs.
Pricing still requires research on costs, competition and demand, so customer profiles do not let staff skip that work.

q.pt: Develop customer profile
q.s: Which of the following is an example of psychographic information an entrepreneur might include in a customer profile:
o: Lives in a suburb of a large metro area
Buys coffee three times each week
q.r: Enjoys hiking and values sustainability. Psychographic information describes customers' lifestyles, values, attitudes, interests and activities, such as enjoying hiking and valuing sustainability. A complete customer profile also includes other kinds of information: age is demographic, living in a suburb is geographic, and buying coffee three times a week is behavioral information about rate of use. Knowing all four helps a business describe its typical customer.
w: Age is demographic information, a population statistic, rather than a description of the customer's values, interests or lifestyle.
Living in a suburb describes where the customer lives, which is geographic information, not psychographic information.
Buying coffee three times a week describes how often the customer buys, which is behavioral information about rate of use.

q.pt: Conduct SWOT analysis for use in the marketing planning process
q.s: In a SWOT analysis, the four letters stand for
q.r: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. A SWOT analysis evaluates a business's internal strengths and weaknesses along with the external opportunities and threats in its environment. Entrepreneurs use it in the marketing planning process to build on what they do well, fix or work around problems, take advantage of favorable conditions, and prepare for dangers. The other options mix in unrelated business terms that are not part of the SWOT framework.
w: Sales, wages, organization and technology are general business terms, not the four factors a SWOT analysis examines.
Strategies, objectives and trends are not part of SWOT; only weaknesses fits, and the framework also covers strengths, opportunities and threats.
Strengths fits, but workloads, outcomes and tactics are not part of the SWOT framework, which also covers weaknesses, opportunities and threats.

q.pt: Conduct SWOT analysis for use in the marketing planning process
q.s: Which of the following would be classified as a strength in a SWOT analysis for Kettle & Crumb Bakery:
o: It holds the largest share of the local bakery market
A national bakery chain plans to open a store nearby
Its ovens are old and frequently break down
A new office park nearby will bring in more workers
q.r: It holds the largest share of the local bakery market. Strengths are internal advantages a business controls, such as market leadership, a strong reputation or skilled employees. Holding the largest local market share is a strength. A national chain opening nearby is an external threat, aging ovens that break down are an internal weakness, and a new office park that brings in potential customers is an external opportunity.
w: A national chain opening nearby is an outside danger the bakery cannot control, which makes it a threat rather than a strength.
Old ovens that keep breaking down are an internal problem, which makes them a weakness, not a strength.
A new office park bringing in workers is a favorable outside condition, which makes it an opportunity rather than an internal strength.

q.pt: Conduct SWOT analysis for use in the marketing planning process
q.s: In a SWOT analysis, which two elements describe factors inside the business that the owner can control?
q.r: Strengths and weaknesses. Strengths and weaknesses are internal factors, such as the business's staff, finances, location and reputation, which the owner can build on or improve. Opportunities and threats are external factors, such as economic trends, competitors and regulations, that the business cannot control but must respond to. The mixed pairs combine one internal and one external factor, so they do not describe only factors inside the business.
w: Opportunities and threats are both external factors, such as the economy and competitors, that the owner cannot control.
Strengths are internal, but opportunities are outside conditions the owner cannot control, so this pair mixes internal and external.
Weaknesses are internal, but threats come from outside the business, so this pair does not describe only factors the owner controls.

q.pt: Conduct competitive analysis
q.s: Nadia owns a yoga studio and suspects that a new studio across town is drawing away some of her members. What should she conduct to find out whether the competitor is taking market share?
q.r: A competitive analysis. A competitive analysis identifies competitors and evaluates their products, prices, promotion and other strengths and weaknesses, including how much of the market they are capturing. It would show Nadia what the new studio offers and why members might be switching. A break-even analysis finds the sales needed to cover costs, a job analysis studies the duties of a position, and ratio analysis evaluates a firm's own financial statements.
w: A break-even analysis finds how many sales are needed to cover costs, but it would not show whether members are leaving for a competitor.
A job analysis studies the duties of a position, which has nothing to do with how a rival studio is affecting Nadia's membership.
Financial ratio analysis looks at Nadia's own financial statements, not at what the new studio offers or how much of the market it is taking.

q.pt: Conduct competitive analysis
q.s: What is a practical, low-cost way for a startup to gather information about its competitors' products and prices?
o: Review secondary data such as trade journals
Hire competitors' employees to reveal trade secrets
Ask competitors to share their financial statements
Wait for customers to report competitors' prices
q.r: Review secondary data such as trade journals. Secondary data, such as competitors' websites, social media pages, advertisements, catalogs and trade journals, are already available and cost little to review, so they are a practical starting point for competitive analysis. Hiring employees to reveal trade secrets is unethical and may be illegal, competitors are unlikely to share private financial statements, and waiting for customers to volunteer information is slow and unreliable.
w: Hiring competitors' employees to reveal trade secrets is unethical and may be illegal, so it is not an acceptable way to gather information.
Competitors are very unlikely to hand over private financial statements to a rival, so this is not a practical approach.
Waiting for customers to mention competitors' prices is slow and unreliable, while existing secondary sources can be reviewed right away.

q.pt: Conduct competitive analysis
q.s: The owner of Grind Time, a coffee shop, views a nearby smoothie bar as a competitor because both sell quick morning drinks to commuters. The smoothie bar represents __________ competition.
q.r: Indirect. Indirect competition comes from businesses that satisfy the same customer need with a different kind of product. A smoothie bar and a coffee shop both meet commuters' need for a quick morning drink, but they sell different products. Direct competition would be another coffee shop, pure competition is a market structure with many sellers of identical products, and price competition means competing mainly by charging less.
w: Direct competition would be another coffee shop selling the same kind of product, but a smoothie bar sells a different drink for the same need.
Pure competition is a market structure with many sellers of identical products, which does not describe a coffee shop and a smoothie bar.
Price competition means competing mainly by charging less, and nothing in the question says the smoothie bar is undercutting Grind Time's prices.

q.pt: Conduct market analysis (market size, area, potential, etc.)
q.s: Before opening a dry-cleaning shop, Marcus maps the neighborhoods within three miles of his location from which he expects to draw most of his customers. Marcus is defining his
q.r: Trading area. A trading area is the geographic area from which a business draws most of its customers. Defining it is part of market analysis, which also looks at the size and potential of the market and whether customers have the ability and willingness to buy. Market share is a company's percentage of total market sales, a sales quota is a sales target, and a price range is a span of prices.
w: Market share is a business's percentage of total market sales, not the map of neighborhoods Marcus expects his customers to come from.
A sales quota is a sales target, usually set for a salesperson or period, not the geographic area a shop draws customers from.
A price range is the span of prices a business charges, which has nothing to do with mapping where customers live.

q.pt: Set marketing goals and objectives
q.s: Bluebird Cleaning Co. sets an objective to add a pet-safe cleaning package to its list of services by next spring. This is an example of a __________ objective.
q.r: Product. Product objectives deal with what a business offers, including adding, improving or dropping goods and services. Adding a pet-safe cleaning package expands the service line, so it is a product objective. Pricing objectives deal with what the business charges, promotional objectives deal with communicating with customers, and distribution objectives deal with how and where the business delivers its products.
w: Pricing objectives deal with what a business charges, but adding a new pet-safe package changes what Bluebird offers, not its prices.
Promotional objectives deal with communicating with customers, while this objective adds a new service to Bluebird's list.
Distribution objectives deal with how and where services reach customers, but this objective is about adding a new cleaning package.

q.pt: Develop marketing plan
q.s: Jada shares her new marketing plan with all six employees of her bike shop. Doing so mainly helps the staff
o: track their individual hours worked each week.
set their own prices for products.
q.r: Work toward shared marketing objectives. A marketing plan is a written document that states the business's marketing objectives and the strategies, budget and schedule for reaching them. Sharing it gives employees a common direction, so everyone's work supports the same goals. Tracking hours is a payroll task, tax returns are prepared from financial records, and employees in a small shop follow the pricing set in the plan rather than setting their own prices.
w: Tracking weekly hours is a payroll task, while a marketing plan lays out objectives, strategies and a budget for the business.
Tax returns are prepared from financial records, not from a marketing plan that sets marketing objectives and strategies.
In a small shop, pricing is set as part of the plan, so sharing it guides employees rather than letting them set their own prices.

q.pt: Forecast sales for marketing plan
q.s: Pet-grooming sales in Eastfield total $1,250,000 a year. Clip & Comb expects its market share to rise from 8% to 10% next year. If total market sales stay the same, what is Clip & Comb's sales forecast for next year?
q.r: $125,000. A sales forecast based on market share equals total market sales multiplied by the company's expected share: $1,250,000 × 0.10 = $125,000. The $100,000 figure uses the old 8% share, $25,000 is only the increase in sales from the higher share, and $225,000 incorrectly adds the two shares together (18%) before multiplying.
w: This is only the increase from the higher share, $1,250,000 times 2%, rather than the total forecast at the new 10% share.
This uses the old 8% share ($1,250,000 times 0.08), but the forecast should use the expected 10% share for next year.
This adds the old and new shares together (18%) before multiplying, but only the expected 10% share should be used.

q.pt: Forecast sales for marketing plan
q.s: Leila asks each of her company's sales representatives to estimate next year's sales in their own territories and then adds the estimates together. Which forecasting method is Leila using?
q.r: Sales force composite. A sales force composite builds a forecast by combining salespeople's estimates for their territories, drawing on their close contact with customers. A jury of executive opinion relies on the combined judgment of top managers, trend analysis projects future sales from past sales patterns, and test marketing measures how a product sells in a limited area before a full launch.
w: A jury of executive opinion relies on the combined judgment of top managers, not on estimates from each sales representative's territory.
Trend analysis projects future sales from past sales patterns, while Leila is adding up her reps' own estimates for their territories.
Test marketing measures sales of a product in a limited area before a full launch, which is not what Leila is doing.

q.pt: Select target market
q.s: Spruce Street Soap Co. decides to focus all of its marketing on one segment: parents looking for gentle skin-care products for babies. This targeting approach is called
q.r: Concentrated marketing. Concentrated marketing focuses all of a business's marketing efforts on a single target segment, which lets a small business become an expert at serving that group. Undifferentiated marketing uses one marketing mix for the entire market, differentiated marketing creates separate mixes for several segments, and direct marketing is a promotional method of communicating straight to individual customers, not a targeting approach.
w: Undifferentiated marketing uses one marketing mix for the whole market, but Spruce Street focuses on just one segment of parents.
Differentiated marketing creates separate mixes for several segments, while Spruce Street aims all its marketing at a single group.
Direct marketing is a way of communicating straight to individual customers, not a decision about how many segments to target.

q.pt: Translate performance measures into financial outcomes
q.s: Tilly's Treats spent $2,000 on a holiday email campaign that produced $10,000 in additional sales. The products sold carry a 40% gross margin. What net contribution did the campaign produce?
q.r: $2,000. Net contribution is the gross profit gained from added sales minus the marketing cost. Gross profit is $10,000 × 0.40 = $4,000, and $4,000 − $2,000 = $2,000. The $4,000 figure ignores the campaign's cost, $6,000 is the cost of the goods sold ($10,000 × 0.60), and $8,000 subtracts the campaign cost from sales without accounting for the cost of goods.
w: This is the gross profit from the added sales ($10,000 times 40%), but it forgets to subtract the $2,000 the campaign cost.
This is the cost of the goods sold ($10,000 times 60%), not the profit left after the campaign's cost is subtracted.
This subtracts the $2,000 campaign cost from $10,000 in sales but ignores the cost of the goods, which takes 60% of sales.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: What is the ultimate goal of a small business's promotional activities?
o: To lower the cost of producing goods
q.r: To increase the business's sales. Promotion informs, persuades and reminds customers about a business and its products, but the ultimate purpose of all these efforts is to increase sales and, in turn, profit. Advertising awards are a by-product at most, promotion adds to costs rather than lowering production costs, and relationships with reporters are a public-relations tool that serves the larger goal of selling more.
w: Advertising awards may come as a side benefit, but promotion exists to bring in customers and sales, not to win industry honors.
Promotion adds to a business's costs rather than lowering what it costs to produce goods, so this cannot be its main goal.
Building relationships with reporters is a public relations tool that serves the bigger goal of selling more, not a goal in itself.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Golden Crust Bakery has served its town for 20 years, yet it still runs radio ads so residents think of it when they want fresh bread. The main purpose of these ads is to
o: inform customers about a new product.
explain how to use the bakery's products.
q.r: Remind customers about the business. Reminder promotion keeps an established business or product top-of-mind so that current customers keep buying. A bakery that residents already know uses ads to stay in their thoughts. Informative promotion introduces something new, persuasive promotion tries to convince customers to choose one product over another, and explaining product use is a kind of informing, none of which fits ads for a well-known business.
w: Informative promotion introduces something new, but these ads are for a bakery residents have known for 20 years, not a new product.
Persuasive promotion tries to win customers away from competitors, while these ads simply keep Golden Crust in residents' minds.
Explaining how to use a product is a form of informing, and fresh bread from a well-known bakery needs no such explanation.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: A new meal-prep company runs ads comparing its prices and ingredients with those of competing services and urging viewers to switch. These ads are mainly intended to
q.r: Persuade. Persuasive promotion tries to convince customers to choose a business's product over competing products, often by comparing features or prices and asking for action. Urging viewers to switch is persuasion. Reminder promotion keeps established products top-of-mind, informative promotion introduces new products or facts, and although some ads entertain, entertainment is a technique rather than the main purpose of promotion.
w: Reminder promotion keeps a well-known business top-of-mind, but this new company is comparing itself with rivals and urging viewers to switch.
Informative promotion introduces new products or facts, while these ads go further by comparing competitors and asking viewers to switch.
Ads can be entertaining, but entertainment is a technique; the main aim of urging viewers to switch is to convince them to choose this company.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Which of the following is an external factor that can affect a business's promotional decisions:
o: The size of the promotional budget
q.r: Government regulation of advertising. External factors are forces outside a business that it cannot control, such as laws, the economy, competitors and technology. Government rules on advertising, including those enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, limit what a business may say and how. The promotional budget, the owner's preferences and the company's marketing objectives are internal factors that the business itself decides.
w: The promotional budget is an amount the business sets for itself, so it is an internal decision rather than an outside force the business cannot control.
The owner's media tastes come from inside the company, and the question asks for a force outside the business, like a law or the economy.
Marketing objectives are goals the business writes for itself, which makes them an internal factor rather than an outside force acting on its promotion.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Which requirement should every promotional message a business sends meet?
o: It must appear in at least two media
It must include a discount or special offer
It must be truthful and not misleading
It must name the competing products
q.r: It must be truthful and not misleading. Sound promotional practice requires honesty. Messages must be truthful and must not mislead customers about a product's features, price or benefits, and the Federal Trade Commission acts against deceptive advertising. Promotions can run in a single medium, many promotions include no discount, and businesses usually are not required to mention competing products at all.
w: A message can run in just one medium, such as a single radio spot, and still be sound promotion as long as it is honest.
Plenty of promotions, like image ads or product announcements, offer no discount at all, so a special offer is not something every message needs.
Businesses usually have no duty to mention rivals in their ads; the rule every message must follow is honesty about the product, not naming competitors.

q.pt: Identify types of public-relations activities
q.s: Each month, Fernwood Garden Center emails subscribers a publication it writes itself, featuring planting tips, staff spotlights and upcoming workshop dates. Which public-relations tool is the business using?
q.r: Newsletter. A newsletter is a regular publication that a business writes and controls, giving it ongoing communication with customers and other publics. Fernwood decides exactly what goes in each issue. A press conference gathers reporters at an event, a media tour takes a spokesperson to several media outlets, and a press release is sent to the media, which then decide whether and how to report the story.
w: A press conference brings reporters together at an event to hear an announcement, but Fernwood is emailing its own publication straight to subscribers.
A media tour sends a spokesperson to visit several news outlets, while Fernwood is simply emailing its own monthly publication to subscribers.
A press release goes to reporters, who decide whether to run the story, but Fernwood sends its own content directly to customers every month.

q.pt: Identify types of public-relations activities
q.s: Tandem Bike Works sponsors and staffs a water station at a fun run that raises money for the local children's hospital. This activity is an example of
q.r: Public relations. Public relations includes planned activities that build goodwill between a business and the community rather than directly selling products. Supporting a charity event is community relations that creates a positive image of the business. Personal selling is person-to-person persuasion to buy, sales promotion uses short-term buying incentives, and direct marketing sends messages to individuals to get a measurable response.
w: Personal selling is a salesperson persuading a customer to buy, and staffing a charity water station is not trying to close any sale.
Sales promotion uses short-term buying incentives like coupons or contests, but Tandem is supporting a hospital fundraiser to build community goodwill.
Direct marketing sends messages to chosen individuals to get a measurable response, while Tandem is helping at a charity event to earn goodwill.

q.pt: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
q.s: Which public-relations channel most easily allows a business and the public to hold two-way conversations?
q.r: Social media. Social media lets a business post information and lets customers and other members of the public respond, comment and ask questions, creating interactive, two-way communication. Businesses use it to answer concerns quickly and build relationships. Press releases, printed brochures and billboards are one-way channels: the business sends the message, but the audience cannot easily reply through the same channel.
w: A press release is sent out to the media in one direction, and the public has no easy way to reply through it.
A printed brochure delivers the business's message to readers, but readers cannot answer back through the brochure, so it is a one-way channel.
A billboard shows a message to people driving or walking past, and they cannot respond to it, so it does not allow two-way conversation.

q.pt: Identify types of public-relations activities
q.s: When Sol Fitness donates free gym memberships to local veterans' groups, the business's main public-relations goal is to
q.r: Build goodwill in the community. Philanthropy, such as donating products or services to worthy causes, is a public-relations activity that builds goodwill, the favorable attitude the public holds toward a business. The goal is a positive image over time, not an immediate sale. Measuring response rates is a feature of direct marketing, and donating free memberships adds to costs rather than lowering them.
w: Donating memberships to veterans' groups is not a sales pitch; Sol Fitness is not asking anyone to buy something on the spot.
Tracking response rates is how direct marketing measures results, but a donation to veterans is meant to create a positive image, not a countable response.
Giving away free memberships actually adds to Sol Fitness's costs, so cutting expenses cannot be the reason behind this donation.

q.pt: Identify types of public-relations activities
q.s: Nguyen Tech Solutions holds monthly town-hall meetings and publishes an internal blog to keep its staff informed and engaged. This type of public-relations activity is
q.r: Employee relations. Employee relations includes public-relations activities directed at a company's own workers, such as meetings, internal blogs and recognition programs that keep them informed, engaged and loyal. Investor relations communicates with shareholders and potential investors, media relations works with journalists and news outlets, and community relations builds goodwill with the people who live where the business operates.
w: Investor relations communicates with shareholders and people who might invest, but Nguyen's town halls and internal blog are aimed at its own staff.
Media relations means working with reporters and news outlets, while these meetings and the internal blog are meant only for the company's workers.
Community relations builds goodwill with local residents, but town halls and an internal blog keep employees, not neighbors, informed.

q.pt: Identify types of public-relations activities
q.s: News reports reveal that the founder of a fast-growing juice company misled the company's investors. Which public-relations activity does the company most need right away?
q.r: Crisis management. Crisis management is the planned communication a business uses to protect its reputation during and after a damaging event, such as a scandal involving its leaders. It typically includes a prepared spokesperson, honest statements and prompt updates. Product sampling and trade promotion are sales-promotion activities, and media buying is purchasing advertising time or space; none addresses the damage to the company's reputation.
w: Product sampling hands out free trials to encourage buying, which does nothing to repair the trust lost after a scandal involving the founder.
Media buying is purchasing ad time or space, but the company's urgent need is to respond honestly to bad news about its founder, not to buy ads.
Trade promotion gives incentives to stores and other channel members, which does not address the reputation damage from the founder misleading investors.

q.pt: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
q.s: A startup preparing to launch its first product assembles a press kit for journalists. Which of the following would it most likely include:
o: Its confidential list of customer names
Its internal budget for next year
A fact sheet about the company
q.r: A fact sheet about the company. A press kit, also called a media kit, is a packet of background materials that helps journalists write accurate stories. It typically contains fact sheets, press releases, photos and biographies of key people. A customer list, employee performance reviews and internal budgets are confidential business records that a company would not share with the media.
w: A customer list is private information the startup must protect, so it would never hand it to journalists in a press kit.
Employee performance reviews are confidential personnel records, and a press kit holds only material meant to help reporters write public stories.
Next year's internal budget is private planning information; a press kit contains background facts the company wants the public to know.

q.pt: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
q.s: Brightwater Kayaks sends a written announcement about its new factory to local newspapers and TV stations, hoping they will report the story. Brightwater is using a
q.r: Press release. A press release, also called a news release, is a written announcement sent to media outlets in the hope that they will publish or broadcast the story. Because the media decide whether to use it, any resulting coverage is publicity. A press conference gathers reporters at an event, a media tour sends a spokesperson to several outlets, and a newsletter goes directly to customers.
w: A press conference gathers reporters in one place to hear an announcement in person, but Brightwater only sent out a written announcement.
A media tour sends a company spokesperson to visit several outlets, while Brightwater simply mailed a written story to newspapers and TV stations.
A newsletter goes directly to a company's customers or subscribers, but Brightwater sent its announcement to the media hoping they would report it.

q.pt: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
q.s: The primary purpose of public-relations communication channels, such as press releases and company blogs, is to
o: inform the public and build goodwill.
set prices for the company's products.
q.r: Inform the public and build goodwill. Public-relations channels carry an organization's news and messages to the public. Their main purpose is to give people information that helps them understand the organization and view it favorably, building goodwill over time. Processing orders and collecting payments are sales and accounting activities, and setting prices is a pricing decision rather than a function of public-relations communication.
w: Processing orders is a sales and operations task, while press releases and blogs exist to share news and shape how the public sees the company.
Setting prices is a pricing decision made elsewhere in the business, not the job of channels that share company news with the public.
Collecting payments is an accounting task, while press releases and company blogs are used to inform people and build a favorable image.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: The owner of Maple & Main Hardware tells employees to "do whatever it takes to make sure every customer leaves satisfied." This shows that the business is
q.r: Customer-oriented. A customer-oriented business puts customers' needs and satisfaction first, which is the attitude behind mottoes such as "the customer is always right." Customer orientation is central to the selling function. A product-oriented business focuses on its products' features, a production-oriented business focuses on making goods efficiently, and a price-oriented business competes mainly by charging less.
w: A product-oriented business focuses on its products' features, but this owner's instruction centers on keeping every customer satisfied.
A production-oriented business focuses on making goods efficiently, which has nothing to do with the owner's push to satisfy every customer.
A price-oriented business competes mainly by charging less, while the owner's message is about customer satisfaction, not low prices.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: Ana buys a set of watercolor paints from Brushstroke Art Supply to use for her own hobby painting at home. Ana is buying the paints for
q.r: Ultimate consumption. Ultimate consumption means a product is bought for the buyer's own personal or household use, which makes it a consumer good. Ana is the final user of the paints. Products bought for resale go to wholesalers and retailers, and products bought for business operations or further production are industrial goods used to run a business or to make other products.
w: Buying for resale means purchasing goods to sell to someone else, but Ana plans to use the paints herself at home.
Business operations purchases are made to run a company, and Ana is buying paints for her personal hobby, not for a business.
Further production means using a product to make other goods for sale, but Ana is the final user painting for fun.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: How does the selling function add value for customers?
o: By lowering the producer's manufacturing costs
By guaranteeing the lowest price on every product
By replacing the need for any other form of promotion
By helping them get products that meet their needs
q.r: By helping them get products that meet their needs. Selling determines what customers need and want and then helps them obtain products that satisfy those needs, at the right place and time. This creates utility, or usefulness, for the customer. Selling does not lower manufacturing costs, it cannot guarantee the lowest price, and businesses still use advertising, sales promotion and other promotional-mix elements alongside selling.
w: Selling does not reduce what it costs the producer to make a product; its value comes from matching customers with products they need.
No selling effort can promise the lowest price on everything; selling adds value by helping customers find and get the right products.
Selling works alongside advertising and other promotion rather than replacing them, so this is not how it adds value for customers.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: Which of the following is a tangible product that a small business might sell:
q.r: A handmade cutting board. Tangible products are goods that have physical form and can be seen and touched, such as a handmade cutting board. Services are intangible activities performed for customers. A guitar lesson, tax preparation and dog walking are all services: the customer pays for the activity and its result rather than for a physical object.
w: A guitar lesson is an activity the customer experiences, not a physical object, which makes it an intangible service rather than a tangible product.
A tax-preparation appointment is a service performed for the customer, so there is no physical item to see or touch.
A dog-walking visit is a service the customer pays someone to perform, so it lacks the physical form of a tangible product.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
q.s: Pinecrest Supply sells cash registers and store shelving to independent retailers, which use them to run their stores. These products are classified as
q.r: Industrial goods. Industrial goods are products that businesses buy to use in their operations, to make other products, or to resell. Cash registers and shelving help retailers run their stores, so they are industrial goods. Consumer goods are bought for personal or household use, and convenience and specialty goods are categories of consumer goods, so none of them describes equipment bought for business use.
w: Consumer goods are bought for personal or household use, but these retailers buy registers and shelving to run their stores.
Convenience goods are low-cost consumer items people buy often, like snacks, not equipment that retailers buy to operate a business.
Specialty goods are unique consumer products shoppers make a special effort to buy, which does not describe store equipment bought for business use.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Moxie Mats mails postcards, each with a unique discount code, to 5,000 past customers so it can count how many orders the mailing produces. This promotion is an example of
q.r: Direct marketing. Direct marketing sends promotional messages straight to targeted individuals, without intermediaries, to produce a measurable response. Unique codes let Moxie Mats count exactly how many orders the postcards generate. Publicity is unpaid media coverage, public relations builds goodwill rather than seeking immediate orders, and personal selling is face-to-face or person-to-person communication with individual customers.
w: Publicity is unpaid news coverage the media choose to run, but Moxie Mats paid to mail postcards straight to its past customers.
Public relations builds goodwill over time, while these coded postcards are meant to bring in orders that Moxie Mats can count.
Personal selling is one-to-one communication between a salesperson and a customer, not a mass mailing of discount postcards.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: For a small business, the main advantage of direct advertising is that it
o: costs nothing to create or send.
reaches the people most likely to buy.
needs no information about its customers.
q.r: Reaches the people most likely to buy. Direct advertising is sent to specific people chosen from mailing lists or customer databases, so it can be aimed at qualified prospects, the people most likely to need and buy the product. That reduces wasted coverage. Direct advertising still has creative, printing and postage or platform costs, response rates are often low and never guaranteed, and targeting depends on good customer information.
w: Direct advertising still has costs for design, printing, postage or online platforms, so it is far from free to create or send.
Response rates for direct advertising are often low, and no method can promise that a large share of people will respond.
Direct advertising depends on good customer information, since a business must know who its likely buyers are in order to target them.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Compared with personal selling, direct mail is usually
o: more effective at closing large sales.
q.r: Less expensive per customer reached. Direct mail can reach many targeted customers for the cost of printing and postage, so it usually costs less per person reached than sending a salesperson. Personal selling, however, is more personal and interactive, lets the salesperson answer questions on the spot, and is generally more effective at closing large or complex sales. Those three strengths belong to personal selling, not direct mail.
w: A printed mailer cannot talk with the customer, so personal selling, with its face-to-face conversation, is the more personal and interactive method.
A salesperson can answer questions on the spot, while a piece of mail cannot respond to anything the reader wants to know.
Large, complex sales usually need a salesperson to handle questions and concerns, which makes personal selling stronger than mail at closing them.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Many startups use email and targeted social media messages for direct marketing mainly because these channels are
o: the most personal form of promotion.
q.r: Affordable and easy to measure. Email and targeted social media messages cost relatively little compared with print and broadcast options, and online tools make it easy to count opens, clicks and orders. These channels are not exempt from regulation; email marketing, for example, must follow the federal CAN-SPAM Act. Personal selling, not email, is the most personal form of promotion, and spam filters and ad blockers can keep messages from being seen.
w: Email and social media marketing must still follow advertising laws, such as the federal CAN-SPAM Act, so they are not exempt from regulation.
Personal selling, with its face-to-face contact, is the most personal form of promotion, not email or targeted social media posts.
Spam filters and ad blockers often stop these messages from being seen, so getting around them is not a reason startups choose these channels.

q.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
q.s: Before Vista Home Solar calls consumers to promote its solar panels, it checks their phone numbers against the National Do Not Call Registry. This step helps the company
q.r: Comply with telemarketing rules. Telemarketing is a direct-marketing channel, and businesses that call consumers must follow federal rules, including honoring the National Do Not Call Registry managed by the Federal Trade Commission. Checking numbers first keeps the company compliant and avoids penalties and ill will. The step does not set a budget, it does not generate news coverage, and it does not group customers by lifestyle.
w: Checking phone numbers against a do-not-call list does not decide how much money the company will spend on advertising.
Publicity comes from media coverage, and screening phone numbers before calling has nothing to do with getting a news story.
Segmenting by lifestyle groups customers by interests and habits, while this step only removes people who asked not to get sales calls.

q.pt: Identify the elements of the promotional mix
q.s: A local TV station airs a news segment about Spark Robotics Academy after its students win a regional competition. Spark did not pay for the story. Spark is receiving
q.r: Publicity. Publicity is unpaid, nonpersonal coverage of a business, such as a news story, that the media choose to run. Spark did not pay for the segment and does not control what is said. Advertising is paid, nonpersonal promotion from an identified sponsor, sales promotion uses short-term incentives such as coupons, and personal selling is person-to-person communication with customers.
w: Advertising is promotion that a sponsor pays for, but Spark did not pay for this news segment and could not control what it said.
Sales promotion uses short-term incentives like coupons or contests, while Spark simply received a free news story about its students' win.
Personal selling is person-to-person communication with customers, not a TV news story the station chose to run on its own.

q.pt: Identify the elements of the promotional mix
q.s: Which element of the promotional mix uses short-term incentives, such as free samples and contests, to encourage immediate buying?
q.r: Sales promotion. Sales promotion includes short-term incentives, such as coupons, samples, contests, premiums and displays, that encourage customers to buy right away. It covers promotional activities other than advertising, personal selling and publicity. Publicity is unpaid media coverage, public relations builds long-term goodwill, and advertising is a paid, nonpersonal message from an identified sponsor that does not by itself offer an incentive.
w: Publicity is unpaid media coverage of a business, and it does not offer customers samples or contests to get them to buy right away.
Public relations builds long-term goodwill with the public, rather than using short-term incentives to spur immediate purchases.
Advertising is a paid message from an identified sponsor; by itself it does not hand out free samples or run contests to trigger quick buying.

q.pt: Identify the elements of the promotional mix
q.s: Haven Kitchens, a startup that designs custom kitchen remodels, needs to answer each homeowner's questions face-to-face and help them decide to buy. Which element of the promotional mix should it rely on most?
q.r: Personal selling. Personal selling is direct, person-to-person communication in which a salesperson learns each customer's needs, answers questions and helps the customer decide to buy, which suits expensive, customized purchases such as kitchen remodels. Publicity is unpaid media coverage that the business does not control. Online advertising is paid, nonpersonal promotion that cannot answer individual questions. Sales promotion uses short-term incentives, such as coupons, to encourage immediate buying.
w: Publicity is unpaid media coverage that Haven Kitchens cannot control, and it cannot answer each homeowner's questions in person.
Online advertising is a paid, one-way message to many people, so it cannot answer each homeowner's individual questions face-to-face.
Sales promotion offers short-term incentives like coupons, which do not give homeowners the face-to-face guidance a custom remodel requires.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: What is the main advantage of television advertising?
o: It is the least expensive medium available
Ads can be changed overnight at no cost
Viewers cannot skip or avoid the ads
Sight, sound and motion make it memorable
q.r: Sight, sound and motion make it memorable. Television combines sight, sound and motion, so ads can demonstrate products and create memorable, believable messages that reach large audiences. Television is one of the most expensive media because of production and airtime costs, changing an ad requires new production work, and viewers can skip, mute or ignore commercials with streaming services and recording devices.
w: Television is one of the most expensive media because of production and airtime costs, so low cost is not its main advantage.
Changing a TV ad usually means new production work and expense, so quick, free changes are not something television offers.
Viewers can mute, skip or record past commercials, especially with streaming, so TV ads are easy to avoid.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: A startup that sells gourmet cooking tools wants to advertise on television but reach mainly cooking enthusiasts. Which advertising medium best meets this goal?
q.r: Cable television. Cable television offers specialized channels, such as food and cooking networks, so advertisers can reach special markets with shared interests. That makes it ideal for a startup targeting cooking enthusiasts. Network television reaches broad, general audiences, outdoor billboards reach everyone who passes a location, and daily newspapers reach general local readers rather than a specific interest group.
w: Network television reaches broad, general audiences, so the startup would pay to reach many viewers who have no interest in cooking.
Billboards are not television at all, and they reach everyone who passes by rather than focusing on cooking enthusiasts.
Daily newspapers reach general local readers and are not television, so they miss the startup's goal of reaching cooking fans through TV.

q.pt: Explain types of advertising media
q.s: Ad-blocking software creates a challenge for advertisers because it
o: keeps digital ads from appearing to users.
raises the price of television commercials.
blocks radio signals in some areas.
q.r: Keeps digital ads from appearing to users. Ad blockers are programs that stop many digital ads, such as pop-ups and banner ads, from appearing in a user's browser or apps. Similarly, spam filters keep unwanted email from reaching inboxes. Advertisers must find other ways, such as content and social media, to reach these users. Ad blockers do not affect television prices, printed magazines or radio signals.
w: Ad blockers are software for browsers and apps, so they have no effect on what TV networks charge for commercials.
Ad-blocking software works only on screens, so it cannot remove ads that are printed on paper in magazines.
Ad blockers filter digital ads on devices; they do not interfere with radio broadcasts or signals.

q.pt: Identify communications channels used in sales promotion
q.s: Pinnacle Blenders offers buyers $20 back if they upload their receipt to the company's website after making a purchase. This sales promotion is a
q.r: Rebate. A rebate is a partial refund that a manufacturer or seller gives a customer after the purchase is made, usually after the customer submits proof of purchase. A coupon reduces the price at the time of purchase, a premium is a free or low-cost item given with a purchase, and a sweepstakes is a game of chance in which entrants can win prizes.
w: A coupon lowers the price at the moment of purchase, but Pinnacle gives the $20 back only after the buyer submits a receipt.
A premium is a free or low-cost item given with a purchase, while Pinnacle is returning part of the purchase price in cash.
A sweepstakes is a game of chance with prizes, but every Pinnacle buyer who uploads a receipt gets the $20, so no luck is involved.

q.pt: Identify communications channels used in sales promotion
q.s: A sports-drink startup pays a mobile game developer to show its logo and bottles throughout a popular racing game. This sales promotion channel is called
q.r: Advergaming. Advergaming is placing brands, products or advertising messages inside video games, where players see them repeatedly while they play. It is especially useful for reaching younger audiences. Sampling gives customers a free trial size of a product, couponing offers a price reduction at purchase, and telemarketing is a direct-marketing method that uses phone calls to reach customers.
w: Sampling hands customers a free trial size of a product, but the startup is placing its logo and bottles inside a mobile game.
Couponing gives buyers a price cut at purchase, while this startup is paying to have its brand shown throughout a racing game.
Telemarketing uses phone calls to reach customers, which has nothing to do with putting a brand inside a video game.

q.pt: Identify communications channels used in sales promotion
q.s: When a manufacturer offers coupons and free samples directly to consumers so that their demand draws the product through stores, it is using a __________ strategy.
q.r: Pull. A pull strategy aims promotion at final consumers so that their demand pulls the product through the channel of distribution, leading retailers to stock it. Consumer sales promotions such as coupons and samples support a pull strategy. A push strategy aims promotion at channel members, often through trade shows and trade allowances, while trade and channel are not names of promotional strategies in this sense.
w: A push strategy aims promotion at stores and other channel members, but these coupons and samples go straight to consumers.
Trade promotions target retailers and wholesalers, and 'trade' is not the name of the strategy that builds consumer demand with coupons and samples.
Every product moves through a channel, so 'channel' does not name the strategy of building consumer demand to draw products through stores.

q.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
q.s: Evergreen Organics runs ads describing its commitment to sustainable farming without mentioning any specific product. This is an example of __________ promotion.
q.r: Institutional. Institutional promotion builds the image and goodwill of a business itself rather than selling specific goods or services. Ads about a company's commitment to sustainable farming promote the organization as a whole. Product promotion focuses on particular goods or services, point-of-purchase promotion uses in-store displays and signs to sell products, and direct promotion is aimed at individual customers to get a measurable response.
w: Product promotion focuses on selling specific goods, but Evergreen's ads describe its farming values without mentioning any product.
Point-of-purchase promotion uses displays and signs in stores to sell products, not ads about a company's commitment to sustainable farming.
Direct promotion targets individual customers to get a measurable response, while Evergreen's ads build its overall image with a broad audience.

q.pt: Describe word-of-mouth channels used to communicate with targeted audiences
q.s: Beacon Bike Rentals gives customers a free hour of riding for every friend they bring in who rents a bike. Beacon is encouraging customers to promote the business through
q.r: Word-of-mouth. Word-of-mouth is communication about a product passed from person to person, and a referral program rewards customers for spreading it. Because the message comes from a trusted friend rather than the business, it is highly credible. Telemarketing uses phone calls from the business, publicity is unpaid media coverage, and advertising is a paid message from an identified sponsor.
w: Telemarketing means the business itself phones potential customers, but Beacon is rewarding customers for bringing friends in.
Publicity is unpaid coverage by news media, while Beacon's referral reward gets customers, not reporters, to spread the word.
Advertising is a paid message from the business itself, but here customers are recommending Beacon to their friends.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: Lakeshore Outfitters, a startup, sells kayaks, paddles, life jackets, camping tents and guided river trips. Taken together, everything the company offers is its
q.r: Product mix. A product mix is all the goods and services a business makes or sells. Lakeshore's kayaks, gear, tents and guided trips together form its product mix, which is organized into product lines. A product line is only one group of closely related products, such as paddling gear. A product item is one specific version of a product. The promotional mix is the combination of promotional activities a business uses, not the products it sells.
w: A product line is just one group of closely related products, such as paddling gear, not everything Lakeshore offers.
The promotional mix is the set of ways a business promotes itself, like advertising, not the goods and services it sells.
A product item is one specific product, such as a single kayak model, rather than the full set of everything Lakeshore offers.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: After reviewing a year of sales, Priya decides her candle shop will stop selling seasonal wreaths and discontinue two slow-selling candle scents. Priya is using the product-mix strategy of
q.r: Contraction. Contraction is a product-mix strategy in which a business drops product lines or product items, usually because they sell slowly or earn little profit. Dropping the wreath line and two scents lets Priya focus on her best sellers. Expansion is the opposite: adding lines or items. Trading up means adding higher-priced, higher-quality products. Alteration means improving existing products rather than removing them.
w: Expansion means adding products, but Priya is dropping wreaths and two candle scents from her shop.
Trading up means adding higher-priced, higher-quality products, while Priya is removing slow sellers rather than adding anything.
Alteration means improving products a business keeps selling, but Priya is discontinuing products instead of changing them.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: Owen's food truck sells three kinds of tacos. Because customers keep asking for more choices, he adds a fish taco and a vegetarian taco to the menu. Which product-mix strategy is Owen using?
q.r: Expansion. Expansion is a product-mix strategy of adding new product lines or adding items to an existing line. Owen added two items to his taco line, which increases the depth of his product mix. Contraction would remove items. Trading down would add lower-priced products to attract bargain hunters. Alteration would change existing tacos, such as a new recipe, rather than add new ones.
w: Contraction means dropping products, but Owen is adding a fish taco and a vegetarian taco to his menu.
Trading down means adding lower-priced products to attract bargain hunters, and Owen is adding choices because customers asked, not to cut prices.
Alteration means changing products already sold, such as a new recipe, but Owen is adding two new tacos.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a product line:
q.r: All of a bakery's cupcakes. A product line is a group of closely related products, such as all of the cupcakes a bakery offers. One mint chocolate cupcake is a product item, a single specific version within the line. Every product a bakery sells is its product mix, which is made up of several lines. A logo and slogan are elements of the bakery's brand, not products.
w: One mint chocolate cupcake is a product item, a single specific version within the cupcake line, not the whole line.
Every product a bakery sells is its product mix, which is made up of several product lines rather than being just one line.
A logo and slogan belong to the bakery's brand identity; they are not products the bakery sells at all.

q.pt: Explain the concept of product mix
q.s: The number of different product lines a business offers is the __________ of its product mix.
q.r: Width. The width of a product mix is the number of product lines a business carries. Depth is the number of product items within each line, such as the sizes and flavors offered. Consistency describes how closely related the product lines are in use, production or distribution. Volume refers to the quantity of goods produced or sold, not the structure of the product mix.
w: Depth counts the items within each line, such as sizes and flavors, not the number of different product lines.
Consistency describes how closely related the product lines are, not how many lines the business offers.
Volume is the quantity of goods produced or sold, which says nothing about how many different product lines a business carries.

q.pt: Plan product mix
q.s: Marcus owns a small shop that sells bicycles, bike helmets and repair services. He wants to add one new product that fits his current product mix. Which product should he choose?
q.r: Bike locks and lights. When planning the product mix, an entrepreneur should choose new items that are compatible with the current product lines. Locks and lights serve the same customers, are used with the products Marcus already sells and can be displayed and sold by his staff. Patio furniture, video game consoles and houseplants would attract different customers, require different knowledge and make the product mix less consistent.
w: Patio furniture would attract different customers and require different knowledge than Marcus's bike business, so it does not fit his product mix.
Video game consoles have no connection to bicycles, so they would not serve Marcus's current customers or fit his shop's mix.
Houseplants have nothing to do with bikes and would need different care and expertise, making Marcus's product mix less consistent.

q.pt: Plan product mix
q.s: Bennett's Bike Shop, known for affordable family bikes, begins carrying premium carbon-fiber racing bikes to attract serious cyclists. Bennett's is
q.r: Trading up. Trading up is adding higher-priced, higher-quality products to the product mix to attract customers who want prestige or superior performance. Premium racing bikes are well above Bennett's usual price range. Trading down is the opposite, adding lower-priced products. Contracting the mix means dropping products, and altering existing products means changing products already in the mix.
w: Trading down means adding lower-priced products, but Bennett's is adding premium racing bikes priced well above its usual family bikes.
Contracting the product mix means dropping products, while Bennett's is adding a new line of racing bikes.
Altering products means changing items already sold, but Bennett's is bringing in new carbon-fiber racing bikes rather than changing its family bikes.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: A fair price is one that
o: satisfies both the buyer and the seller.
is the lowest price available anywhere in the market.
covers the seller's costs exactly and earns no profit.
is set for the product by government regulators.
q.r: Satisfies both the buyer and the seller. A fair price is one the buyer is willing to pay and the seller is willing to accept: the customer believes the product is worth the money, and the business earns enough to make the sale worthwhile. A fair price does not have to be the lowest available price. A business needs profit to survive, so breaking even is not the test. Government sets prices only in rare, regulated situations.
w: A fair price does not have to be the lowest anywhere; it just needs to be one the buyer will pay and the seller will accept.
Breaking even leaves the seller with no profit, and a business needs profit to survive, so that price would not satisfy the seller.
Government sets prices only in rare, regulated cases, so fairness depends on buyer and seller agreeing, not on regulators.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: The overall goals that a business wants to accomplish through its pricing decisions are its
q.r: Pricing objectives. Pricing objectives are the overall goals that guide a business's pricing decisions, such as earning a certain profit, increasing sales or market share, or matching competitors. Pricing policies are general guidelines, such as whether to offer discounts, that help carry out the objectives. Price lines are a set of distinct price points for related products. Pricing tactics are short-term moves, such as a weekend sale.
w: Pricing policies are general guidelines, such as whether to give discounts, that help carry out the overall goals rather than being the goals themselves.
Price lines are a set of distinct price points for related products, not the overall goals behind pricing decisions.
Pricing tactics are short-term moves like a weekend sale, while the question asks about the broad goals that guide pricing.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: When an entrepreneur sets the price of a new product, the most basic requirement is that the price must
o: be lower than every competitor's price.
stay the same for the life of the product.
be one at which the product will sell.
be identical in every market the business serves.
q.r: Be one at which the product will sell. A price that customers will not pay produces no sales, no matter how carefully it was calculated, so the most basic test of a price is whether the product will sell at it while the business covers its costs over time. A price does not have to be the lowest in the market. Prices often change over a product's life and may differ from one market to another.
w: A new product does not have to undercut every rival; many businesses charge more because of quality or service and still sell well.
Prices often change over a product's life as costs, competition and demand shift, so staying the same is not a basic requirement.
Businesses often charge different prices in different markets, so an identical price everywhere is not the most basic requirement.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: Pricing is an important marketing function for a small business because the price of a product directly affects the business's
q.r: Sales revenue and profit. Revenue equals the price of each unit times the number of units sold, so price directly determines how much money comes in and whether the business earns a profit. Price also affects how customers judge a product's value. The legal form of ownership, the organizational chart and the business name are management decisions that pricing does not directly determine.
w: The legal form of ownership, such as a partnership or corporation, is chosen when a business is organized, not determined by its prices.
An organizational chart shows who reports to whom, which a product's price does not directly change.
A business name is a branding and legal choice, and the price of a product has no direct effect on it.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: A tutoring service charges a session fee, a landlord charges rent and a bank charges interest on loans. Each of these terms is another name for
q.r: Price. Price is the value, usually stated in money, that a buyer gives and a seller accepts in exchange for a good or service. It goes by many names, including fees, rent, interest, tuition, fares and premiums. Profit is the money left after expenses are subtracted from revenue. Cost is what the seller spends to make or buy a product. Revenue is the total income the seller receives from sales.
w: Profit is the money left after expenses are subtracted from revenue, not the amount a customer pays for tutoring, rent or a loan.
Cost is what the seller spends to provide a product, while fees, rent and interest are what buyers pay the seller.
Revenue is all the income a seller takes in from many sales, whereas a fee, rent or interest charge is the price of one exchange.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: A late frost destroyed much of the region's strawberry crop just as demand for local strawberries reached its peak. Farm stands raised their strawberry prices. Which factor affected this pricing decision?
q.r: Supply and demand. When supply falls short and demand stays high, buyers compete for the limited product and prices rise. The frost created a shortage at the same time customers wanted strawberries most. Government regulation would involve a law or agency limiting prices. Industry standards are customary pricing practices, such as a traditional markup. Promotional costs are expenses of advertising and selling, which did not change here.
w: Government regulation would mean a law or agency limiting prices, but here a frost caused a shortage while demand was high.
Industry standards are customary pricing practices, like a usual markup, and they do not explain a price jump caused by a crop shortage.
Promotional costs are advertising and selling expenses, which did not change; the frost cut supply while demand peaked.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: Tessa prices the merchandise in her new gift shop by applying the same percentage markup that gift shops traditionally use. Tessa is basing her prices on
q.r: Industry standards. Many industries have customary markups or pricing practices that businesses follow, and entrepreneurs often use them as a starting point when they set prices. Tessa is using the markup traditional in her trade. Elastic demand describes how sharply demand reacts to price changes. Government regulations are laws that limit pricing. A sales-oriented objective aims to grow sales or market share, often with low prices.
w: Elastic demand describes how strongly customers react to price changes, but Tessa is simply copying the markup gift shops traditionally use.
Government regulations are laws that limit pricing, while Tessa is following a customary markup used throughout her trade.
A sales-oriented objective aims to grow sales or market share, often through low prices, but Tessa is just applying her industry's usual markup.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: When Coastline Car Wash raised its basic wash price by $1, many customers switched to a competitor down the street, and Coastline's sales dropped sharply. Demand for Coastline's car wash is
q.r: Elastic. Demand is elastic when a small change in price causes a large change in the quantity customers buy. Car washes have close substitutes nearby, so customers switch when the price rises. Inelastic demand changes very little when price changes, as with necessities that have few substitutes. Derived demand is business demand that comes from consumer demand for another product. Joint demand exists when two products are used together.
w: Inelastic demand barely changes when price rises, but Coastline lost many customers over just a $1 increase.
Derived demand is business demand that comes from consumer demand for another product, which does not describe drivers switching car washes.
Joint demand exists when two products are used together, and the question is about customers leaving after one price increase.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a profit-oriented pricing objective:
o: Increasing the business's market share by 5%
Keeping prices equal to competitors' prices
Selling 1,000 more units than last year
q.r: Earning a 20% return on investment. Profit-oriented pricing objectives focus on profit, such as maximizing profit or earning a target return on the money invested in the business. Increasing market share and selling more units are sales-oriented objectives because they focus on sales volume. Keeping prices equal to competitors' prices is a status quo, or competition-oriented, objective that aims to avoid price wars.
w: Growing market share is a sales-oriented objective because it focuses on how much the business sells compared with rivals, not on profit.
Matching competitors' prices is a status quo objective meant to avoid price wars, not a goal focused on earning profit.
Selling 1,000 more units is a sales-oriented objective about volume, and it does not say how much profit those sales should earn.

q.pt: Explain factors affecting pricing decisions
q.s: Dana buys handmade mugs for $12.00 each. She adds the 40% markup on cost that is standard for gift shops. What selling price will Dana set for each mug?
q.r: $16.80. A markup on cost is calculated by multiplying the cost by the markup percentage and adding the result to the cost: $12.00 × 0.40 = $4.80, and $12.00 + $4.80 = $16.80. The $4.80 figure is only the markup, not the price. The $20.00 figure results from dividing $12.00 by 0.60, which treats the markup as a percentage of the retail price. The $12.40 figure adds 40 cents instead of 40%.
w: $4.80 is only the markup ($12.00 x 0.40); Dana must add it to the $12.00 cost to get the selling price of $16.80.
$20.00 comes from dividing $12.00 by 0.60, which treats the 40% as a markup on the retail price instead of on cost.
$12.40 adds just 40 cents to the cost instead of 40% of $12.00, which is $4.80.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Every channel of distribution starts with the __________ and ends with the final user.
q.r: Producer. A channel of distribution is the path a product and its ownership take from the producer, who makes or grows it, to the final user, who may be an ultimate consumer or an industrial user. Wholesalers, retailers and agents are intermediaries. They may appear in the middle of a channel, but no channel begins with them, and some channels are direct and use no intermediaries at all.
w: A wholesaler is a middleman that buys from producers, so it sits in the middle of a channel and never starts one.
A retailer sells to final users near the end of a channel, so it cannot be where every channel begins.
An agent helps producers sell without owning the goods, so it appears in the middle of some channels, not at the start of all of them.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Kiran represents several small furniture makers. He finds stores to sell their tables and chairs and earns a commission on each sale, but he never owns the furniture. Kiran is
q.r: An agent. An agent is an intermediary who helps producers buy or sell products, usually for a commission, but does not take title to, or ownership of, the goods. Kiran works on behalf of the furniture makers. A wholesaler buys large quantities and owns the goods before reselling them. A retailer buys products to resell to ultimate consumers. An industrial user buys products for use in its own operations.
w: A wholesaler buys large quantities and owns the goods before reselling them, but Kiran never owns the furniture he helps sell.
A retailer buys products and resells them to consumers, while Kiran only connects furniture makers with stores for a commission.
An industrial user buys products to use in its own operations, but Kiran sells furniture on behalf of the makers.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: By placing large orders with producers and handling distribution to many stores, wholesalers help producers
q.r: Lower their per-unit costs. Large orders allow producers to manufacture in big batches, which spreads fixed costs over more units, and producers can sell to a few wholesalers instead of many small stores. Products still must be transported, often by the wholesaler at a cost. Retailers set their own prices. Producers still need to promote their products so that customers ask for them.
w: Products must still be moved from producers to stores, and wholesalers often pay for that shipping, so transportation costs do not disappear.
Retailers decide the prices they charge shoppers, so wholesalers do not set retail prices for the stores.
Producers still need to promote their products so customers ask for them, even when wholesalers handle distribution.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Which of the following is an example of an industrial user:
o: A family buying mulch for its backyard garden
A landscaper buying mulch for clients' yards
A garden center buying mulch to resell to shoppers
A distributor buying truckloads of mulch for garden centers
q.r: A landscaper buying mulch for clients' yards. An industrial user is a business or organization that buys goods or services to use in its operations or to make other products. The landscaping company uses the mulch to provide its service. A family buying for its own garden is an ultimate consumer. The garden center is a retailer, and the distributor is a wholesaler, because both buy to resell.
w: A family buying mulch for its own garden is an ultimate consumer, using the product personally rather than in a business.
A garden center buys mulch to resell to shoppers, which makes it a retailer, not a business that uses the mulch itself.
A distributor buys truckloads to resell to garden centers, which makes it a wholesaler rather than a user of the mulch.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Jasmine sells her handmade soaps only through her own website and ships them straight to customers' homes. Jasmine is using a(n) __________ channel of distribution.
q.r: Direct. In a direct channel of distribution, the producer sells straight to the final user with no intermediaries. Jasmine makes the soap and sells it to consumers herself. An indirect channel uses one or more intermediaries, such as wholesalers or retailers, between the producer and the final user. Agent and wholesale channels are both kinds of indirect channels because they include an intermediary.
w: An indirect channel includes middlemen like wholesalers or stores, but Jasmine sells and ships straight to her customers herself.
An agent channel uses a middleman who helps sell the goods, while Jasmine has no one between her and her customers.
A wholesale channel sends products through a wholesaler before they reach customers, but Jasmine sells directly through her own website.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
q.s: Midstate Supply buys large quantities of school supplies from manufacturers, stores them in its warehouse and resells them to office supply stores. Midstate is a(n)
q.r: Wholesaler. A wholesaler is an intermediary that buys goods in large quantities from producers, takes ownership of them and resells them to retailers, other intermediaries or business users. Midstate buys from manufacturers and sells to stores. A retailer sells to ultimate consumers. An agent helps sell goods without owning them. An industrial user buys products to use in its own operations rather than to resell.
w: A retailer sells to final consumers, but Midstate sells its supplies to office supply stores, not to shoppers.
An agent helps sell goods without owning them, but Midstate buys the supplies, owns them and stores them in its warehouse.
An industrial user buys products to use in its own operations, while Midstate buys school supplies in order to resell them.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of channel management
q.s: Brightway Snacks gives the grocery stores that carry its granola bars free display racks and coupons that the stores feature in their weekly flyers. Brightway and the grocers are sharing the channel activity of
q.r: Promoting products. Channel members share distribution activities, and promotion is one of them. When a producer supplies displays and coupons that retailers feature in their own flyers, both members work together to build customer interest and sales. Financing involves providing credit to make purchases possible. Storing inventory means holding goods until they are needed. Transporting means physically moving goods from one place to another.
w: Financing means providing credit so purchases can happen, but Brightway is supplying display racks and coupons to boost customer interest.
Storing inventory means holding goods until they are needed, which is not what free racks and flyer coupons do.
Transporting means physically moving goods from place to place, while displays and coupons are tools to promote the granola bars.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of channel management
q.s: Channel members add value to products mainly by
o: raising the selling price of every product.
changing the designs of the products they handle.
q.r: Performing distribution tasks efficiently. Intermediaries specialize in activities such as buying, selling, storing, transporting, financing and promoting, so they can often do these jobs better and more cheaply than producers could alone. Higher prices do not add value by themselves. Channel members usually do not redesign products. Every channel begins with a producer, so intermediaries cannot replace producers.
w: Charging more does not add value by itself; intermediaries add value by doing distribution jobs well and at lower cost.
