Intermediaries usually handle products as they are made, so redesigning products is not how they add value.
Every channel starts with a producer, so intermediaries cannot replace producers; they add value by handling distribution tasks.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of channel management
q.s: Coordinating the activities of the businesses in a channel of distribution so that products flow smoothly to customers is called
q.r: Channel management. Channel management is the process of planning, coordinating and controlling the activities of channel members so that products reach customers efficiently. Risk management deals with reducing and handling possible losses. Product planning decides which goods and services to offer. Market research gathers and analyzes information about markets and customers to support marketing decisions.
w: Risk management focuses on reducing and handling possible losses, not on coordinating channel members so products flow to customers.
Product planning decides which goods and services to offer, not how the businesses in a channel work together to move them.
Market research gathers information about customers and markets, but it does not coordinate the businesses that move products to customers.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channel strategies
q.s: Which of the following businesses is most likely to use exclusive distribution:
o: A maker of large farm combines
A maker of sugar-free chewing gum
A company that bottles spring water
q.r: A maker of large farm combines. Exclusive distribution is a channel strategy that places a product with only one dealer in a given area. It fits expensive, specialized products that require expert selling, service and parts support, such as farm combines. Chewing gum, bottled water and paper towels are low-priced convenience goods that customers buy often and expect to find everywhere, so they call for intensive distribution.
w: Chewing gum is a cheap item people buy often and expect to find everywhere, so it calls for intensive distribution, not one dealer per area.
Bottled spring water is a low-priced convenience good customers want in many stores, which fits intensive rather than exclusive distribution.
Paper towels are inexpensive items bought frequently in many stores, so limiting them to one dealer per area would hurt sales.

q.pt: Select channels of distribution
q.s: A bakery that sells fresh bread to local stores usually uses a short channel of distribution because the product is
q.r: Perishable. Perishable products spoil quickly, so they need to reach consumers fast. A short channel, with few or no intermediaries, moves fresh bread to stores while it is still fresh. Low production cost does not require a short channel. Products sold nationally often use longer channels to reach distant markets. Standardized products that keep well can travel through longer channels without losing value.
w: A low production cost does not require a short channel; the bakery needs speed because fresh bread goes stale quickly.
Products sold nationally often use longer channels to reach distant markets, and this bakery sells fresh bread to local stores.
Standardized products that keep well can travel through long channels, but fresh bread spoils, which is why a short channel fits.

q.pt: Select channels of distribution
q.s: Fizzle Pop, a startup, makes a low-priced soft drink that customers buy often and with little shopping effort. Which distribution approach should Fizzle Pop use?
q.r: Intensive distribution. Intensive distribution places a product in as many suitable outlets as possible. It fits convenience goods, such as soft drinks, that customers buy often and expect to find wherever they shop. Selective distribution uses a limited number of outlets and suits shopping goods. Exclusive distribution uses one dealer per area and suits expensive, specialized goods. Selling only directly would sharply limit where customers could buy.
w: Selective distribution uses a limited number of outlets and suits shopping goods, but customers expect to find a cheap soft drink everywhere.
Exclusive distribution gives one dealer per area and suits expensive, specialized goods, not a low-priced drink people buy often.
Selling only directly would greatly limit where people could buy Fizzle Pop, while a drink bought often needs to be in many stores.

q.pt: Select channels of distribution
q.s: Northwind Audio sells its mid-priced headphones only through a few carefully chosen electronics stores in each city. Northwind is using
q.r: Selective distribution. Selective distribution places a product in a limited number of carefully chosen outlets in each area. It suits shopping goods, such as headphones, that customers compare before buying. Intensive distribution would place the headphones in as many outlets as possible. Exclusive distribution would use only one dealer per area. Direct distribution would mean Northwind sells straight to consumers with no stores in between.
w: Intensive distribution would put the headphones in as many stores as possible, but Northwind uses only a few chosen stores in each city.
Exclusive distribution would use just one dealer per area, while Northwind sells through several stores in each city.
Direct distribution would mean Northwind sells straight to consumers, but it uses electronics stores as middlemen.

q.pt: Explain the nature of channel strategies
q.s: Peak Threads, a small apparel startup, sells through its own website, a weekend pop-up shop and several independent boutiques. Peak Threads is using a __________ strategy.
q.r: Multichannel distribution. A multichannel distribution strategy reaches customers through two or more channels at the same time, such as online sales, the company's own shop and independent retailers. It helps a startup reach different customer groups. A single-channel strategy would use only one path to customers. Exclusive distribution limits a product to one dealer per area. Contraction is a product-mix strategy, not a channel strategy.
w: A single-channel strategy uses only one path to customers, but Peak Threads sells through its website, a pop-up shop and boutiques.
Exclusive distribution limits a product to one dealer per area, while Peak Threads reaches customers through several different channels.
Contraction is a product-mix strategy of dropping products, so it does not describe how Peak Threads reaches its customers.

q.pt: Evaluate channel members
q.s: Lena's company ships its organic sauces to stores through two regional distributors. To decide which distributor to keep, Lena should mainly compare the distributors'
o: advertising budgets for their own businesses.
number of employees in their offices.
costs and service to her retail customers.
q.r: Costs and service to her retail customers. When evaluating channel members, a producer looks mainly at cost efficiency and customer service: how much it costs to use the member and how well the member delivers, handles orders and supports the stores that buy the product. A distributor's own advertising budget, its distance from the owner's home and the size of its office staff do not show how well it serves the channel.
w: How much a distributor spends promoting its own business does not show how well or how cheaply it serves Lena's retail customers.
The distance from Lena's home has nothing to do with how well a distributor serves stores or what it costs to use.
Having more office employees does not prove better service; Lena should judge each distributor on its costs and how well it serves her stores.

q.pt: Explain the role of customer service in positioning/image
q.s: The owner of a new boutique hotel wants every employee to understand the level of service guests should receive. What is the best way for the owner to communicate this expectation?
o: Post the standards on the hotel's website only
Let each employee decide how to serve guests
Reduce the number of front-desk employees
Train staff on its service standards
q.r: Train staff on its service standards. Training employees is how management communicates the level of service it expects and gives employees the skills to deliver it consistently, which builds the hotel's image. Posting standards online informs guests but does not prepare employees. Letting each employee decide leads to inconsistent service. Cutting front-desk staff would likely lower service levels.
w: Posting standards on the website tells guests what to expect, but it does not prepare employees to deliver that service.
Letting each employee decide leads to uneven service from guest to guest, which defeats the owner's goal of a shared standard.
Cutting front-desk staff would likely lower service levels and does nothing to communicate what service guests should receive.

q.pt: Explain the role of customer service in positioning/image
q.s: When should the manager of a busy downtown café schedule more employees to work?
o: When the café is designing a new logo
When sales are slower than usual
q.r: During expected busy periods. Customer service affects a business's image, and long waits during rush periods hurt that image. Scheduling more employees when demand for service is expected to be high, such as lunch hours or local events, keeps service fast and friendly. Designing a logo does not create a need for more staff. Slow periods call for fewer employees, and staffing should match customer demand rather than employee requests.
w: Designing a new logo is a branding task that does not bring in more customers to serve, so it creates no need for extra staff.
Slow sales periods have fewer customers, so the café would need fewer employees then, not more.
Staffing should match customer demand; scheduling extra people just because employees want hours could leave the café overstaffed at slow times.

q.pt: Explain the role of customer service in positioning/image
q.s: Slice House lets customers order pizza through an app and pay at the table with a tablet, so they wait less and leave faster. Slice House is using __________ to improve its customer service.
q.r: Technology. Businesses use technology, such as online ordering, mobile apps and tablet payment, to make service faster, more accurate and more convenient, which strengthens the business's image. Price discounts lower what customers pay but do not speed service. Intermediaries are channel members, such as wholesalers. Product-mix contraction is the strategy of dropping product lines or items.
w: Price discounts lower what customers pay, but Slice House's app and tablets make service faster, not cheaper.
Intermediaries are channel members like wholesalers, and ordering apps and table tablets are not middlemen.
Product-mix contraction means dropping products, while Slice House is adding ordering and payment tools to speed up service.

q.pt: Determine services to provide customers
q.s: When deciding which customer services to offer, such as delivery or gift wrapping, a startup should first consider
o: which services are cheapest to provide.
which services the owner enjoys most.
q.r: What its target customers value. Services add value only when customers want them, so a business starts by learning its target market's expectations and then chooses services that meet them at a reasonable cost. Competitors' prices and the cost of each service matter later in the decision, but they do not show whether customers want the service. The owner's personal preferences are not a sound basis for the decision.
w: A competitor's prices matter later, but they do not show whether this startup's own customers want delivery or gift wrapping.
Cost matters once the startup knows which services customers want, but a cheap service adds no value if customers do not care about it.
The owner's personal preferences may not match what customers want, so they are not a sound basis for choosing services.

q.pt: Identify company's unique selling proposition
q.s: A business's unique selling proposition should answer which customer question?
o: How many years has the business been open?
Who owns the business and the building it uses?
Where does the company keep its extra inventory?
Why should I choose you over a competitor?
q.r: Why should I choose you over a competitor? A unique selling proposition (USP) states what makes the business or its product different from and better than the competition, such as lower prices, higher quality or special service. The age of the business, its ownership and the location of its inventory may be useful facts, but they do not explain the benefit that sets the business apart from competitors.
w: How long a business has been open may be a useful fact, but it does not explain what makes the business better than its competitors.
Who owns the business and its building does not tell customers what benefit sets the business apart from its competitors.
Where inventory is stored is an internal detail that does not give customers a reason to pick this business over a competitor.

q.pt: Identify company's unique selling proposition
q.s: Valley Tire's ads promise, "We will beat any competitor's price on the same tire, guaranteed." Valley's unique selling proposition is built mainly on its
q.r: Pricing strategy. A unique selling proposition can rest on price, quality, service, convenience or a special feature. Valley Tire sets itself apart by promising to beat competitors' prices, so its USP is based on its pricing strategy. The ad says nothing about the tires being better than others, about where the store is located or about teaching customers to use or maintain products.
w: Valley's ad promises to beat competitors' prices and says nothing about its tires being better made than others.
The ad does not mention where Valley's store is or how easy it is to reach; it focuses on beating competitors' prices.
Nothing in the ad is about teaching customers to use or care for tires; Valley stands out by promising lower prices.

q.pt: Identify company's unique selling proposition
q.s: Abby wants to sharpen her café's unique selling proposition but has little money for research. What is a low-cost way for her to learn more about her target market?
o: Ask employees who serve customers daily
Hire a national marketing research firm
Buy a month of television advertising
Lower all of her prices for a full month
q.r: Ask employees who serve customers daily. Front-line employees hear customers' comments and questions every day, so asking them, for example in a brainstorming session, is an inexpensive way to learn what customers value and what sets the café apart. A national research firm would be costly. Television advertising sends a message but does not gather information. Cutting prices changes sales but does not reveal why customers choose the café.
w: A national research firm would cost far more than Abby can afford, so it does not fit her need for a low-cost method.
TV advertising sends Abby's message out to viewers but gathers no information about her customers, and it is expensive.
Cutting prices might change sales, but it costs Abby money and still does not reveal why customers choose her café.

q.pt: Build corporate brands
q.s: Maya is building the corporate brand for her new home-cleaning company. Her brand promise should be based on
o: the slogan used by the market leader.
what it can deliver every time.
whatever customers most want to hear.
the lowest price available in the area.
q.r: What it can deliver every time. A brand promise is the benefit or experience a company commits to providing whenever customers deal with it. If the company cannot keep the promise, customers lose trust and the brand suffers. Copying a market leader's slogan does not set the company apart. Promising whatever customers want to hear invites broken promises. A low price is only one possible promise, and it may not be sustainable.
w: Copying the market leader's slogan would not set Maya's company apart and may promise something her business cannot deliver.
Promising whatever customers want to hear invites broken promises, which would make customers lose trust in Maya's brand.
A low price is only one possible promise, and Maya may not be able to sustain it every time, which could damage her brand.

q.pt: Build product/service brand
q.s: Rosa's sauce company uses the same name, logo, colors and recipe quality on every jar it sells. This consistency mainly helps the product's brand
q.r: Earn recognition and loyalty. A product brand is built when customers see the same name, look and quality every time, so they recognize the product quickly and trust it enough to buy it again. Even well-known brands still need promotion to stay in customers' minds. Consistency does not remove competitors from the market. Channel length depends on the product and the market, not on brand consistency.
w: Even well-known brands keep promoting to stay in customers' minds, so a consistent look does not make Rosa's promotion unnecessary.
Consistent branding helps customers recognize Rosa's sauce, but other sauce makers are still in the market competing for buyers.
How long a channel is depends on the product and market, so using the same name and logo does not shorten it.

q.pt: Create processes for ongoing opportunity recognition
q.s: To spot new business opportunities, Elan Tech forms a group of employees from sales, engineering, finance and customer support who meet monthly to share ideas. This group is a
q.r: Cross-functional team. A cross-functional team brings together employees from different departments so that problems and opportunities are viewed from many angles. This makes it a useful process for ongoing opportunity recognition. A focus group is a small group of customers who discuss a product for research purposes. A board of directors is elected to oversee a corporation. A sales team includes only salespeople.
w: A focus group is a small group of customers who discuss a product for research, but Elan's group is made up of its own employees.
A board of directors is elected to oversee a corporation, not a monthly idea-sharing group of employees from different departments.
A sales team includes only salespeople, while Elan's group mixes employees from sales, engineering, finance and customer support.

q.pt: Evaluate customer experience
q.s: The owner of a family restaurant visits tables to ask guests about their dining experience. What should she do while gathering this feedback?
o: Explain why any complaints are mistaken
Offer every guest a free dessert
Keep each conversation under ten seconds
q.r: Listen and ask follow-up questions. Evaluating the customer experience depends on accurate feedback. Active listening, which means giving full attention, asking questions and confirming understanding, shows guests that their opinions matter and uncovers useful details. Arguing with complaints discourages honest feedback. Free desserts may please guests but do not gather information. Rushing conversations prevents the owner from learning what guests really think.
w: Arguing that complaints are wrong discourages guests from being honest, which defeats the purpose of asking about their experience.
A free dessert might please guests, but it gathers no information about what they think of the restaurant.
Rushing through each conversation keeps the owner from hearing the details that would show what guests really think.

q.pt: Identify internal and external service standards
q.s: A software startup requires its support staff to respond to every customer email within two hours. This requirement is an example of a
q.r: Company-defined service standard. A company-defined, or internal, service standard is a measurable target the business sets for its own employees, such as a two-hour response time. Customer-defined, or external, standards are based on what customers say they expect. A warranty is a promise about a product's quality or performance. A pricing objective is a goal for pricing decisions.
w: A customer-defined standard is based on what customers say they expect, but this two-hour rule is a target the company set for its staff.
A warranty is a promise about a product's quality or performance, not a rule for how quickly staff must answer emails.
A pricing objective is a goal for pricing decisions and has nothing to do with how fast support staff reply to customers.

q.pt: Determine initial feasibility of product idea
q.s: Before investing in his idea for a mobile phone-repair van, Dev checks whether enough customers want the service and whether he can provide it at a profit. Dev is
q.r: Judging the idea's feasibility. Judging initial feasibility asks whether a product idea is likely to work: whether enough customers want it and whether the business can provide it profitably with available resources. Evaluating channel members means judging intermediaries such as wholesalers. Contracting a product mix means dropping products. Pricing objectives are goals that guide pricing decisions after the idea moves forward.
w: Evaluating channel members means judging middlemen like wholesalers, but Dev is checking whether his repair-van idea can work at all.
Contracting a product mix means dropping existing products, while Dev is checking whether a new idea is worth starting.
Pricing objectives are goals that guide prices once a business moves forward, but Dev is still testing whether customers want the service at all.

q.pt: Determine stakeholder expectations
q.s: Before opening a second location, Carla wants to learn what her investors expect the expansion to accomplish over the long term. Which question should she ask them?
o: Which vendor should supply the new furniture?
How much did the first location cost to open?
What problems should this project solve?
Who should work the register on opening day?
q.r: What problems should this project solve? Asking stakeholders what problems a project should solve reveals the long-term results they expect, which helps Carla set goals that match their expectations. Questions about furniture vendors and opening-day staffing deal with short-term operating details that Carla can decide herself. The cost of the first location is a past fact, not an expectation about the new project.
w: Choosing a furniture vendor is a short-term detail Carla can decide herself, and it does not reveal what investors expect the expansion to achieve.
The first location's cost is a fact from the past, not a view of what the investors hope the second location will accomplish.
Who works the register on opening day is a small staffing detail, not a question about the long-term results investors expect.

q.pt: Determine stakeholder expectations
q.s: Jada is launching a bookkeeping service for small businesses. A useful first step in learning what her future clients will expect from her is to
o: set her fees well below every competitor's.
wait until clients complain to ask questions.
copy a competitor's client contract word for word.
q.r: Read current industry trend information. Industry trends, such as new software, regulations and shifting client needs, signal what customers in a field will expect from a provider. Knowing them helps Jada plan services that meet those expectations. Low fees do not reveal what clients expect. Waiting for complaints means learning expectations only after failing to meet them. Copying a competitor's contract ignores her own clients' needs.
w: Setting very low fees is a pricing choice, and it tells Jada nothing about what her future clients expect from a bookkeeping service.
Waiting for complaints means Jada would learn what clients expect only after she has already let them down.
Copying another firm's contract word for word ignores the needs of Jada's own clients and does not help her learn their expectations.

q.pt: Determine stakeholder expectations
q.s: The most important part of managing stakeholder expectations is
o: promising every stakeholder the same results.
q.r: Understanding what each stakeholder expects. A business cannot meet, balance or adjust expectations it does not know, so understanding them comes first. Promising every group the same results ignores the fact that groups want different things. Limiting communication makes misunderstandings more likely. Owners are only one stakeholder group; customers, employees, lenders and others also have expectations that affect the business.
w: Different stakeholder groups want different things, so promising them all the same results ignores what each group actually expects.
Limiting communication makes it harder to learn what stakeholders want and makes misunderstandings more likely.
The owner is only one stakeholder; customers, employees, lenders and others also have expectations that affect the business.

q.pt: Determine stakeholder expectations
q.s: Employees of Greenleaf Grocers want stable schedules, customers want fair prices, and the bank wants its loan repaid on time. This shows that
o: all stakeholders expect the same things.
each group has its own expectations.
q.r: Each group has its own expectations. Each stakeholder group has its own interests in the business, so its needs and expectations differ from those of other groups. Managers must identify each group's expectations and balance them. The example shows three groups wanting three different things, so they do not all expect the same thing. Employees and lenders are stakeholders too, and expectations change over time as conditions change.
w: The example shows employees, customers and the bank each wanting something different, so stakeholders clearly do not expect the same things.
The employees and the bank in the example are stakeholders too, since each has an interest in how Greenleaf performs.
Nothing in the example says expectations stay fixed, and in reality they shift as conditions change; the point is that each group wants something different.

q.pt: Determine stakeholder expectations
q.s: Before starting a website redesign, Omar and his client sign an agreement listing the deliverables, deadlines and budget. This written agreement mainly helps Omar
o: avoid paying sales tax on the project.
q.r: Manage the client's expectations. Agreeing in writing on deliverables, deadlines and budget makes expectations clear and realistic, so both parties know what will be delivered and when, and misunderstandings are less likely. A project agreement has no effect on sales tax. Pricing objectives are broad goals for pricing decisions. A product mix is the full set of goods and services a business offers.
w: A project agreement listing deliverables and deadlines has no effect on whether sales tax applies to Omar's work.
Pricing objectives are broad goals for pricing, while this agreement spells out what Omar will deliver, when and for how much.
A product mix is the full set of goods and services a business offers, not an agreement about one client's project.

q.pt: Establish strategic relationships with others
q.s: A graphic designer agrees to create a logo for a new accounting firm. In return, the firm prepares the designer's business tax return at no charge. This arrangement is an example of a
q.r: Strategic relationship. A strategic relationship is a mutually beneficial business relationship in which each party provides something the other needs to reach its goals. The designer and the firm each trade a skill the other lacks. A mentoring relationship involves an experienced person guiding a less experienced one. A sole proprietorship is a form of business ownership. An internship is a temporary work-based learning position.
w: A mentoring relationship has an experienced person guiding a less experienced one, but here two businesses trade skills as equals.
A sole proprietorship is a business owned by one person, which describes a form of ownership, not a skill-trading arrangement.
An internship is a temporary work-based learning position, not two businesses exchanging a logo for tax preparation.

q.pt: Establish strategic relationships with others
q.s: What is the main benefit of a strategic relationship for a small business?
o: Each party gains resources or skills it lacks
The business no longer needs any customers
One party controls all of the other's decisions
q.r: Each party gains resources or skills it lacks. Strategic relationships let small businesses share costs, knowledge, equipment, space or customer contacts that would be hard to obtain alone, so both parties grow stronger. Every business still needs customers. In a strategic relationship, each party stays independent instead of controlling the other. Partnerships may help a business compete, but they do not remove competitors from the market.
w: A strategic relationship helps a business grow, but every business still needs customers to buy what it offers.
In a strategic relationship, both parties stay independent, so neither one takes control of the other's decisions.
Partnering may help a small business compete better, but it does not remove its competitors from the market.

q.pt: Establish strategic relationships with others
q.s: When looking for a business to form a strategic relationship with, an entrepreneur should look for one that
o: wants to keep all of the benefits for itself.
has goals and values compatible with her own.
has no experience in her industry.
q.r: Has goals and values compatible with her own. Strategic relationships work when both parties want similar results, trust each other and gain something of value, so compatible goals and values are essential. A business that wants to keep all of the benefits for itself does not create a mutually beneficial exchange. Lack of relevant experience limits what a partner can offer. Refusing to share information prevents the trust that partnerships require.
w: A strategic relationship must benefit both sides, so a partner that wants to keep all the benefits would not create a fair exchange.
A partner with no experience in her industry would have little useful knowledge or skill to bring to the relationship.
Refusing to share information blocks the trust a strategic relationship needs to work.

q.pt: Share best practices with key individuals and groups
q.s: Methods or techniques that have consistently produced better results than other approaches are called
q.r: Best practices. Best practices are proven methods that consistently get better results than other approaches, so businesses share and adopt them more widely. Trade secrets are confidential business information, such as recipes or formulas, that a company protects rather than shares. Industry trends are patterns of change within a field. Company policies are rules that guide employees' decisions and actions.
w: Trade secrets are confidential information, such as recipes or formulas, that a company protects rather than proven methods it shares.
Industry trends are patterns of change in a field, not methods that have proven to get better results than other approaches.
Company policies are rules that guide employees' decisions, not methods proven to produce better results than other approaches.

q.pt: Share best practices with key individuals and groups
q.s: The owner of a growing landscaping company wants to build a culture in which crews learn from one another and cooperate. Which action would help most?
o: Reward only the crew with the highest sales
Assign every crew to a different supervisor
Hold sessions for crews to share methods
q.r: Hold sessions for crews to share methods. Sharing best practices spreads proven methods across the company and shows employees that cooperation is valued, which builds a learning, cooperative culture. Rewarding only one crew encourages competition rather than cooperation. Keeping methods confidential prevents others from improving. Assigning separate supervisors does nothing by itself to help crews learn from one another.
w: Rewarding only the top-selling crew encourages crews to compete against one another, which works against a culture of cooperation.
Keeping each crew's methods secret stops crews from learning from one another, the opposite of what the owner wants.
Giving each crew its own supervisor does nothing by itself to help crews share what they know or cooperate.

q.pt: Share best practices with key individuals and groups
q.s: Logan, an experienced employee at a print shop, shows new coworkers a faster way to set up orders. Sharing this best practice is likely to
o: reduce Logan's value to the shop.
slow down the shop's order processing.
q.r: Build stronger working relationships. When employees share know-how, coworkers feel supported, trust grows and the whole team performs better, which strengthens working relationships. Sharing expertise usually increases an employee's value because it shows leadership and helps the business. Helpful sharing tends to reduce conflict rather than create it. A faster setup method speeds up order processing instead of slowing it.
w: Sharing know-how usually increases Logan's value because it shows leadership and helps the whole shop work better.
Helpful sharing like Logan's tends to build trust among coworkers, so it is more likely to reduce conflict than create it.
Logan is teaching a faster way to set up orders, so sharing it should speed up the shop's work rather than slow it down.

q.pt: Leverage business relationships
q.s: Nadia asks a supplier she has worked with for years to introduce her to the buyer for a regional grocery chain. Nadia is
q.r: Leveraging a business relationship. Leveraging means using an existing relationship to gain something of value, such as an introduction, referral or information. Nadia is drawing on years of trust with her supplier to reach a new customer. Outsourcing means hiring another business to perform work. Delegating means assigning tasks and authority to an employee. Contracting the product mix means dropping products.
w: Outsourcing means hiring another business to do work for you, but Nadia is asking her supplier for an introduction, not to produce anything.
Delegating means assigning tasks and authority to an employee, while Nadia is asking an outside supplier for help reaching a new buyer.
Contracting the product mix means dropping products, which has nothing to do with Nadia asking for an introduction to a grocery buyer.

q.pt: Explain management's role in customer relations
q.s: What is management's main role in a small business's customer relations?
o: Leaving all service decisions to customers
q.r: Setting and modeling service policies. Management shapes customer relations by creating customer-service policies, training staff and showing through its own behavior how customers should be treated. Managers cannot personally handle every customer contact in a growing business. Customers give feedback, but management makes service decisions. Limiting employee contact with customers weakens relationships rather than building them.
w: Managers cannot personally handle every customer contact as a business grows; they guide relations by setting policies and training staff.
Customers give useful feedback, but management is responsible for making service decisions, not handing them all to customers.
Limiting employees' contact with customers weakens relationships, while management's role is to build them through good service policies.

q.pt: Encourage team building
q.s: The owner of a busy café wants her staff to work together smoothly during the holiday rush. Which action would best encourage team building?
o: Post individual sales rankings each day
Assign all tasks without explaining them
Meet with staff to set shared goals
Schedule employees so they rarely work together
q.r: Meet with staff to set shared goals. Team building helps employees develop trust, shared goals and cooperation. When staff help set common goals, they understand how their work fits together and feel responsible for the team's success. Daily individual rankings encourage competition among coworkers. Unexplained assignments reduce understanding and commitment. Keeping employees apart prevents them from learning to work together.
w: Posting daily individual rankings pushes employees to compete with each other, which works against team building.
Assigning tasks without explaining them leaves staff unsure how their work fits together and lowers their commitment.
Keeping employees apart on the schedule prevents them from learning to work together, the opposite of team building.

q.pt: Adapt management style to the personality type of others
q.s: Theo manages two employees at his bike shop. One wants detailed, step-by-step instructions, and the other prefers the freedom to work independently. What should Theo do?
o: Adapt his management style to each employee
Manage both employees in exactly the same way
Give detailed instructions only to the newer employee
Let both employees work without any direction
q.r: Adapt his management style to each employee. Effective managers adjust how they direct and communicate with employees to fit each person's personality and needs. Theo can give detailed guidance to one employee and more independence to the other, so both perform well. Managing both identically ignores their differences. Seniority alone does not determine the kind of direction a person needs. Removing all direction would frustrate the employee who wants detail.
w: Managing both employees the same way ignores that one wants detailed instructions and the other wants independence.
The question never says which employee is newer; Theo should base his approach on each person's needs, not on seniority.
Giving no direction at all would frustrate the employee who wants step-by-step instructions.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of supply chain management
q.s: At which stage of the supply chain does a furniture startup cut, assemble and finish raw lumber into tables and chairs?
q.r: Manufacturing. The manufacturing, or making, stage of the supply chain is where raw materials and components are turned into finished products, such as lumber becoming tables and chairs. It follows the planning and sourcing stages and comes before delivering. Sourcing is finding and selecting the suppliers that provide the lumber. Planning involves forecasting demand and deciding how much to produce. Delivering involves storing, transporting and distributing the finished furniture to customers.
w: Sourcing is the stage where the startup finds and selects suppliers for the lumber, not where the wood is cut and assembled into furniture.
Planning involves forecasting demand and deciding how much to produce, which happens before any lumber is turned into tables and chairs.
Delivering covers storing and shipping finished furniture to customers, which comes after the tables and chairs have been made.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of supply chain management
q.s: What is the primary goal of supply chain management?
o: To gain a competitive advantage by delivering customer value efficiently
To reduce the number of suppliers a business works with
To eliminate the need for a business to hold inventory
To transfer production responsibilities to outside suppliers
q.r: To gain a competitive advantage by delivering customer value efficiently. Supply chain management (SCM) coordinates sourcing, production and delivery so that a business can provide value to customers at the lowest reasonable cost and in the shortest reasonable time. Doing this better than rivals gives the business a competitive advantage. Reducing the number of suppliers or holding less inventory may be tactics within SCM, but they are not its overall goal. Shifting production to outside suppliers does not describe the purpose of SCM.
w: Cutting the number of suppliers is one tactic a business might use within its supply chain, but it is a means to an end, not the overall purpose of managing the chain.
Holding less inventory can be part of an efficient supply chain, but almost every business still needs some stock, and wiping it out is not what supply chain management aims for.
Shifting production to outside suppliers is outsourcing, a single sourcing decision; supply chain management is about coordinating the whole flow to deliver customer value efficiently.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of supply chain management
q.s: Which of the following sets of activities does supply chain management oversee:
o: Recruitment, training and evaluation of employees
Production, shipment and distribution of products
q.r: Production, shipment and distribution of products. Supply chain management oversees the flow of goods from raw materials to the final consumer, which includes sourcing materials, producing products, shipping them and distributing them to customers. Recruiting, training and evaluating employees are human resources management activities. Advertising, publicity and personal selling are promotion activities. Auditing, tax preparation and payroll are accounting activities.
w: Recruiting, training and evaluating employees are human resources tasks about managing people, not about moving products from raw materials to the customer.
Advertising, publicity and personal selling are promotion activities that communicate with customers; they do not involve making or moving the product itself.
Auditing, taxes and payroll are accounting tasks that track money, while supply chain management oversees the physical flow of goods to customers.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of supply chain management
q.s: Priya owns a skincare startup that relies on an ingredient supplier, a contract manufacturer and a shipping company. Which practice will best help her keep the supply chain running efficiently?
o: Monitoring the performance of every supply chain partner
Choosing the lowest-priced partner for each activity
Letting each partner set its own delivery schedule
Communicating only with the contract manufacturer
q.r: Monitoring the performance of every supply chain partner. A supply chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so effective supply chain management requires tracking each partner's quality, timeliness and cost. Monitoring lets Priya spot problems early and correct them before they reach customers. Choosing partners only on price can lower quality and reliability. Letting each partner set its own schedule prevents coordination. Communicating with only one partner leaves the rest of the chain unmanaged.
w: Picking the cheapest partner for each step can lower quality and reliability, and it does nothing to keep the supplier, manufacturer and shipper working together smoothly.
If each partner sets its own delivery schedule, the steps will not line up, so ingredients and shipments may arrive at the wrong times for Priya's business.
Talking only to the contract manufacturer leaves the ingredient supplier and shipping company unmanaged, so problems in those links could go unnoticed until customers feel them.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of supply chain management
q.s: Marcus is opening a coffee roastery and is comparing green-bean growers on price, quality and reliability before choosing one. Marcus is engaged in the supply chain activity called __________.
q.r: Sourcing. Sourcing is the supply chain activity of finding, evaluating and selecting the suppliers that will provide needed goods and services. Comparing bean growers on price, quality and reliability is sourcing. Delivering is moving finished products to customers. Manufacturing is turning raw materials, such as green beans, into finished products, such as roasted coffee. Returning involves handling products that come back through the supply chain, also called reverse logistics.
w: Delivering means moving finished products to customers, but Marcus has not made anything yet and is still comparing growers to decide who will supply the beans.
Manufacturing would be roasting the green beans into finished coffee, which happens later; comparing growers on price, quality and reliability is choosing a supplier.
Returning deals with products coming back through the supply chain, such as customer returns, and has nothing to do with selecting a bean grower before opening.

q.pt: Explain the impact of supply chains on business performance
q.s: An electric-scooter startup's only battery supplier shuts down after a warehouse fire, and no other supplier can deliver batteries for two months. What is the most likely effect on the startup?
o: Production of finished scooters will have to stop
Customer demand for its scooters will increase
Its delivery lead times will become shorter
q.r: Production of finished scooters will have to stop. A supply chain disruption is an unexpected event that interrupts the flow of goods. When a manufacturer cannot get a critical component, it cannot complete its products, so production stops until supply is restored. This is why many businesses line up backup suppliers. A disruption usually raises costs rather than lowering them, lengthens lead times rather than shortening them, and does not increase customer demand.
w: Losing the only battery supplier makes inputs harder and usually more expensive to get, so the startup's production costs would rise, not fall.
A fire at a supplier's warehouse does not make customers want scooters more; if anything, the startup may lose sales because it cannot fill orders.
Without batteries the startup cannot finish scooters, so customers would wait longer for orders, making lead times longer rather than shorter.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of supply chain management
q.s: Which career area involves overseeing the flow of a product from raw-material suppliers to the end user?
q.r: Supply chain management. Supply chain managers coordinate the flow of materials, products and information from suppliers through production and distribution to the end user. Their work affects the business's costs, delivery speed and customer satisfaction. Public relations focuses on building goodwill between the business and the public. Marketing research gathers and analyzes information about markets and customers. Human resources management handles hiring, training and managing employees.
w: Public relations builds goodwill between a business and the public; it does not manage how materials and products move from suppliers to end users.
Marketing research gathers and analyzes information about customers and markets, which can inform decisions but does not oversee the product's physical flow.
Human resources management handles hiring, training and managing employees, not the movement of products from raw-material suppliers to the final customer.

q.pt: Explain the impact of supply chains on business performance
q.s: Lena owns a small neighborhood bookstore with limited shelf space and little extra cash. Which supply approach best fits her business when customers ask for titles she does not carry?
o: Stocking every new title her distributor releases
Buying large quantities to earn volume discounts
Ordering specific titles as customers request them
Renting a separate warehouse for extra inventory
q.r: Ordering specific titles as customers request them. A small retailer with limited space and cash cannot hold a large inventory, so ordering items to fill individual customer requests keeps inventory costs low while still meeting customer needs. Supply chain choices directly affect a business's costs and customer satisfaction. Stocking every new release, buying in large quantities and renting a warehouse all tie up cash and space the bookstore does not have and raise inventory carrying costs.
w: Stocking every new release would take shelf space and cash that Lena does not have, and many of those titles might never sell in a small shop.
Volume discounts lower the price per book, but buying in bulk ties up the limited cash and space Lena has, and it does not target the specific titles customers want.
Renting a warehouse adds a new monthly cost, which is the opposite of what a small shop with little extra cash needs just to fill occasional special requests.

q.pt: Explain the impact of supply chains on business performance
q.s: When making decisions about suppliers, transportation and storage, supply chain managers usually give top priority to __________.
q.r: Controlling costs. Purchasing, transportation, warehousing and handling make up a large share of a business's expenses, so supply chain managers focus on keeping those costs under control while still meeting customer needs. Lower supply chain costs improve profit and can become a competitive advantage. Expanding product lines and increasing advertising are marketing decisions. Raising selling prices is a pricing decision, not a supply chain priority.
w: Deciding to add new products is a marketing and product-planning choice; when picking suppliers, shipping and storage, supply chain managers focus on keeping those costs down.
Advertising is a promotion decision about communicating with customers, and it is not what drives choices about suppliers, transportation or storage.
Setting selling prices is a pricing decision, while supply chain managers work on lowering the cost of getting goods to customers rather than charging customers more.

q.pt: Explain the impact of supply chains on business performance
q.s: Two online pet-supply startups sell the same products at the same prices, but Pawsome Supply's distribution network delivers orders in one day while its rival takes five. Pawsome's supply chain is giving it a(n) __________.
q.r: Competitive advantage. A competitive advantage is an edge that helps a business outperform its rivals. Because the two startups match on products and prices, Pawsome's faster delivery, created by its supply chain, is what sets it apart and can win customers. This shows how supply chain performance affects business performance. A supply chain disruption is an interruption in the flow of goods. A reverse logistics system manages returns. Nothing in the scenario points to a sourcing problem.
w: A disruption is an interruption in the flow of goods, but Pawsome's network is working well and delivering faster than its rival, not breaking down.
Reverse logistics handles returned products, and nothing in the question mentions returns; Pawsome's edge comes from fast outbound delivery.
A sourcing problem would mean trouble finding or choosing suppliers, yet the question describes Pawsome succeeding through faster delivery, not struggling with suppliers.

q.pt: Discuss business process thinking and its impact
q.s: Before launching a pop-up shop, Jordan writes down the project's goals, lists the people, money and materials he will need, and maps each activity in order. Jordan is using __________.
q.r: Business process thinking. Business process thinking treats work as a structured process made up of goals, resources (inputs) and activities that lead to an output. By defining the goals, resources and ordered activities of the pop-up shop, Jordan is approaching the project as a process rather than as a set of unrelated tasks. A SWOT analysis examines strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Trend analysis compares data across time periods. Brainstorming generates many ideas without evaluating them.
w: A SWOT analysis sizes up strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, but Jordan is laying out goals, resources and ordered steps for doing the work.
Trend analysis compares data over several time periods, and Jordan is not looking at past numbers; he is planning the steps of a new project.
Brainstorming produces lots of ideas without judging them, while Jordan is organizing specific goals, resources and activities into a planned sequence.

q.pt: Discuss business process thinking and its impact
q.s: A key benefit of defining clear business processes is that work is performed with greater __________.
q.r: Standardization. A business process sets out the steps for completing a task, so employees perform the task the same way each time. This standardization produces consistent quality, reduces errors and makes results predictable. Processes are meant to reduce unpredictability, not increase it. They also cut down on duplicated effort, and they connect work across people and departments rather than isolating it.
w: A clear process lays out the same steps every time, so it makes results more predictable, not less.
Defined processes show who does each step, which helps prevent people from doing the same work twice rather than causing more duplication.
Processes connect work across people and departments through planned steps and handoffs, so they reduce isolation instead of increasing it.

q.pt: Discuss business process thinking and its impact
q.s: Sofia, a manager who uses business process thinking, has just been assigned to launch her company's new subscription box. What should she focus on first?
o: Choosing the colors and design of the packaging
Identifying who was to blame for problems in past launches
Defining the steps the team will follow to complete the project
Asking each employee to work independently on new ideas
q.r: Defining the steps the team will follow to complete the project. A manager who uses business process thinking views a project as a structured sequence of activities. Her first focus is to define those steps, along with the goals and resources involved, so everyone knows what to do and in what order. Choosing packaging colors is a detail that comes later. Assigning blame does not move the project forward. Having employees work independently ignores the connected, step-by-step nature of a process.
w: Packaging colors and design are details that come later; a process thinker first sets out the steps, goals and resources that the whole launch will follow.
Blaming people for past launches does not plan the new subscription box, and process thinking looks at fixing steps rather than finding someone at fault.
Having everyone work alone on ideas ignores how the steps of a process connect, which is exactly what Sofia should be mapping out first.

q.pt: Discuss business process thinking and its impact
q.s: How does business process thinking help an entrepreneur after a project is finished?
o: It shows why the project succeeded or failed
It lets the owner skip planning for the next project
It identifies which employee to blame for each error
It reduces the need to gather customer feedback
q.r: It shows why the project succeeded or failed. Because process thinking breaks a project into defined goals, resources and steps, an entrepreneur can review each step afterward to see what worked and what did not. This makes it easier to repeat successes and fix weak steps next time. The review improves future planning rather than replacing it, focuses on fixing steps rather than blaming people, and works best when it includes customer feedback rather than ignoring it.
w: Reviewing a finished project should make the next plan better, not replace it; the entrepreneur still needs to plan each new project.
Process thinking reviews which steps worked and which did not, so the focus is on fixing weak steps rather than pointing fingers at an employee.
A good project review uses customer feedback to judge each step, so process thinking makes feedback more useful rather than less needed.

q.pt: Discuss business process thinking and its impact
q.s: In a business process, the point at which work passes from one person or department to another is called a(n) __________.
q.r: Handoff. A handoff is the point in a business process where work moves from one person, team or department to the next, such as when a salesperson passes a customer order to the shipping team. Business process thinking pays close attention to handoffs because delays and errors often happen there. An input is a resource that enters a process. An output is the product, service or information a process produces. A constraint is a limitation on how a process can operate.
w: An output is the product, service or information a process produces at the end, not the moment work passes from one person to the next.
A constraint is a limit on how a process can run, such as time or budget, rather than the point where work changes hands.
An input is a resource, like materials or information, that goes into a process; it is not the transfer of work between people or departments.

q.pt: Describe the factors that influence business process design
q.s: The owner of a small auto-detailing business changes how employees dispose of used cleaning chemicals after the state passes a new hazardous-waste rule. Which type of factor is influencing the design of this process?
q.r: Regulatory. Regulatory factors are laws and government rules that a business must follow, and they often dictate how a process must be performed. A new state hazardous-waste rule forces the owner to redesign the disposal process to comply. Human factors relate to employees' abilities, fatigue and safety. Technological factors relate to the equipment and software available. Competitive factors relate to what rival businesses are doing.
w: Human factors involve workers' skills, fatigue and safety, but the owner changed the process because a new state rule required it.
Technological factors involve new equipment or software, and nothing in the question says the shop got new tools; a new hazardous-waste law drove the change.
Competitive factors come from what rival businesses do, yet the owner changed chemical disposal to follow a state rule, not to match a competitor.

q.pt: Describe the factors that influence business process design
q.s: Packers at an online candle company make more mistakes late in their 10-hour shifts, so the owner adds rotating breaks to the packing process. To which type of process design factor is the owner responding?
q.r: Human. Human factors are the abilities, limitations and needs of the people who perform a process, including fatigue, skill level and comfort. Because tired packers make more errors, adding breaks redesigns the process around employees' physical limits. Regulatory factors come from laws and government rules. Technological factors involve equipment and software. Financial factors involve the money available to run the process.
w: Regulatory factors are laws and government rules, but the owner added breaks because tired packers were making mistakes, not because a law required it.
Technological factors involve equipment or software, and the fix here is rest breaks for workers rather than any new machine or program.
Financial factors involve the money available to run a process, while this change responds to workers getting tired late in long shifts.

q.pt: Describe the factors that influence business process design
q.s: Human, regulatory and technological factors all influence the design of a business's __________.
q.r: Processes. Business process design is shaped by human factors (the abilities and needs of workers), regulatory factors (laws and rules the business must follow) and technological factors (the equipment and software available). Together, these factors determine how steps, people and tools fit together. Brand names, advertising slogans and mission statements communicate a business's identity and purpose; they are not designed around worker fatigue, regulations or equipment.
w: A brand name is chosen to identify and market the business, and it is not shaped by worker fatigue, safety laws or the equipment available.
Advertising slogans are creative marketing messages, not step-by-step ways of doing work that must fit around workers, rules and technology.
A mission statement explains a business's purpose, while human, regulatory and technological factors shape how the actual work steps are designed.

q.pt: Describe the factors that influence business process design
q.s: What is the intended result of business process design?
o: Fewer rules for employees to follow on the job
Greater structure and consistency in how work is done
More variety in how each employee completes a task
Greater freedom for each department to set its own steps
q.r: Greater structure and consistency in how work is done. Business process design plans the steps, people, technology and information for a process so that work is performed in an organized, repeatable way. The result is consistent quality, fewer errors and more predictable output. Fewer rules, more variation among employees and more freedom for each department to set its own steps all work against the structure and consistency that process design is meant to create.
w: Process design actually sets out rules and steps for doing work, so its purpose is more structure, not fewer rules for employees.
Letting each employee do a task in their own way creates inconsistent results, which is exactly what process design tries to prevent.
If each department set its own steps, work would not fit together smoothly, which defeats the structure and consistency process design aims for.

q.pt: Describe the factors that influence business process design
q.s: A family-owned bakery redesigns its order-taking process after installing a tablet-based point-of-sale system that sends orders directly to the kitchen. Which factor shaped the new process design?
q.r: Technological. Technological factors are the equipment, software and other tools a business has available, and they strongly influence how a process is designed. Installing a point-of-sale system that sends orders straight to the kitchen changes the steps for taking and filling orders. Regulatory factors are laws and government rules. Human factors are employees' skills, fatigue and comfort. Competitive factors are the actions of rival businesses.
w: Regulatory factors are laws and rules, but the bakery redesigned order-taking because it installed a new point-of-sale system, not because of a new law.
Human factors involve employees' skills and comfort, but the change here was triggered by new tablet equipment that sends orders to the kitchen.
Competitive factors come from rivals' actions, and nothing in the question mentions a competitor; the new system itself reshaped the order process.

q.pt: Explain the causes of business process changes
q.s: After a landscaping startup adopts scheduling software, its crews receive their daily routes on their phones instead of from a printed list. This shift is an example of a(n) __________.
q.r: Business process change. A business process change is a modification to how work gets done. Adopting new scheduling software changed the steps crews follow to receive their routes, so the process itself changed. New technology is one of the most common causes of process change. A supply chain disruption is an unexpected interruption in the flow of goods. A budget variance is a difference between planned and actual amounts. A SWOT analysis is a planning tool.
w: A supply chain disruption is an unexpected interruption in getting goods, while the landscaping startup simply chose to change how crews receive their routes.
A budget variance is a gap between planned and actual money amounts, and nothing in the question compares spending to a budget.
A SWOT analysis is a planning tool for reviewing strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, not an actual change in how daily work gets done.

q.pt: Explain the causes of business process changes
q.s: Most business process changes are made in order to __________.
o: give managers more control over employees.
reduce the number of customers served.
q.r: Improve performance. Most business process changes are made to help the business perform better, whether by working faster, cutting costs, raising quality or better meeting customer needs. Other causes, such as new technology, competition and new regulations, usually lead back to this same goal. Process changes are not primarily about increasing managers' control, creating new job titles or serving fewer customers.
w: Some changes may shift how managers oversee work, but the main reason businesses change processes is to work better, not to tighten control over employees.
A process change might create a new role now and then, but new job titles are a side effect, not the purpose behind most changes.
Businesses change processes to serve customers better and grow, so cutting the number of customers served runs against the usual goal.

q.pt: Explain the causes of business process changes
q.s: A small accounting firm buys software that automatically reads and sorts clients' receipts, so employees no longer enter receipt data by hand. What directly caused this business process change?
q.r: New technology. When a business adopts new software or equipment, the way employees perform their work changes to take advantage of it. Here, the receipt-reading software eliminated manual data entry, directly causing the process change. New regulations, customer complaints and employee turnover can all prompt process changes, but nothing in the scenario suggests a new law, unhappy clients or employees leaving the firm.
w: New regulations are laws or rules, and the question does not mention any; the firm changed because new software now reads receipts automatically.
Unhappy clients can prompt change, but the question gives no sign of complaints; the process changed because the firm bought receipt-reading software.
Employees leaving the firm can force changes, but here the staff simply stopped typing receipt data because new software took over that task.

q.pt: Explain the causes of business process changes
q.s: After a rival print shop opened nearby and drew away customers with lower prices, Rosa redesigned her shop's ordering and production steps to cut costs and win customers back. What prompted Rosa's process change?
q.r: Competition. Pressure from competitors is a common cause of business process change. When a rival's lower prices drew customers away, Rosa redesigned her processes to lower costs and regain her competitive advantage. New regulations would involve a law or government rule. New technology would involve adopting new equipment or software. Employee fatigue is a human factor, and nothing in the scenario points to tired workers.
w: New regulations would mean a new law or government rule, but Rosa changed her steps because a nearby rival was taking her customers with lower prices.
New technology would involve adopting new equipment or software, yet the question says Rosa reacted to a rival's lower prices.
Employee fatigue is about tired workers, and nothing in the question points to that; Rosa changed her process to compete with a new rival.

q.pt: Explain the causes of business process changes
q.s: Rather than adjusting a few steps, the owner of a meal-kit startup scraps the entire packing process and designs a new one from scratch. This approach to process change is called __________.
q.r: Reengineering. Reengineering is a radical form of business process change in which a business redesigns a process from the ground up rather than making small adjustments. Scrapping the packing process and starting over is reengineering. Process improvement makes smaller, gradual changes to an existing process. Standardization is doing a task the same way every time. Benchmarking compares a business's practices with those of top performers.
w: Process improvement makes small, gradual changes to an existing process, while this owner threw out the whole packing process and started over.
Standardization means doing a task the same way every time, which describes a result of a process, not the act of redesigning one from scratch.
Benchmarking compares a business's practices with those of top performers; it may inspire a redesign but is not the redesign itself.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of business analysis
q.s: A consultant studies how a growing bakery takes and fills catering orders, identifies the steps that cause late deliveries, and helps the owner put fixes in place. The consultant is performing __________.
q.r: Business analysis. Business analysis is the practice of identifying a business's needs and problems, studying how the business operates and recommending or implementing solutions that add value. Finding the steps that cause late deliveries and helping fix them is business analysis. Public relations builds goodwill with the public. Marketing research gathers information about customers and markets. Quality inspection checks finished products against standards but does not redesign how the business works.
w: Public relations builds goodwill with the public, while the consultant is studying the bakery's order steps and fixing what causes late deliveries.
Marketing research gathers information about customers and markets, but the consultant is examining internal operations to solve a delivery problem.
Quality inspection checks finished products against standards, but the consultant is redesigning how orders are handled, not inspecting the food.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of business analysis
q.s: Which planning tool would help the owner of a new fitness studio examine her internal strengths and weaknesses together with her external opportunities and threats?
q.r: SWOT analysis. A SWOT analysis evaluates a business's internal strengths and weaknesses along with the external opportunities and threats it faces, all in one tool. It helps an entrepreneur see where the business stands and plan accordingly. A PESTEL analysis looks only at external political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal factors. A Gantt chart shows a project's tasks on a timeline. Break-even analysis finds the sales level at which revenue equals total costs.
w: A PESTEL analysis looks only at outside factors such as politics, the economy and technology, so it would miss the studio's internal strengths and weaknesses.
A Gantt chart lays out project tasks on a timeline; it schedules work but does not evaluate strengths, weaknesses, opportunities or threats.
Break-even analysis finds the sales level where revenue covers total costs, which is useful for pricing but does not review the studio's overall position.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of business analysis
q.s: Why might the owner of a T-shirt printing business compare her company's financial data from each of the last three years?
q.r: To detect trends. Comparing financial data across several periods, called trend analysis, shows whether sales, costs and profits are rising, falling or holding steady. Spotting these patterns helps the owner identify problems and opportunities early and make better decisions. Payroll taxes are calculated from the current period's wages. An advertising theme is a creative marketing decision. A patent protects an invention and does not require comparing years of financial data.
w: Payroll taxes are figured from the current period's wages, so the owner would not need three years of financial data to calculate them.
An advertising theme is a creative marketing choice, not something found by lining up several years of the company's financial results.
A patent protects an invention, and applying for one has nothing to do with comparing the business's financial records across years.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of business analysis
q.s: Kenji asks, "If we install inventory software, how many more orders could our current staff fill each day?" Kenji is analyzing a way to increase his business's __________.
q.r: Efficiency. Efficiency is producing more output, or the same output faster, with the same or fewer resources. Kenji's if-then question tests whether new software would let the same staff fill more orders, which is an efficiency question. This kind of what-if analysis is a common business analysis tool. Liabilities are debts the business owes. Overhead costs are general operating expenses such as rent. Employee turnover is the rate at which employees leave a business.
w: Liabilities are debts the business owes, and Kenji's question is about filling more orders with the same staff, not about borrowing or owing money.
Overhead costs are general expenses like rent, and Kenji is trying to get more work done with the same people, not to raise those costs.
Employee turnover is how often workers leave a business, while Kenji is asking how much more his current staff could accomplish with new software.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of business analysis
q.s: A business analyst compares a startup's current on-time delivery rate of 80% with its goal of 95%. This comparison is known as __________.
q.r: Gap analysis. Gap analysis compares a business's current performance with its desired performance to measure the difference, or gap, which here is 15 percentage points. Identifying the gap is often an early step in business analysis. Root cause analysis comes next, finding the underlying reason the gap exists. A SWOT analysis examines strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Break-even analysis finds the sales level at which revenue equals total costs.
w: Root cause analysis looks for the underlying reason a problem exists, which usually comes after you have measured the gap between 80% and 95%.
A SWOT analysis reviews strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, not a direct comparison of a current measure with a target.
Break-even analysis finds the sales level where revenue equals costs, and it has nothing to do with comparing on-time delivery rates.

q.pt: Negotiate lease or purchase of facility
q.s: Why do many entrepreneurs with limited cash choose to lease a building rather than buy one?
o: Leasing builds equity in the property
Buying usually requires a large down payment
Rent on a leased building stays the same when the lease renews
Landlords usually waive the security deposit for startups
q.r: Buying usually requires a large down payment. Purchasing a building typically requires paying a sizable portion of the price in cash up front, plus closing costs, which can drain the money a new business needs for inventory, equipment and payroll. Leasing usually requires only a security deposit and the first month's rent. Leasing does not build equity; ownership does. Rent often increases when a lease is renewed, and most landlords require a security deposit from new tenants.
w: Leasing does not build equity, because the tenant never owns any part of the building; only buying builds equity in the property.
Rent on a leased building often goes up when the lease is renewed, so it is not a reason cash-strapped owners would choose to lease.
Most landlords do require a security deposit from new tenants, including startups, so a waived deposit is not why entrepreneurs lease.

q.pt: Negotiate lease or purchase of facility
q.s: Devon is negotiating a three-year lease for his new yoga studio and expects to need more space if the business grows. Which lease term should he try to include?
o: A personal guarantee covering the full lease amount
A clause letting the landlord end the lease on short notice
A rent increase whenever the landlord's property taxes rise
An option to renew or expand into adjoining space
q.r: An option to renew or expand into adjoining space. A renewal or expansion option gives a growing business the right to extend the lease or take more space on agreed terms, so Devon can grow without moving or facing a sudden rent hike. A personal guarantee puts Devon's own assets at risk. A clause letting the landlord end the lease on short notice threatens the studio's location, and a rent increase tied to property taxes adds unpredictable costs. Each of these favors the landlord.
w: A personal guarantee puts Devon's own savings and property at risk if the studio cannot pay rent, which helps the landlord, not his growth plans.
A clause letting the landlord end the lease on short notice could force the studio to move suddenly, the opposite of the stability Devon needs to grow.
Tying rent increases to the landlord's property taxes adds unpredictable costs for Devon and does nothing to secure room for future growth.

q.pt: Negotiate lease or purchase of facility
q.s: Amara has $20,000 to open a smoothie shop and needs most of it for blenders, refrigeration and opening inventory. Which facility option is most appropriate for her?
o: Make a large down payment on a storefront
Pay cash for a small building
Pay a security deposit and lease a storefront
Buy land and build a new store
q.r: Pay a security deposit and lease a storefront. Because Amara's cash is limited and needed for equipment and inventory, leasing lets her open with a small upfront cost, usually a security deposit and the first month's rent. She keeps the rest of her money working in the business. Making a large down payment, paying cash for a building or buying land and building would all consume far more cash than she has available.
w: A large down payment would eat up much of Amara's $20,000, leaving too little for the blenders, refrigeration and inventory she needs to open.
Paying cash for a building, even a small one, would likely take more than Amara's entire $20,000 and leave nothing for blenders, refrigeration and opening inventory.
Buying land and building a new store would cost far more than $20,000 and take a long time, so it does not fit Amara's limited budget.

q.pt: Develop expense control plans
q.s: The owner of a small coworking space wants to lower what she pays for janitorial and landscaping services. Which expense-control method should she use?
o: Renewing current contracts without reviewing them
Hiring the first provider she finds online
Switching to a new provider every month
Obtaining competitive bids from several providers
q.r: Obtaining competitive bids from several providers. Competitive bidding asks multiple vendors to quote prices for the same services, which lets the owner compare costs and quality and choose the best value. It also gives her leverage to negotiate lower prices with her current providers. Renewing contracts without review misses chances to save. Hiring the first provider she finds skips comparison entirely. Switching providers every month adds disruption and setup costs.
w: Renewing contracts without reviewing them keeps the current prices in place, so the owner misses any chance to find a lower cost.
Hiring the first provider found online skips any comparison of prices or quality, so there is no reason to expect lower costs.
Switching providers every month adds disruption and setup hassle, and it is not a planned way to compare prices and get the best value.

q.pt: Develop expense control plans
q.s: Which expense-control tactic can also help a small gift shop increase its sales?
o: Turning off the security lighting at night
Placing high-margin items in the most visible display space
Scheduling fewer cashiers during peak hours
Delaying payments to vendors past their due dates
q.r: Placing high-margin items in the most visible display space. Using display space effectively makes every square foot of the store work harder, so the shop earns more sales per square foot from the rent it already pays. Prominent placement of profitable items cuts wasted space and raises sales at the same time. Turning off security lighting creates risk. Fewer cashiers at peak times causes lost sales. Delaying vendor payments can bring late fees and damage supplier relationships.
w: Turning off security lighting may save a little on electricity, but it raises the risk of theft and does nothing to bring in more sales.
Cutting cashiers during peak hours saves on wages, but long lines drive away shoppers, so the gift shop would likely lose sales instead of gaining them.
Paying vendors late holds on to cash briefly, but it can bring late fees and hurt supplier relationships, and it does not increase sales.

q.pt: Describe the role of management in the achievement of quality
