q.s: The owner of a medical-device startup adopts a quality program that stresses preventing defects and measuring process performance precisely, with a goal of nearly error-free output. Which program is the owner using?
q.r: Six Sigma. Six Sigma is a quality-management approach that uses careful measurement and statistical analysis to prevent defects and reduce variation in processes, aiming for no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities. Management leads the effort by setting goals and supporting training. Theory X is a management view that employees dislike work and need close supervision. Just-in-time inventory is an inventory-control method. Sales forecasting predicts future sales.
w: Theory X is a belief that employees dislike work and need close supervision; it is a management attitude, not a measurement-based program for near-perfect quality.
Just-in-time inventory keeps stock low by receiving materials right when needed; it controls inventory but is not a defect-prevention quality program.
Sales forecasting predicts future sales, which helps with planning but has nothing to do with preventing defects in the startup's devices.

q.pt: Describe the role of management in the achievement of quality
q.s: What should managers do first when developing a quality assurance plan?
q.r: Create quality standards. Quality standards are specific, measurable requirements that define what acceptable work looks like. Managers must set them first because every later step depends on them: employees are trained to meet the standards, products are inspected against them and performance is rewarded based on them. Inspecting products, training employees and rewarding results all come after the standards are in place.
w: Inspecting finished products only works once you know what acceptable quality looks like, so it comes after the standards are created.
Employees can only be trained to meet quality standards after those standards exist, so training is a later step in the plan.
Rewarding results requires a standard to measure results against, so it cannot come before managers decide what quality means.

q.pt: Establish safety policies and procedures
q.s: How does a procedure requiring employees to report every workplace accident and near miss benefit a small manufacturing business?
o: Managers can investigate causes and prevent repeat incidents
Employees can spend less time following safety rules
The business can cut back on safety training
The business's insurance premiums will automatically drop
q.r: Managers can investigate causes and prevent repeat incidents. Incident reports create a written record of what happened, where and why. Reviewing them lets managers identify hazards and patterns, correct unsafe conditions and update safety procedures before someone else is hurt. Reporting does not reduce the need for employees to follow safety rules or for the business to provide safety training, and it does not automatically lower insurance costs.
w: Reporting accidents is an added safety step, so it does not free employees from following safety rules; it helps make those rules better.
Incident reports often show where more training is needed, so they support safety training rather than letting the business cut it.
Better safety records may help with insurance over time, but reporting incidents does not automatically lower premiums; its main value is preventing repeat accidents.

q.pt: Establish safety policies and procedures
q.s: As part of its fire-safety procedures, what should a new restaurant owner make sure every employee knows?
o: How to reset the point-of-sale system
Where the fire extinguishers are located
Where the security cameras store footage
q.r: Where the fire extinguishers are located. Fire-safety procedures require employees to know where fire extinguishers are and how to use them, so a small fire can be put out quickly before it spreads. Employees should also know evacuation routes and emergency exits. Resetting the point-of-sale system, knowing supplier delivery days and knowing where camera footage is stored are operational matters, not fire-safety essentials.
w: Resetting the point-of-sale system is a routine register task and would not help anyone put out a fire or get to safety.
Knowing weekend supplier deliveries helps with ordering, but it plays no part in responding to a kitchen fire.
Knowing where camera footage is stored is a security matter, not something employees need to stop a small fire or protect people.

q.pt: Establish efficient operating systems
q.s: Liam writes step-by-step instructions, with photos, for every task in his bike repair shop. What is a key benefit of documenting work processes this way?
o: New employees are easier to train
Customers are willing to pay higher prices
The shop needs fewer safety policies
q.r: New employees are easier to train. Process documentation gives new workers a clear, consistent reference for how each task should be done, which shortens training time and reduces mistakes. It also keeps work consistent when experienced employees are absent or leave. Documentation supports, but does not replace, supervision. It does not cause customers to pay higher prices, and it does not reduce the need for safety policies.
w: Written instructions support supervision but do not replace it, since someone still needs to check work and help employees with problems.
Customers pay based on the value of the repair, and internal instructions do not by themselves make them willing to pay more.
Documenting how tasks are done does not reduce the need for safety policies; the shop still needs rules to keep workers safe.

q.pt: Use budgets to control operations
q.s: While reviewing her monthly budget reports, the owner of a small landscaping company notices that a growing number of customer accounts are more than 60 days past due. This signals a problem with __________.
q.r: Collections. Accounts receivable are amounts customers owe the business. When many accounts are past due, the business is not collecting what it is owed on time, which hurts cash flow and can lead to bad debts. Comparing budgeted and actual results helps owners catch such problems early and act, for example by tightening credit terms. Production, purchasing and advertising problems would show up as costs that differ from budget, not as unpaid customer accounts.
w: A production problem would show up as making the product or service poorly or at higher cost, not as customers failing to pay their bills.
Purchasing problems involve buying supplies for the business, while past-due accounts mean customers are not paying what they owe.
Advertising problems would show up as weak marketing results or overspending on ads, not as customer accounts sitting unpaid for over 60 days.

q.pt: Establish policies to protect company information and intangibles
q.s: The owner of a software startup wants to prevent employees, including those who later leave the company, from sharing its customer list and product plans. Which policy is most appropriate?
o: Posting the information on the company intranet
Registering the customer list as a trademark
Requiring employees to sign non-disclosure agreements
Offering employees shares of company stock
q.r: Requiring employees to sign non-disclosure agreements. A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) is a legal contract in which the signer promises not to reveal a business's confidential information, and it can remain in force after employment ends. NDAs help protect trade secrets such as customer lists and product plans. Posting the information on an intranet makes it easier to access, not harder. Trademarks protect brand names and logos, not customer lists. Stock ownership may build loyalty but creates no legal duty of confidentiality.
w: Posting the customer list and product plans on the intranet makes them easier for employees to see and copy, which is the opposite of protecting them.
A trademark protects brand names and logos, not a private customer list, so registering one would not stop employees from sharing the information.
Giving employees stock may build loyalty, but it creates no legal promise to keep information secret, especially after someone leaves.

q.pt: Conduct break-even analysis
q.s: A startup that sells phone cases has fixed costs of $12,000 per month. Each case sells for $25 and costs $10 to produce. How many cases must the business sell each month to break even?
q.r: 800 cases. The break-even point is the number of units a business must sell for total revenue to equal total costs. Break-even point in units = fixed costs / (selling price per unit - variable cost per unit) = $12,000 / ($25 - $10) = $12,000 / $15 = 800 cases. Dividing by the $25 price gives 480, dividing by the $10 cost gives 1,200, and dividing by the $35 sum of price and cost gives about 343; none of these uses the $15 contribution margin per case.
w: About 343 comes from dividing $12,000 by $35, which wrongly adds the price and cost instead of subtracting the $10 cost from the $25 price.
480 comes from dividing $12,000 by the $25 selling price alone, which ignores that each case costs $10 to make.
1,200 comes from dividing $12,000 by the $10 production cost, but break-even uses the $15 left over from each sale after that cost.

q.pt: Negotiate service and maintenance contracts
q.s: A bakery owner can buy an annual maintenance contract that covers all oven repairs for a flat fee, or pay for each repair as needed. When is the flat-fee contract usually the better choice?
o: When the ovens are new and rarely need repairs
When the ovens are heavily used and break down often
When the owner plans to replace the ovens within months
When the owner wants to pay only for repairs that occur
q.r: When the ovens are heavily used and break down often. A flat-fee maintenance contract turns repair costs into a predictable payment, which saves money when equipment needs frequent service and makes expenses easier to budget. New ovens that rarely need repairs would make the fee cost more than the repairs themselves. Ovens that will soon be replaced do not justify a year of coverage, and paying only for repairs that occur describes the pay-as-needed option.
w: New ovens that rarely break would cost little to repair as needed, so the flat fee would likely be more than the repairs themselves.
If the ovens will be replaced within months, paying for a full year of coverage would waste money on months the bakery will not use.
Paying only for repairs that actually happen describes the pay-as-needed choice, not a reason to buy the flat-fee contract.

q.pt: Evaluate strategies for protecting business' digital assets (e.g., website, social media, email, etc.), customer data, and other protected information
q.s: Which strategy best protects a small online boutique's social media accounts and customer data from unauthorized access?
o: Requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication
Sharing one login among all employees
Using the same password for every account
Storing passwords in a shared spreadsheet
q.r: Requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication. Strong, unique passwords make accounts hard to guess, and two-factor authentication requires a second proof of identity, such as a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough. Together they protect digital assets and customer data. Sharing one login removes accountability, reusing a password lets one breach expose every account, and a shared password spreadsheet can easily be copied or leaked.
w: Sharing one login means no one knows who did what, and if any employee leaks it, the boutique's accounts and customer data are open.
Reusing one password means a single breach unlocks every account, putting all of the boutique's digital assets at risk at once.
A shared spreadsheet of passwords can easily be copied, forwarded or leaked, giving anyone who sees it access to every account.

q.pt: Interpret financial statements
q.s: Marisa owns a startup skate shop. Her beginning inventory was $24,000, she purchased $51,000 of merchandise during the year, and her ending inventory was $19,500. What was her cost of goods sold?
q.r: $55,500. Cost of goods sold is found by adding purchases to beginning inventory and subtracting ending inventory: $24,000 + $51,000 - $19,500 = $55,500. This is the cost of the merchandise Marisa actually sold during the year. $75,000 is the cost of goods available for sale, before ending inventory is subtracted. $94,500 wrongly adds ending inventory, and $46,500 reverses the beginning and ending inventory amounts.
w: $46,500 swaps the inventory amounts, adding the $19,500 ending inventory and subtracting the $24,000 beginning inventory instead of the other way around.
$75,000 is beginning inventory plus purchases, which is the cost of goods available for sale before the $19,500 ending inventory is subtracted.
$94,500 adds the ending inventory to beginning inventory and purchases, but merchandise still on hand at year-end was not sold and must be subtracted.

q.pt: Interpret financial statements
q.s: On an income statement, net sales minus cost of goods sold equals __________.
q.r: Gross margin. Gross margin, also called gross profit, is what remains after the cost of goods sold is subtracted from net sales. It shows how much the business earns on its merchandise before paying operating expenses. Net income is found only after operating expenses are also subtracted. Operating expenses are the costs of running the business, and owner's equity appears on the balance sheet, not the income statement.
w: Net income is what remains after operating expenses are also subtracted, so it comes one step below net sales minus cost of goods sold.
Operating expenses are the costs of running the business, like rent and wages; they are subtracted from gross margin, not the result of this calculation.
Owner's equity is the owner's claim on the business and appears on the balance sheet, not as a line calculated on the income statement.

q.pt: Interpret financial statements
q.s: Which of the following is an example of an operating expense on a small business's income statement:
o: Cash the owner invests in the business
Money received from a bank loan
q.r: Sales commissions paid to employees. Operating expenses are the costs of running a business other than the cost of the goods it sells, such as wages, rent, utilities, advertising and commissions. They are subtracted from gross margin to find net income. Merchandise purchased for resale is part of the cost of goods sold. An owner's investment increases owner's equity, and loan proceeds create a liability; neither is an expense.
w: Merchandise bought to resell is counted in cost of goods sold, not in operating expenses, which are the costs of running the business.
Cash the owner puts into the business increases owner's equity; it is an investment, not a cost of operating.
Money from a bank loan creates a debt the business must repay, so it is a liability, not an operating expense.

q.pt: Interpret financial statements
q.s: Ellery Outfitters' income statement shows that its gross margin increased this year, but its net income decreased. Which change most likely explains this result?
o: Net sales rose while cost of goods sold held steady
Cost of goods sold fell as a share of sales
The owner invested more cash in the business
Operating expenses rose by more than gross margin did
q.r: Operating expenses rose by more than gross margin did. Net income equals gross margin minus operating expenses. If gross margin grew but net income shrank, operating expenses such as wages, rent or advertising must have grown faster than gross margin. Higher net sales with steady cost of goods sold and a lower cost of goods sold would both raise gross margin but do not explain the drop. An owner's investment affects owner's equity, not the income statement.
w: Higher sales with steady cost of goods sold would help explain why gross margin rose, but it does not explain why net income fell.
Cost of goods sold falling as a share of sales would also push gross margin up, so it does not account for the drop in net income.
An owner's cash investment changes owner's equity on the balance sheet, not income or expenses on the income statement.

q.pt: Develop company's/department's budget
q.s: Each year, the owner of Lantern Lane Bakery starts every budget category at $0 and requires each expense, even rent, to be justified before it is included. This is __________ budgeting.
q.r: Zero-based. Zero-based budgeting builds a new budget from nothing each period, so every expense must be justified rather than carried over. It forces owners to question spending but takes more time. Incremental budgeting adjusts the previous period's amounts up or down. A flexible budget changes with the level of activity, such as sales volume, and a capital budget plans purchases of long-term assets such as equipment.
w: Incremental budgeting adjusts last year's amounts up or down, but this owner starts every category at $0 and justifies each expense from scratch.
A flexible budget changes with activity levels like sales volume, and it does not require every expense to be justified from zero each year.
A capital budget plans purchases of long-term assets like ovens or equipment, not every yearly expense category such as rent.

q.pt: Develop company's/department's budget
q.s: After a startup's budget has been prepared and put into use, what is the final step in the budgeting process?
q.r: Evaluating and revising the budget. Budgeting does not end once the plan is in use. The final step is to compare actual results with budgeted amounts, find the reasons for any differences, and revise the budget so it stays realistic. Gathering past records, forecasting sales and estimating operating expenses are earlier steps that take place before the budget is prepared and implemented.
w: Forecasting sales happens early, before the budget is built, so it cannot be the final step once the budget is already in use.
Estimating operating expenses is part of preparing the budget, which the question says has already been done.
Gathering past financial records is one of the first steps, used as a starting point before the budget is prepared.

q.pt: Develop company's/department's budget
q.s: Owen runs a seasonal kayak-rental business, and his sister runs a dental office that is busy all year. Their budgets are built very differently, mainly because the way a business approaches budgeting depends on its
q.r: Type of business. A business's type shapes its revenue patterns, major costs and planning needs, so it largely determines how the budget is built. A seasonal kayak business must plan for months with little income, while a dental office has steadier monthly revenue and staff costs. The accounting software used, the bank's location and the owner's personal spending habits do not determine a business's budgeting approach.
w: Accounting software is just a tool for recording numbers; it does not explain why a seasonal kayak business and a year-round dental office budget so differently.
Where the bank is located has no real effect on budgeting, while seasonal versus steady revenue clearly does.
Personal spending habits concern the owner's own money, but the difference here comes from how each business earns revenue and pays costs.

q.pt: Develop company's/department's budget
q.s: To build next year's budget, Priya takes this year's amount for each expense category and increases it by 3%. Priya is using
q.r: Incremental budgeting. Incremental budgeting starts with the current period's budget or actual results and adjusts each amount up or down, often by a set percentage. It is quick and simple but can carry forward unnecessary spending. Zero-based budgeting starts every category at zero. Bottom-up forecasting combines individual sales estimates into a total, and ratio analysis compares line items on financial statements.
w: Zero-based budgeting starts every category at $0 and justifies it, but Priya is starting from this year's amounts and raising them 3%.
Bottom-up forecasting adds up individual sales estimates into a total, while Priya is adjusting existing expense categories by a set percentage.
Ratio analysis compares related numbers on financial statements to judge performance; it is not a method for building next year's budget.

q.pt: Monitor business's profitability
q.s: Which profitability ratio shows the percentage of each sales dollar that a business keeps as net income?
q.r: Net profit margin. Net profit margin is calculated by dividing net income by net sales. It shows how many cents of each sales dollar remain as profit after all expenses, so owners track it to monitor profitability. Return on equity is also a profitability ratio, but it compares net income with the owners' investment rather than with sales. The current ratio measures liquidity, and the debt-to-equity ratio measures how much the business relies on borrowed money.
w: The current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities to measure liquidity, so it says nothing about how much of each sales dollar becomes profit.
Debt-to-equity shows how much a business relies on borrowed money compared with the owner's investment, not how much of sales is kept as profit.
Return on equity is a profitability ratio, but it compares net income with the owner's investment, not with each dollar of sales.

q.pt: Monitor business's profitability
q.s: To find out whether her web-design startup earned a net profit last quarter, Tamsin should look at the bottom line of the
q.r: Income statement. The income statement lists revenues and subtracts expenses for a period of time, and its last line, the bottom line, shows net profit or net loss. Business owners review it regularly to monitor profitability. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and owner's equity on one date. The cash flow statement tracks cash received and paid, and a sales forecast predicts future sales rather than reporting results.
w: The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and owner's equity on one date, but it does not total a quarter's revenue and expenses to show net profit.
A cash flow statement tracks cash coming in and going out, which can differ from profit, so its last line is not the net profit Tamsin needs.
A sales forecast predicts future sales; it does not report what Tamsin's startup actually earned last quarter.

q.pt: Monitor business's profitability
q.s: Harbor Bloom Florist earned net income of $27,000 on net sales of $225,000. Its total assets are $300,000, and its owner's equity is $180,000. What is its return on equity?
q.r: 15%. Return on equity equals net income divided by owner's equity: $27,000 / $180,000 = 0.15, or 15%. Each dollar the owner has invested earned 15 cents of profit. Dividing net income by total assets gives 9%, which is return on assets. Dividing by net sales gives 12%, the net profit margin. 60% compares owner's equity with total assets and is not a profitability ratio.
w: 9% comes from dividing $27,000 by $300,000 in total assets, which is return on assets, not return on the owner's $180,000 of equity.
12% comes from dividing $27,000 by $225,000 in net sales, which is the net profit margin rather than return on equity.
60% divides $180,000 of owner's equity by $300,000 of total assets, which leaves net income out and so is not return on equity.

q.pt: Prepare cash flow statements
q.s: Juniper Pet Grooming began June with $3,600 in cash. It expects cash receipts of $9,400 and cash payments of $8,100 during June. How much cash will Juniper have available before making any payments?
q.r: $13,000. Cash available equals the beginning cash balance plus cash receipts: $3,600 + $9,400 = $13,000. This is the total the business can draw on during the month. $4,900 is the projected ending balance after the $8,100 in payments is subtracted. $5,800 subtracts beginning cash from receipts, and $21,100 wrongly adds the payments to cash available.
w: $4,900 is the ending balance after subtracting $8,100 in payments, but the question asks for cash available before any payments are made.
$5,800 subtracts the $3,600 beginning balance from receipts, but beginning cash should be added to receipts, not taken away.
$21,100 wrongly adds the $8,100 in payments, which are cash going out, to the cash available.

q.pt: Prepare cash flow statements
q.s: During March, Coastline Coffee Cart collected $14,250 in cash receipts and paid $11,780 in cash for operating expenses. What was its net cash flow for March?
q.r: $2,470. Net cash flow equals cash receipts minus cash payments: $14,250 - $11,780 = $2,470. Because more cash came in than went out, the cash flow is positive and the cart's cash balance grew. A result of -$2,470 reverses the subtraction. $11,780 is only the cash paid out, and $26,030 incorrectly adds receipts and payments together.
w: -$2,470 reverses the subtraction, taking receipts away from payments, but more cash came in than went out, so March's flow is positive.
$11,780 is only the cash paid out for expenses; net cash flow needs those payments subtracted from the $14,250 collected.
$26,030 adds receipts and payments together, but cash paid out should be subtracted from cash received.

q.pt: Prepare cash flow statements
q.s: What is the primary purpose of a small business's cash flow statement?
o: To show what the business owns and owes on one date
To compare net sales with the cost of goods sold
To list each employee's rate of pay
To track cash received and paid out over a period
q.r: To track cash received and paid out over a period. A cash flow statement tracks cash receipts and cash payments over a period, helping the owner see whether there will be enough cash to pay bills as they come due. Showing what a business owns and owes on one date is the job of the balance sheet. Comparing net sales with cost of goods sold happens on the income statement, and pay rates belong in payroll records.
w: Showing what a business owns and owes on one date is the job of the balance sheet, not a statement that follows cash over a period.
Comparing net sales with cost of goods sold is done on the income statement to find gross margin, not on the cash flow statement.
Employee pay rates are kept in payroll records; a cash flow statement shows total cash in and out, not each person's wage.

q.pt: Describe types of financial statement analysis (e.g., ratio analysis, trend analysis, etc.)
q.s: Trevor compares his catering company's current assets with its current liabilities, and its net income with its net sales, to judge liquidity and profitability. Which type of financial statement analysis is Trevor using?
q.r: Ratio analysis. Ratio analysis compares related line items from the financial statements, such as current assets to current liabilities (the current ratio) or net income to net sales (profit margin). The results help owners judge liquidity, profitability and efficiency. Trend analysis tracks figures across several periods. Vertical analysis expresses each item as a percentage of one base amount, and cost-benefit analysis weighs the costs and benefits of a decision.
w: Trend analysis compares figures across several periods, but Trevor is comparing related items from the same period, like assets to liabilities.
Vertical analysis shows each item as a percentage of one base amount, while Trevor is pairing specific items to measure liquidity and profitability.
Cost-benefit analysis weighs the costs and benefits of a decision, not related numbers pulled from financial statements.

q.pt: Describe types of financial statement analysis (e.g., ratio analysis, trend analysis, etc.)
q.s: To compare her small boutique with a competitor ten times its size, Nadia restates every line of both businesses' income statements as a percentage of net sales. Nadia is preparing
q.r: Common-size statements. Common-size statements show every amount as a percentage of a base figure, such as net sales on the income statement or total assets on the balance sheet. Because percentages remove differences in size, Nadia can fairly compare her boutique with a much larger business. Pro forma statements project future results, cash budgets plan cash receipts and payments, and consolidated statements combine a parent company with its subsidiaries.
w: Pro forma statements project future results, but Nadia is restating current income statements as percentages to compare two businesses.
A cash budget plans future cash receipts and payments; it does not convert every income statement line into a percentage of net sales.
Consolidated statements combine a parent company with businesses it owns, while Nadia is comparing two separate businesses side by side.

q.pt: Describe types of financial statement analysis (e.g., ratio analysis, trend analysis, etc.)
q.s: Lucas lines up his startup's net sales, expenses and net income for each of the past four years to see whether each one is rising or falling over time. This is
q.r: Trend analysis. Trend analysis compares financial data across several periods to reveal patterns of growth or decline, often expressing each year as a percentage of a base year. It helps owners spot problems early and plan ahead. Vertical analysis compares items within a single statement to one base amount. Ratio analysis compares related line items with each other, and break-even analysis finds the sales level at which revenue equals total costs.
w: Vertical analysis compares items within one statement to a single base amount, while Lucas is following the same figures across four years.
Ratio analysis compares related items, like net income to sales, rather than tracking whether each figure rises or falls over several years.
Break-even analysis finds the sales level where revenue equals total costs, which is not the same as watching figures change across four years.

q.pt: Discuss factors to consider in choosing between debt and equity capital
q.s: What is a key advantage of using debt financing rather than equity financing to fund a new business?
o: The money does not have to be repaid
No interest or fees are charged
The owner keeps full ownership and control
q.r: The owner keeps full ownership and control. With debt financing, the business borrows money and must repay it with interest, but the lender receives no ownership. The entrepreneur therefore keeps control over business decisions and keeps all of the profits that remain after the debt is paid. Money that does not have to be repaid describes equity financing. Loans do carry interest and fees, and lenders do not share in a business's losses.
w: Money that never has to be repaid describes equity financing; a loan must be paid back on schedule.
Loans do carry interest and often fees, which is a cost of debt, not an advantage over equity.
Lenders expect repayment no matter how the business does, so they do not share losses the way equity investors do.

q.pt: Discuss factors to consider in choosing between debt and equity capital
q.s: Kiara's app startup will not earn revenue for at least two years, so she cannot make monthly loan payments in the meantime. Which type of financing best fits her situation?
q.r: Equity capital from investors. Equity capital does not require repayment on a set schedule; investors receive a share of ownership and are rewarded through future profits or the eventual sale of the business. That suits a startup with no early revenue. A short-term bank loan and a credit card cash advance are debt that requires regular payments with interest. Trade credit covers purchases of goods for a short period, not years of development.
w: A short-term bank loan requires regular payments with interest, which Kiara cannot make while her app earns no revenue.
Trade credit lets a business pay suppliers for goods within about 30 to 60 days, not cover two years of app development with no income.
A credit card cash advance is expensive debt that must be paid back monthly, which Kiara has no revenue to do.

q.pt: Discuss factors to consider in choosing between debt and equity capital
q.s: One factor favoring debt over equity financing is that the interest a business pays on a loan is generally __________.
o: repaid to the business at year-end.
added to the owner's equity account.
q.r: Deductible as a business expense. Interest on business loans is generally a deductible expense, which lowers taxable income and reduces the true cost of borrowing. Profits paid out to equity investors are not deductible, so this tax advantage is one factor that favors debt. Interest is not returned to the business, and because it is an expense it reduces owner's equity rather than adding to it. Ordinary loan interest is not converted into ownership shares.
w: Interest is paid to the lender and is not given back to the business at year-end; it is a real cost of borrowing.
Interest is an expense, so it lowers profit and owner's equity rather than being added to the owner's equity account.
Ordinary loan interest does not turn into ownership shares; giving lenders shares would make the deal more like equity financing.

q.pt: Describe the nature of cost-benefit analysis
q.s: In a cost-benefit analysis, a cost or benefit that is real but difficult to measure in dollars, such as improved employee morale, is considered
q.r: Intangible. Intangible costs and benefits, such as morale, customer goodwill or a company's reputation, affect a decision but cannot easily be assigned a dollar value. Decision-makers should still consider them alongside the numbers. Tangible items can be measured in dollars, such as an equipment price. Fixed costs stay the same regardless of output, and direct costs can be traced to a specific product or activity.
w: Tangible costs and benefits can be measured in dollars, like an equipment price, while improved morale is real but hard to put a number on.
Fixed costs stay the same no matter how much a business produces, which describes cost behavior, not whether something can be measured in dollars.
Direct costs can be traced to a specific product or activity, but morale is a benefit that cannot easily be given a dollar value.

q.pt: Describe the nature of cost-benefit analysis
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a benefit a business owner would weigh in a cost-benefit analysis of new scheduling software:
q.r: Increased employee productivity. Cost-benefit analysis lists the expected benefits of a decision, such as higher productivity, time savings, lower operating costs or increased sales, and compares them with the expected costs. If benefits outweigh costs, the purchase is usually worthwhile. The monthly subscription fee, staff training time and installation charges are all costs of adopting the software, not benefits.
w: The monthly subscription fee is money the owner must pay for the software, so it goes on the cost side of the analysis.
Time spent training staff is a cost of adopting the software, since workers are learning instead of doing their regular jobs.
One-time installation charges are an upfront cost of getting the software, not a benefit it provides.

q.pt: Describe the nature of cost-benefit analysis
q.s: Rosa estimates that a new convection oven for her bakery will cost $8,000 and will produce benefits worth $11,500 over its useful life. Based on cost-benefit analysis, what should Rosa conclude?
o: Benefits exceed costs by $3,500, which supports buying it
Costs exceed benefits by $3,500, so she should not buy it
The oven should be rejected because it requires spending
She cannot decide until costs and benefits are equal
q.r: Benefits exceed costs by $3,500, which supports buying it. Cost-benefit analysis compares expected costs with expected benefits: $11,500 - $8,000 = $3,500 more in benefits than costs. When benefits outweigh costs, the action is generally worth taking, although Rosa should also consider intangibles. The costs do not exceed the benefits here. Every purchase requires spending, so that alone is no reason to reject it, and costs and benefits need not be equal to make a decision.
w: This reverses the numbers: the $11,500 in benefits is more than the $8,000 cost, so costs do not exceed benefits.
Every purchase requires spending, so that alone is no reason to reject the oven when its benefits are larger than its cost.
Cost-benefit analysis looks for benefits that exceed costs; Rosa does not need the two amounts to be equal before deciding.

q.pt: Spot problems in/issues with financial statements
q.s: Abigail's balance sheet lists total assets of $86,000, total liabilities of $31,000 and owner's equity of $49,000. What should she conclude?
o: The business cannot pay its debts
The balance sheet contains an error
The balance sheet is accurate and complete
q.r: The balance sheet contains an error. The accounting equation states that assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity. Here, $31,000 + $49,000 = $80,000, which is $6,000 less than the $86,000 in assets, so an amount was recorded or added incorrectly. The difference is not profit, which is reported on the income statement. Assets far exceed liabilities, so nothing shows she cannot pay her debts, and a statement that does not balance cannot be accurate.
w: The $6,000 gap is a mismatch in the accounting equation, not profit, since profit is reported on the income statement.
Abigail's $86,000 in assets is far more than her $31,000 in liabilities, so nothing here shows the business cannot pay its debts.
A balance sheet is accurate only when assets equal liabilities plus equity, and here $31,000 plus $49,000 is only $80,000.

q.pt: Forecast sales
q.s: Each salesperson at Ridgeline Solar estimates next year's sales for his or her own territory, and the owner adds the estimates together to create the company's sales forecast. This is
q.r: Bottom-up forecasting. Bottom-up forecasting builds a company total by combining individual forecasts, such as those for each salesperson, territory or product. The people closest to customers supply the estimates. Top-down forecasting starts with a large figure, such as industry or company sales, and divides it into smaller units. Zero-based budgeting justifies every expense from zero, and trend analysis studies financial data over several periods.
w: Top-down forecasting starts with a large total, like industry sales, and divides it into smaller parts, but Ridgeline builds up from each salesperson's estimate.
Zero-based budgeting is a way of planning expenses by justifying each one from zero, not a way of forecasting sales.
Trend analysis studies past financial data over several periods, while Ridgeline is adding up salespeople's estimates of next year's sales.

q.pt: Explain the purposes and importance of obtaining business credit
q.s: A supplier lets Gianna's new boutique receive $5,000 of merchandise now and pay for it within 30 days. This is an example of
q.r: Trade credit. Trade credit is short-term financing a supplier gives a business by allowing it to receive goods now and pay later, often within 30 to 60 days. It helps a new business stock its shelves and sell merchandise before paying for it. Equity financing involves selling ownership. Factoring is selling accounts receivable for cash, and commercial paper is a short-term, unsecured debt instrument issued by large corporations.
w: Equity financing means selling part ownership of the business, but the supplier is simply letting Gianna pay for goods later.
Factoring is selling accounts receivable to get cash, not receiving merchandise from a supplier with 30 days to pay.
Commercial paper is short-term unsecured debt issued by large corporations, not a supplier's payment terms for a small boutique.

q.pt: Identify risks associated with obtaining business credit
q.s: What is a major risk to a business owner who obtains a secured loan?
o: The lender may claim the pledged collateral if payments stop
The lender becomes a part owner of the business
The interest rate is usually higher than on an unsecured loan
The loan cannot be paid off before its due date
q.r: The lender may claim the pledged collateral if payments stop. A secured loan is backed by collateral, such as equipment, inventory or property, that the borrower pledges to the lender. If the borrower defaults, the lender may take and sell that collateral, which could cost the owner assets the business needs. Lenders do not become owners; that happens with equity financing. Secured loans usually carry lower rates than unsecured loans, and many loans can be paid off early.
w: Lenders do not become part owners through a loan; giving up ownership happens with equity financing, not with a secured loan.
Because collateral lowers the lender's risk, secured loans usually carry lower interest rates than unsecured loans, not higher ones.
Many loans can be paid off early, and being unable to prepay is not the main risk that comes from pledging collateral.

q.pt: Obtain insurance coverage
q.s: Fern Street Design pays 70% of each employee's $7,800 annual health insurance premium. Employees pay the rest through equal deductions from 26 biweekly paychecks. How much is deducted from each paycheck?
q.r: $90. The employee's share is 30% of the premium: $7,800 x 0.30 = $2,340 per year. Spread over 26 paychecks, $2,340 / 26 = $90 per paycheck. $210 is the employer's 70% share divided by 26 ($5,460 / 26). $300 divides the entire premium by 26, and $195 divides the employee's share by 12 months instead of 26 pay periods.
w: $195 divides the employee's $2,340 share by 12 months instead of by the 26 biweekly paychecks given in the question.
$210 is the company's 70% share ($5,460) divided by 26, but the deduction should come from the employee's 30% share.
$300 divides the full $7,800 premium by 26, forgetting that the company pays 70% and the employee pays only 30%.

q.pt: Describe the financial needs of a business at different stages of its development
q.s: Which of the following is a financial need typical of a business in its expansion stage:
o: Money to test whether a business idea is feasible
Seed funds to register the business name
Funds to open a second location
Cash to cover the costs of closing the business
q.r: Funds to open a second location. In the expansion stage, an established business grows by adding locations, products, equipment or markets, which requires significant new capital, often from loans or investors. Money to test feasibility and seed funds to register the business are needs of the startup stage. Cash to cover closing costs is a need of a business that is winding down.
w: Testing whether an idea is feasible happens before a business even launches, so it is a startup-stage need, not an expansion need.
Seed money to register a business name is needed when the business is just being formed, long before it is ready to expand.
Cash to cover closing costs is needed when a business is winding down, the opposite of the growth that defines expansion.

q.pt: Analyze critical banking relationships
q.s: When choosing a bank for her new graphic-design business, what quality should Danielle look for most in a banker?
o: An office close to her home
Knowledge of her type of business
A personal connection to her family
The longest list of branch locations
q.r: Knowledge of her type of business. A banker who understands the business and its industry can give useful advice, anticipate its cash needs, and make a stronger case for its loan requests. Building that relationship early helps an entrepreneur obtain credit when it is needed. Convenience, family connections and the number of branches may be pleasant, but none of them help the banker evaluate or support the business's financial needs.
w: An office near home is convenient, but convenience does not help a banker understand Danielle's business or support its credit needs.
A family connection may feel comfortable, but it does not give the banker the knowledge to advise on a graphic-design business's finances.
Lots of branches is a convenience, but it does not help the banker evaluate or support the financial needs of Danielle's business.

q.pt: Explain sources of financial assistance
q.s: To get cash quickly, Hollis Manufacturing sells its accounts receivable at a discount to a company that will then collect payments from Hollis's customers. The company buying the receivables is a(n)
q.r: Factor. A factor is a financial company that buys a business's accounts receivable for less than their face value, giving the business immediate cash and taking on the job of collecting from customers. Factoring is a common source of short-term financial assistance. Venture capitalists and angel investors provide equity capital in exchange for ownership, and a credit union is a member-owned financial institution that takes deposits and makes loans.
w: A venture capitalist invests money in exchange for part ownership; it does not buy a company's unpaid customer bills at a discount.
An angel investor puts personal money into a business for ownership, not for the right to collect Hollis's accounts receivable.
A credit union is a member-owned institution that takes deposits and makes loans; buying receivables and collecting them is what a factor does.

q.pt: Calculate financial ratios
q.s: Willow & Wick Candles has current assets of $48,000 and current liabilities of $20,000. What is its current ratio?
q.r: 2.4:1. The current ratio equals current assets divided by current liabilities: $48,000 / $20,000 = 2.4, written 2.4:1. The business has $2.40 in current assets for every $1 of short-term debt, a sign of good liquidity. 0.42:1 divides liabilities by assets. 1.4:1 divides working capital ($28,000) by current liabilities, and 24:1 misplaces the decimal point.
w: 0.42:1 divides the $20,000 in liabilities by the $48,000 in assets, which flips the current ratio formula.
1.4:1 divides working capital ($28,000) by current liabilities instead of dividing total current assets by current liabilities.
24:1 misplaces the decimal point; $48,000 divided by $20,000 is 2.4, not 24.

q.pt: Explain loan evaluation criteria used by lending institutions
q.s: Before approving a loan, a loan officer reviews how much of her own money Shayla has invested in her startup. Which of the five Cs of credit is the loan officer evaluating?
q.r: Capital. Capital is the money the owner has personally invested in the business. Lenders want to see that the owner has a financial stake and shares the risk. Character refers to the borrower's trustworthiness and credit history. Collateral is property pledged to secure the loan, and capacity is the borrower's ability to repay from cash flow. The fifth C, conditions, covers the economy and the loan's purpose.
w: Character is the borrower's trustworthiness and credit history, but this loan officer is looking at how much of Shayla's own money is in the business.
Collateral is property pledged to back the loan, not the amount of personal money Shayla has already invested.
Capacity is the ability to repay the loan from cash flow, while the officer is reviewing Shayla's personal investment in the startup.

q.pt: Discuss limitations of using financial statements to assess business performance
q.s: Which of the following is a limitation of using financial statements to judge a startup's performance:
o: They are not useful for comparing results across periods
They leave the business's debts off the balance sheet
They report only transactions that were paid in cash
They leave out factors such as customer loyalty
q.r: They leave out factors such as customer loyalty. Financial statements report measurable dollar amounts from past periods. They omit nonfinancial factors, such as customer loyalty, employee skill or a strong reputation, that affect future success, so owners should look beyond the numbers. Statements are useful for comparing periods; that is how trend analysis works. The balance sheet lists debts as liabilities, and accrual-based statements include credit transactions, not just cash.
w: Financial statements are actually very useful for comparing periods; that is exactly how trend analysis works.
The balance sheet does list a business's debts as liabilities, so leaving debts off is not a real limitation of using financial statements to judge a startup.
Statements prepared on the accrual basis include sales and purchases made on credit, not only transactions paid in cash.

q.pt: Make critical decisions regarding acceptance of bank cards
q.s: What is a primary reason a small retailer decides to accept credit and debit cards even though it must pay processing fees?
o: Card sales lower the business's income taxes
Card networks refund the fees at year-end
Card sales do not need to be recorded
q.r: Card acceptance can increase sales. Many customers prefer the convenience of paying with cards, so a business that accepts them can attract more customers and larger purchases, and it receives payment quickly from the card processor. The owner weighs these gains against the processing fees. Accepting cards does not lower the business's income taxes. Card networks do not refund processing fees, and card sales must be recorded like any other sale.
w: Accepting cards does not lower income taxes; card sales are taxable sales like any other.
Card networks do not refund processing fees at year-end; the fees are an ongoing cost the retailer weighs against more sales.
Card sales must be recorded like any other sale, so avoiding recordkeeping is not a reason to accept cards.

q.pt: Describe relationship among innovation, learning, and change
q.s: At Brightleaf Snacks, a startup, the marketing, production, and finance staff meet weekly to share customer feedback. Their discussions led to a new resealable package. This shows how __________ among departments can drive innovation.
q.r: Collaboration. When people from different departments work together and share information, they combine their knowledge and see problems from several angles, which often produces new ideas such as the resealable package. Collaboration is a common source of innovation and change. Competition sets people against each other, centralization concentrates decision-making in a few hands, and specialization narrows each person's focus rather than combining ideas.
w: Competition sets people against each other, while the Brightleaf departments are sharing feedback and working together toward a new idea.
Centralization puts decisions in a few hands, which is the opposite of several departments meeting and sharing ideas.
Specialization narrows each person's focus to one area, but the new package came from combining knowledge across departments.

q.pt: Describe relationship among innovation, learning, and change
q.s: Which of the following best describes the relationship between learning and innovation:
o: Learning provides the knowledge that makes innovation possible
Innovation must happen before employees can learn
Learning and innovation are unrelated activities
Innovation reduces a business's need for learning
q.r: Learning provides the knowledge that makes innovation possible. People cannot create new or improved products and processes without first gaining new information and skills, so learning is essential to innovation. Innovation then brings change, which creates a need for more learning. Innovation does not have to come before learning, the two activities are closely connected, and innovation increases rather than reduces the need for learning.
w: It usually works the other way: people must first gain knowledge and skills before they can create something new.
Learning and innovation are closely connected, since new knowledge fuels new ideas and new ideas lead to more learning.
Innovation brings change, and change creates more need for learning, so innovation does not reduce it.

q.pt: Describe relationship among innovation, learning, and change
q.s: After five years of repairing bicycles and studying which parts fail first, Darnell uses that understanding to design a sturdier frame for his new business. Darnell is applying his
q.r: Knowledge. Knowledge is the information and expertise a person retains from study and experience and can apply to new problems. Darnell's years of repair work gave him an understanding of part failures that he is now using to innovate. Instinct is an unlearned reaction, authority is the right to make decisions, and seniority is rank based on length of service; none describes retained, applied expertise.
w: Instinct is an unlearned reaction, but Darnell's understanding came from five years of repairs and study.
Authority is the right to make decisions; it does not explain how Darnell learned which parts fail first.
Seniority is rank based on length of service, but Darnell is using what he learned, not his position, to design a sturdier frame.

q.pt: Describe relationship among innovation, learning, and change
q.s: When a small catering business adopts a new online ordering system, its employees must master new skills. This illustrates that change often creates a need for
q.r: Learning. Change, such as new technology or procedures, requires employees to gain new knowledge and skills so they can perform effectively. That learning can in turn lead to further innovation. Downsizing is reducing the number of employees, which this change does not require. Complacency is satisfaction with the way things are, the opposite of what change demands. Regulation refers to government rules, which are not involved here.
w: Downsizing means cutting employees, and nothing in the question suggests jobs are being cut; workers are learning a new ordering system.
Complacency is being satisfied with how things are, the opposite of what employees need when they must master a new system.
Regulation refers to government rules, and adopting an online ordering system is a business choice that requires new skills, not new laws.

q.pt: Describe relationship among innovation, learning, and change
q.s: A business owner who encourages employees to keep developing new skills and sharing ideas is most likely to benefit from increased
q.r: Innovation. Continuous learning gives employees fresh knowledge, and sharing ideas spreads that knowledge across the business. Together these create the conditions for new or improved products, services, and processes. Turnover, the rate at which employees leave, usually falls when people feel they are growing. Complacency and bureaucracy discourage new ideas rather than result from a learning culture.
w: Turnover is the rate at which employees leave, and it usually falls when people feel they are growing and their ideas are valued.
Complacency is contentment with the status quo, which is what a culture of learning and idea sharing works against.
Bureaucracy means layers of rules and procedures that slow down new ideas, not a result of encouraging learning and sharing.

q.pt: Explain the nature of change management
q.s: What is the primary goal of change management?
o: To prevent changes to established procedures
To gain stakeholders' support for and adoption of a change
To replace employees who question new policies
To reduce the cost of all business operations
q.r: To gain stakeholders' support for and adoption of a change. Change management is the process of planning, communicating, and supporting people through a change. Its main aim is buy-in, so employees, owners, and other stakeholders accept the change and it succeeds. Change management does not block change, it does not focus on replacing employees, and cutting costs may be a reason for a change but is not the goal of managing it.
w: Change management guides people through a change; it does not block changes to established procedures.
Replacing employees who ask questions creates fear and resistance, while change management works to win people's support.
Cutting costs may be one reason for making a change, but the goal of managing the change is getting people to accept and use it.

q.pt: Explain the nature of change management
q.s: Tamsin is moving her bakery's staff to a new scheduling app. To reduce employees' resistance to the change, what should Tamsin do early in the process?
o: Explain why the change is needed and how it will affect them
Announce the change on the day it takes effect
Limit discussion of the change to managers only
Discipline employees who ask questions about the change
q.r: Explain why the change is needed and how it will affect them. Early, honest communication builds awareness, answers concerns, and helps employees see the benefit, which reduces resistance and builds buy-in. Announcing the change at the last minute or keeping it among managers leaves employees uninformed and anxious. Disciplining employees for asking questions increases fear and resistance.
w: Announcing the change on the day it takes effect gives employees no time to understand or prepare, which tends to increase resistance.
Keeping discussion among managers leaves the staff who must use the app uninformed and anxious, making resistance more likely.
Disciplining employees for asking questions makes them fearful and less willing to accept the change, which increases resistance.

q.pt: Explain the nature of change management
q.s: In the ADKAR model of change management, the stage in which employees understand why a change is needed is
q.r: Awareness. ADKAR stands for awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, and reinforcement. The first stage, awareness, means people understand the reason for the change. Desire is wanting to support the change, ability is being able to perform the new behaviors, and reinforcement is the rewards and recognition that keep the change in place. Each of these comes after awareness.
w: Desire is wanting to support the change, which comes after people understand why it is needed.
Ability is being able to perform the new behaviors, a later stage that comes after awareness and knowledge.
Reinforcement is the final stage, using rewards and recognition to keep the change in place, not the stage of understanding why it is needed.

q.pt: Explain the nature of change management
q.s: Ravi, operations manager at a growing online retailer, plans training on a new warehouse system, schedules regular check-ins, and answers employees' concerns as the switch takes place. Ravi is practicing
q.r: Change management. Ravi is planning, communicating, and supporting employees through a transition so the new system is accepted and used. Crisis management deals with sudden emergencies that threaten the business. Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a loss to another party, such as an insurer. Quality control checks products or services against standards. None of these describes guiding people through a planned change.
w: Crisis management handles sudden emergencies that threaten a business, while this is a planned switch to a new warehouse system.
Risk transfer shifts the cost of a possible loss to someone else, such as an insurer, which has nothing to do with training and supporting employees.
Quality control checks products or services against standards, while the question describes helping employees adjust to a new system.

q.pt: Explain the nature of change management
q.s: Why should a business owner recognize and reward employees who successfully use a newly adopted process?
o: To reduce the business's total payroll costs
To reinforce the change so employees do not return to old habits
To discourage feedback about the new process
To eliminate the need for employee training
q.r: To reinforce the change so employees do not return to old habits. Reinforcement is the final stage of the ADKAR change model; recognition and rewards help a change stick. Without reinforcement, employees often slip back into familiar routines. Rewards add to costs rather than reduce payroll, feedback should be encouraged during change, and recognition does not replace the training employees need to build knowledge and ability.
w: Rewards and recognition add to costs, if anything, so they are not a way to lower total payroll.
Recognizing success encourages people to keep using the new process, and feedback about it should be welcomed, not discouraged.
Rewarding employees for using the process does not replace training, which they still need to build the knowledge to do it well.

q.pt: Explain the nature of managerial ethics
q.s: Which of the following is an example of unethical managerial behavior:
o: Disciplining an employee who repeatedly arrives late to work
Recognizing an employee who exceeds her quarterly sales objectives
Giving worse shifts to an employee who reports safety violations
Requiring all employees to follow the company's dress code
q.r: Giving worse shifts to an employee who reports safety violations. Punishing a whistle-blower, an employee who reports wrongdoing, is retaliation. It discourages honest reporting and is often illegal. Disciplining repeated lateness, recognizing strong sales performance, and enforcing a dress code that applies to everyone are normal, fair management actions.
w: Disciplining an employee who is repeatedly late is a fair, normal response to a real performance problem, not unethical behavior.
Recognizing an employee who beats her sales objectives rewards good performance, which is fair and appropriate management.
Requiring everyone to follow the same dress code applies one rule equally to all employees, which is fair management.

q.pt: Explain the nature of managerial ethics
q.s: Lena, a manager at a small marketing firm, must choose a vendor for a large printing contract. One of the vendors bidding is owned by her brother. What is the most ethical action for Lena to take?
o: Choose her brother's company if its price is competitive
Choose the other vendor without explaining her reason
Ask her brother to lower his bid before others submit
Disclose the relationship and remove herself from the decision
q.r: Disclose the relationship and remove herself from the decision. Lena has a conflict of interest because a family relationship could influence a business decision. Disclosing it and letting someone else decide protects the firm's objectivity and her reputation. Choosing her brother still lets the relationship influence the outcome, silently rejecting him hides the conflict, and sharing bidding information with him is unfair to the other vendors.
w: Even if the price is competitive, Lena would still be letting a family relationship affect a business decision she should not be making alone.
Quietly choosing the other vendor hides the conflict of interest instead of disclosing it, so the firm never knows about the relationship.
Asking her brother to lower his bid gives him an unfair advantage over the other vendors and makes the conflict of interest worse.

q.pt: Explain the nature of managerial ethics
q.s: Owen manages a landscaping company's equipment. Every weekend he uses the company's trailer to move furniture for people who pay him. Owen's behavior is unethical because he is
q.r: Misusing company resources. Company equipment, vehicles, and money belong to the business and should be used only for business purposes. Owen is using the trailer for personal profit, which adds wear and risk without the owner's approval. Antitrust laws deal with unfair competition, delegation is assigning tasks to others, and favoritism is unfair treatment of certain employees; none fits Owen's actions.
w: Antitrust laws deal with unfair competition between businesses, not an employee using a company trailer for personal side jobs.
Delegating means assigning tasks to others, but Owen is personally using company equipment for his own paid work.
Favoritism is unfairly treating certain employees better, while Owen's issue is using the company's trailer to make money for himself.

q.pt: Explain the nature of managerial ethics
q.s: A manager who regularly gives the best assignments to the employees he socializes with outside of work is showing
q.r: Favoritism. Favoritism is giving better treatment to certain employees because of personal feelings rather than performance. It damages morale and trust and violates managerial ethics, which call for treating everyone fairly. Impartiality is the opposite, treating all employees equally. Empowerment is giving employees decision-making authority, and delegation is assigning tasks; neither involves unfair preference.
w: Impartiality means treating all employees equally, which is the opposite of handing the best work to friends.
Empowerment means giving employees authority to make decisions, not giving better assignments to people the manager socializes with.
Delegation is assigning tasks to others, which is normal; the problem here is choosing who gets the best tasks based on friendship.

q.pt: Explain the nature of managerial ethics
q.s: Why is it important for business managers to behave ethically?
o: Ethical behavior guarantees that a business will earn a profit
Employees tend to follow the standards their managers model
Laws require managers to share all company information
Ethical managers do not have to follow company policies
q.r: Employees tend to follow the standards their managers model. Managers set the tone for the business; when they act honestly and fairly, employees are more likely to do the same, which builds trust with customers and staff. Ethical behavior supports long-term success but cannot guarantee profit. Managers must protect confidential information rather than share everything, and ethical managers follow company policies.
w: Ethical behavior builds trust and supports long-term success, but no business practice can promise a profit, since sales and costs depend on many other factors.
No law requires managers to share all company information; in fact, they are expected to protect confidential information, so this is not why ethical behavior matters.
Ethical managers are expected to follow company policies and set an example, not ignore the rules that everyone else is asked to follow.

q.pt: Analyze operating results in relation to budget/industry
q.s: Copper Kettle Cafe had net sales of $250,000 and cost of goods sold of $170,000 last year. Similar cafes average a 35% gross profit percentage. What was Copper Kettle's gross profit percentage, and how does it compare?
o: 32%, which is below the industry average
68%, which is above the industry average
47%, which is above the industry average
q.r: 32%, which is below the industry average. Gross profit is net sales minus cost of goods sold: $250,000 - $170,000 = $80,000. Gross profit percentage is gross profit divided by net sales: $80,000 / $250,000 = 32%, three points below the 35% average. The owner should look at costs and prices. 68% is cost of goods sold divided by sales, and 47% divides gross profit by cost of goods sold instead of sales.
w: 68% comes from dividing cost of goods sold ($170,000) by net sales ($250,000), which shows the share of sales spent on goods, not the gross profit percentage.
35% is just the industry average copied from the question; Copper Kettle's own gross profit of $80,000 divided by $250,000 in sales works out lower.
47% comes from dividing the $80,000 gross profit by cost of goods sold instead of by net sales, so it uses the wrong base for the percentage.

q.pt: Analyze operating results in relation to budget/industry
q.s: Northgate Supply's customers take an average of 52 days to pay their accounts, while the industry average is 30 days. What should the owner do?
o: Extend customers' payment period to 60 days
Increase the amount of inventory on hand
Tighten credit terms and follow up on overdue accounts sooner
Stop comparing collections with the industry
q.r: Tighten credit terms and follow up on overdue accounts sooner. Comparing operating results with industry averages shows that Northgate collects its accounts receivable much more slowly than similar businesses, which ties up cash. Speeding collections improves cash flow. Lengthening payment periods would make the problem worse, buying more inventory uses cash the business is already short of, and ignoring the comparison removes a useful warning sign.
w: Giving customers 60 days would let them pay even more slowly, widening the gap with the 30-day industry average and tying up more of Northgate's cash.
Buying more inventory spends cash, and Northgate is already short of cash because its customers pay slowly, so this does nothing to fix the collection problem.
The industry comparison is what revealed that Northgate collects far more slowly than similar businesses, so dropping it would just hide a real warning sign.

q.pt: Analyze operating results in relation to budget/industry
q.s: Businesses analyze their operating results to control costs and operate efficiently mainly so that they can
q.r: Remain competitive. A business that operates efficiently keeps its costs low, which allows it to offer competitive prices and still earn a profit. Analyzing results against the budget and industry shows where money is wasted. Efficiency does not let a business avoid taxes it owes, no analysis can eliminate all risk, and efficient operations often require fewer, not more, employees.
w: Controlling costs can raise profits, but it does not let a business skip taxes it legally owes, so tax avoidance is not the purpose of analyzing results.
Analyzing operating results can reduce some risks, but no amount of analysis can remove every risk a business faces.
Running efficiently often means doing the same work with fewer people, so adding employees is not the goal behind controlling costs.

q.pt: Analyze operating results in relation to budget/industry
q.s: Hollis Fitness budgeted $4,000 for monthly utilities but actually spent $5,200. Comparing actual results with the budget helps the owner
o: identify a $1,200 favorable variance to reward.
identify a $1,200 unfavorable variance to investigate.
identify a $9,200 unfavorable variance to investigate.
conclude that no corrective action is needed.
q.r: Identify a $1,200 unfavorable variance to investigate. A variance is the difference between budgeted and actual amounts: $5,200 - $4,000 = $1,200. Because the business spent more than planned, the variance is unfavorable, and the owner should find the cause and correct it. A favorable variance occurs when spending is below budget. $9,200 adds the two amounts instead of subtracting them, and overspending calls for action.
w: Spending $5,200 against a $4,000 budget means Hollis spent more than planned, which makes the $1,200 difference unfavorable rather than something to reward.
$9,200 comes from adding the budgeted and actual amounts together; a variance is found by subtracting them, which gives $1,200.
Hollis went $1,200 over the utilities budget, and overspending is exactly the kind of result that calls for finding the cause and correcting it.

q.pt: Explain external planning considerations
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a government action that encourages small-business growth:
o: Raising tariffs on imported materials that companies use
Offering subsidies to companies that open in rural areas
Increasing licensing fees for new businesses
Adding reporting requirements for small employers
q.r: Offering subsidies to companies that open in rural areas. A subsidy is financial help from the government, such as a grant or tax break, that lowers a business's costs and encourages growth. Entrepreneurs consider such external factors when planning. Higher tariffs raise the cost of imported materials, higher licensing fees raise start-up costs, and added reporting requirements increase paperwork; each makes growth harder.
w: Higher tariffs make imported materials cost more, which raises a company's expenses and makes it harder, not easier, for a small business to grow.
Raising licensing fees increases what it costs to start a business, which discourages new businesses instead of helping them grow.
More reporting requirements add paperwork and time for small employers, which is a burden on growth rather than encouragement.

q.pt: Explain external planning considerations
q.s: While planning her children's clothing store, Ana learns that the number of young families in her trading area is shrinking. Which type of external planning consideration is she examining?
q.r: Demographic. Demographic considerations involve population characteristics such as age, family size, income, and location. A shrinking number of young families means fewer potential customers for a children's clothing store, so Ana may need to adjust her location, products, or sales goals. Political considerations involve government actions and laws, technological considerations involve new equipment and processes, and competitive considerations involve the actions of rival businesses.
w: Political considerations deal with government actions and laws, but Ana is looking at a change in who lives in her trading area, not at any new law.
Technological considerations involve new equipment and processes, while Ana is studying how many young families live near her store.
Competitive considerations focus on what rival stores are doing, but a shrinking number of young families is a population change, not a competitor's action.

q.pt: Explain external planning considerations
q.s: Which of the following is an external factor a startup should consider when planning:
o: Rising interest rates on business loans
The skills of the company's current employees
The layout of the company's office
q.r: Rising interest rates on business loans. External planning considerations are factors outside the business's control, such as economic conditions, government actions, competition, and technology. Higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing and can change expansion plans. Employees' skills, the owner's schedule, and the office layout are internal factors the business can control or change itself.
w: Employees' skills are inside the business, which can train or hire to change them, so they are an internal factor rather than an external one.
The owner's work schedule is a personal choice inside the business that the owner fully controls, so it is not an external planning factor.
The office layout is something the startup arranges for itself, which makes it an internal factor rather than a condition outside the business.

q.pt: Track performance of business plan
q.s: Six months after opening, Juniper Pet Grooming has far fewer customers than its business plan projected. What should the owner analyze first?
o: Whether the business name should be changed
Whether the plan's operating strategies are working
Whether to close the business immediately
q.r: Whether the plan's operating strategies are working. Tracking a business plan means comparing actual results with planned results and then examining the strategies, such as pricing, promotion, and hours, that were supposed to produce them. That analysis shows what to adjust. Renaming the business is a guess rather than an analysis, competitors' profits do not explain Juniper's shortfall, and closing after one missed projection is premature.
w: Changing the name is a guess at a fix; the owner first needs to compare results with the plan and see which strategies, like pricing or promotion, are falling short.
Competitors' profits do not explain why Juniper has fewer customers than its own plan projected; the owner needs to examine Juniper's own strategies.
Closing right away after one missed projection is premature, because the owner has not yet found out why customers are fewer or tried to fix it.

q.pt: Track performance of business plan
q.s: Two years after launch, Mara compares her company's actual sales, expenses, and customer counts with the figures she projected before opening. Mara is using her __________ as a benchmark.
q.r: Business plan. A new business's business plan contains its objectives and financial projections, so it serves as the benchmark for measuring success. Comparing actual results with the plan shows where the business is ahead or behind. A mission statement states the business's purpose but has no figures, an organizational chart shows reporting relationships, and an employee handbook explains policies for workers.
w: A mission statement explains a business's purpose but contains no sales, expense, or customer projections that Mara could compare her actual results against.
An organizational chart shows who reports to whom, not the projected sales and expenses Mara made before opening.
An employee handbook explains workplace policies for staff and has no financial projections for Mara to measure her results against.

q.pt: Track performance of business plan
q.s: What should an entrepreneur do when tracking shows that the business is not meeting the objectives in its business plan?
o: Wait until the end of the year to review results
Abandon all of the objectives in the plan
Identify the causes and adjust strategies or the plan
q.r: Identify the causes and adjust strategies or the plan. Tracking performance is useful only if the owner acts on it. Finding out why results fall short, then changing tactics or revising unrealistic objectives, keeps the business on course. Waiting until year-end lets problems grow, abandoning every objective leaves the business without direction, and stopping data collection removes the information needed to make decisions.
w: Waiting until year-end lets the problems keep growing for months, when tracking is meant to catch shortfalls early enough to fix them.
Missing some objectives is a reason to adjust, not to drop every objective, which would leave the business with no direction at all.
Stopping data collection removes the very information the entrepreneur needs to figure out why the business is falling short.

q.pt: Identify and benchmark key performance indicators (e.g., dashboards, scorecards, etc.)
q.s: What is the main purpose of a management dashboard?
o: To display key performance indicators at a glance
To record every customer transaction in detail
To replace the company's business plan
q.r: To display key performance indicators at a glance. A dashboard pulls the most important measures, such as sales, cash, and customer satisfaction, into one visual display so managers can quickly see how the business is performing and spot problems. Personnel records and detailed transaction records are kept in other systems, and a dashboard tracks progress toward the plan rather than replacing it.
w: Personnel records are stored in separate employee files, while a dashboard summarizes a few key business measures so managers can check performance quickly.
A dashboard shows summary measures at a glance; recording every transaction in detail is the job of the sales or accounting system.
A dashboard helps managers track progress toward the business plan's goals, so it works alongside the plan rather than replacing it.

q.pt: Identify and benchmark key performance indicators (e.g., dashboards, scorecards, etc.)
q.s: Sunfield Home Goods' scorecard lists the goal "Improve customer satisfaction." Which measure would best track progress toward this goal?
o: Number of employees hired each month
Average cost of inventory on hand
Number of customer complaints received each month
q.r: Number of customer complaints received each month. A key performance indicator should directly measure the goal it tracks. Fewer complaints over time signal that customers are more satisfied. Hiring numbers relate to staffing, advertising spending measures promotion effort rather than results, and average inventory cost relates to operations; none of them tells the owner whether customers are happier.
